5th Metatarsal Base Fracture

Foot & Ankle · 1 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequencyamong the commonest foot fractures · base fractures = 25% of all metatarsal fractures · 90% are zone 1

Whoathletes, military recruits, manual labourers · runners, dancers

Anatomy & blood supply

Regionstuberosity → base → metadiaphysis → diaphysis → neck → head

Base + tuberositycancellous, highly vascular · tuberosity = insertion of peroneus brevis + lateral band of plantar fascia

Metadiaphysisno tendon attachments · vascular watershed between metaphyseal vessels and diaphyseal nutrient artery (terminal capillaries)

Diaphysisdorsal curve in distal ⅓ · peroneus tertius inserts dorsally

Shear force (OB)fracture lies in the hypovascular zone between peroneus brevis and peroneus tertius insertions → tendons shear across fracture site

Functionlateral border of forefoot · lever during push-off

Mimicsopen apophysis or os peroneum → comparison radiographs

Genes & lab markers

CMT (cavovarus → 5th MT stress fracture)duplication on chromosome 17
✗ Wrong options: absent dystrophin (muscular dystrophy, equinovarus) · PITX1 (clubfoot) · PTT insufficiency (flatfoot) · tarsal coalition

Nonunion / refracture labsvitamin D deficiency (hypovitaminosis D) · thyroid (hormonal) deficiency

Female athlete triad (TO)disordered eating + menstrual irregularities + ↓ BMD → ↑ metatarsal stress fractures (TO)

2Mechanism

Zone Mechanism
1 Plantarflexion + hindfoot inversion → avulsion by peroneus brevis, lateral band of plantar fascia or long plantar ligament
2 Forefoot adduction (Orthobullets, OB) · strong abduction force to forefoot → bending moment at metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction (TO) — read the options · acute inversion injury (OB)
3 Repetitive microtrauma → stress fracture

Associated conditionsLisfranc / midfoot injury · lateral ankle ligament laxity · cavus foot + varus hindfoot

Hindfoot varus / cavusoverloads lateral column → stress fracture distal to 4/5 articulation

3Presentation

Symptompain over lateral border of forefoot, worse with WB · stress fracture: antecedent pain, rapid ↑ workload / training change

Exampoint tenderness at base · rare skin tenting (zone 1) · varus hindfoot, cavus, lateral shoe-tread wear, 5th MT head callosity

Checklateral ligament instability · is varus hindfoot correctable · pain with resisted eversion (peroneal weakness)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
X-ray AP, lateral, oblique foot Diagnosis; location + displacement decide fixation
X-ray chronicity Intramedullary sclerosis + no periosteal callus = chronic · callus forms medially first → laterally
Plantar fracture gap Poor prognosis for nonop union
Cavovarus signs Plantarflexed 1st MT, high Meary angle
Bone scan Suspected stress fracture, equivocal X-ray → diaphyseal uptake
MRI Equivocal X-ray / scan → high-signal stress reaction + oedema
CT Healing in delayed / nonunion or after fixation · not at time of injury (X-ray suffices)
Screw planning (TO) AP = screw diameter · lateral = screw length (TO)

Lawrence & Botte anatomic zones (also called Torg anatomic zones)

Zone Name Location Key facts
1 Pseudo-Jones Proximal tubercle avulsion; may enter cubometatarsal (5th TMT) joint; proximal to 4–5 intermetatarsal joint Well vascularised; nonunion rare, usually asymptomatic (fibrous)
2 Jones Metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction; enters 4th–5th intermetatarsal articulation Watershed; acute; nonunion 15–30%
3 Proximal diaphyseal Distal to 4–5 articulation; proximal 1.5 cm of diaphysis (TO) Stress fracture in athletes; cavovarus, sensory neuropathy; ↑ nonunion

Jones location1.5–3 cm from proximal tip (OB) · ~2.5 cm distal to base (OB) · intra-articular at 4–5 intermetatarsal facet; does not extend distal to it or into metatarsocuboid joint

Joint enteredJones → intermetatarsal (4–5) joint · avulsion → tarsometatarsal joint (OB) · one OB explanation calls the Jones joint "4th–5th tarsometatarsal" — read the options

Zone 2 vs 3 (TO)some studies: no distinction needed, treatment + outcome the same (TO)

Torg radiographic classification (stress fractures, zone 3)

Type Orthobullets TO Age
I Narrow line, no IM sclerosis Acute fracture Acute
II Widened line + IM sclerosis Periosteal reaction, widening, some IM sclerosis Delayed union
III Widened (obliterated) canal, no callus IM sclerosis + blunted fracture edges Nonunion

5Management

Proximal 5th MT fracture
  • Zone 1→protected WB, stiff-soled shoe / boot
    • rotational displacement / skin tenting→fixation
  • Zone 2, non-athlete / recreational→NWB short-leg cast 6–8 wk
    • failed 6–8 wk nonop or displaced→IM screw
  • Zone 2, elite / competitive athlete→early IM screw
  • Zone 3→NWB cast ~8 wk
    • athlete, cavovarus, sclerosis (Torg II–III), not healing 8–12 wk→IM screw ± graft

Operative criteria

Nonoperative Operative (IM screw)
Zone 1 without rotational displacement — even elite athletes / dancers Zone 1 with rotational displacement or skin tenting · gross displacement / articular involvement in young active (TO)
Zone 2 in non-athlete / recreational athlete (e.g. 45-yo recreational soccer) Zone 2 in elite / competitive athlete (collegiate, Olympic, professional) — even acute + nondisplaced
High-school / recreational athlete until 6–8 wk nonop failed Non-elite after failed 6–8 wk nonop or unacceptable displacement
Zone 3 acute, low demand Zone 3 in athletes, cavovarus, sclerosis / nonunion (Torg II–III) · not healing at 8–12 wk (TO) · occupation can't tolerate NWB (TO)

Zone 1 avulsion – weight bearing in a hard-soled shoe

Treatmentprotected / immediate WB in stiff- (hard-) soled shoe, postoperative shoe, walking boot or short-leg walking cast, advance as pain allows

Outcomeunion by 8 wk · fibrous unions rarely symptomatic · early RTW, symptoms up to 6 months

Soft dressing (TO)compressive dressing + WB in cast boot → shorter recuperation, better foot score than cast (TO)

Elite dancer, zone 1protected WB, stiff-soled shoe, gradual return
✗ Wrong options: immediate return to competition · NWB short-leg cast (unnecessary) · IM screw (true Jones only) · resection + peroneus brevis advancement

57-yo, inversion off curb, zone 1immediate WB in postoperative shoe
✗ Wrong options: acute fragment excision · IM screw · NWB cast · K-wires

Which pattern → immediate WB in boot?zone 1
✗ Wrong options: Lisfranc (unstable) · displaced 1st MT fracture (no intermetatarsal ligament → surgery) · zone 2 (NWB if nonop)

Symptomatic zone 1 nonunionfragment excision + peroneus brevis reattachment
✗ Wrong options: acutely

Zone 1 ORIF (TO)rarely; displaced intra-articular in highly competitive · plate, screw or tension-band (TO)

Acute Jones (zone 2) – IM screw in athletes vs casting

NonopNWB short-leg cast 6–8 wk (Orthobullets, OB) · then WB cast until union (TO) · advance WB with callus (~4–6 wk) · NWB cast > walking cast for healing

Zone 2 outcome Value
Nonunion, nonop 15–30% (Orthobullets) · 10–30% (OB) · 25% (OB) · up to 33% (OB) · > 30% in some studies (OB) — read the options
Union with cast 72–93% (OB) · healing rate 75% (TO)
Refracture after nonop 33% (Orthobullets) · ~30% (OB)
Union with IM screw Approaching 100%
Reoperation after ORIF (Yates) 8.5% — refracture, persistent nonunion, symptomatic hardware

What IM screw achievesimproved union rate (primary advantage) · faster / decreased time to union · earlier return to play / work · minimises nonunion + prolonged activity restriction · better patient-reported scores in athletes

What it does not do↓ pain · ↓ HO · ↑ ROM · ↓ cost · eliminate refracture · avoid hardware complications · ↓ sural irritation (more with surgery) · prevent midfoot arthritis (not a sequela)

✗ Casting traps> 95% union with cast (false) · asymptomatic fibrous nonunion with cast (that's zone 1; zone 2 nonunion usually symptomatic) · "casting unacceptable" (false — still valid if avoiding surgery) · "ORIF ≈ casting" (false) · "ORIF high hardware failure" (false)

Bone graftnot required in primary fixation · use in revision / nonunion / refracture (± BMAC)

✗ Other wrong answers for athlete JonesK-wires (not supported) · tubular plate (long lines into zone 3 / multifragmentary diaphyseal) · MRI · taping + immediate RTS · Brostrom · Lisfranc repair · midfoot fusion

TO answer key (TO)painful 5th MT base stress fracture in runner: "All correct" = internal fixation always required + more in females with menstrual abnormalities + RICE is first treatment (TO) · conflicts with OB/Orthobullets (cast for non-athletes) — read the options

RICE (TO)rest, ice, compression, elevation = primary treatment in all fractures (TO)

Competitive athletes (TO)early ORIF to ↓ disability time (TO)

Stress fractures, delayed union & nonunion – fixation

Zone 3 nonop (TO)chronic (canal obliteration, sclerosis) → NWB casting ~8 wk may work (TO) · Orthobullets: NWB 6–8 wk (often 6–7 wk) · ESWT union ≈ internal fixation (reports)

Refracture common in zone 3 (TO)risk factors: cavovarus, hypovitaminosis D, metatarsus adductus, curved 5th MT with prominent base (TO)

Two proven operations, zones 2–3 (TO)IM screw (5.5 mm) · corticocancellous inlay bone graft after clearing canal of sclerotic bone (TO)

Delayed union after 6 wk cast, widened line (15-yo)percutaneous IM screw
✗ Wrong options: ORIF (not needed) · electrical stimulation alone · more casting · hard-sole shoe

Zone 3, 11 wk, sclerotic edges, minimal callusORIF ± bone grafting
✗ Wrong options: MRI · bone stimulator (controversial) · continued cast / boot

HS quarterback, refracture after 8 wk NWB bootIM compression screw
✗ Wrong options: plate · fragment excision (zone 1) · NWB + stimulator · midfoot fusion

Zone 3, triathlete wants running at 6 wkIM screw
✗ Wrong options: boot / hard-soled shoe / early PT (zone 1) · NWB cast (non-athletes)

Nonunion risk factor (dancer, 4 months)fracture location (zone 2–3)
✗ Wrong options: NSAIDs · high calcium · early WB · female sex

Nonunion treatmentrevision IM screw + bone graft · plate = salvage after failed IM screw

IM screw technique & failure

Positionsupine, bump under hip, fluoroscopy

Approachshort incision proximal to tuberosity, parallel to sole · blunt dissection past sural branches · between peroneus longus + brevis

Start point"high and inside" = superior + medial on tuberosity · K-wire not past MT curvature

Screw> 4 mm diameter · 4.5, 5.5 or 6.5 mm partially threaded (solid or cannulated) · largest diameter the canal accepts (max fill + compression, ↓ refracture) · 5.5 mm (TO)

Checkall threads cross fracture · no distal cortical perforation · tap measures length

Screw error Result
< 4.5 mm (not including 4.5) Delayed / nonunion
Too long Straightens curved shaft → fracture gapping + distal / medial cortical perforation → failure, nonunion
Too short No compression
Prominent head Sural nerve irritation

RehabNWB 1–3 wk → protected WB (from ~2 wk) → running + impact at 6 wk if pain-free + radiographic callus · RTP average 4–6 wk

Failure risk factorselite athletes · return to sport before radiographic union · early unprotected WB in athletes · too-long screw
✗ Wrong options: female · age < 20 or > 40 · solid vs cannulated · 4.5 mm or > 4.5 mm screw · no bone graft · no ultrasound stimulator · partially threaded

Bent 5.0 mm screw at 12 wkcause = return to play before radiographic union · fix = remove + larger IM screw

NFL QB, failure at 8 wktoo long partially threaded screw
✗ Wrong options: WB at 2 wk · impact at 6 wk · no BMAC · largest screw

IM screw vs plateIM more rigid + less hardware prominence (OB) · plate equivalent strength in early data (Orthobullets) — read the options

Plate (3 mm, plantar-lateral)same indications; salvage after failed IM screw; reduces plantar gap / rotation

Association with cavovarus foot (CMT)

Cavus foot↑ refracture + ↑ nonunion even after successful treatment
✗ Wrong options: ↓ nonunion · earlier / later RTS

Varus hindfootoverloads lateral column → zone 3 stress fracture distal to 4/5 articulation

Refracture treatmentinternal fixation + correct cavovarus · leave screw in until end of athletic career (removal ↑ refracture)

6Complications

Complication Key facts
Nonunion Zone 2 15–30%; zones 2–3 (watershed); screw < 4.5 mm; vitamin D / thyroid deficiency → revision IM screw + graft
Failure of fixation Elite athlete, RTS before radiographic union, screw length (too long → gapping) → revision fixation
Refracture 33% zone 2 nonop; cavovarus, stress fracture, vitamin D, screw removal → fix + correct cavovarus
Painful hardware Rare; prominent head → modified shoewear
Sural nerve injury Dorsolateral branch within 2–3 mm of tuberosity · prevent: tissue protector + countersink head
Chronic pain Zone 1 nonunion after nonop → fragment excision + peroneus brevis reattachment

Achilles Tendon Rupture

Foot & Ankle · 2 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology & risk factors

Incidence18 : 100,000 / yr · missed in up to 25%

Demographicsmen · 30–40 yr (Orthobullets) · males 30–39 (TO)

Classic patientepisodic athlete, "weekend warrior" (basketball, tennis, pickleball, volleyball)

Risk factor Source
Fluoroquinolones Orthobullets, TO
Steroids — local injections + systemic Orthobullets, TO
Hypercholesterolaemia, gout, RA TO
Long-term dialysis, renal transplantation TO
Chronic tendinopathy with Haglund disease TO
Foot / ankle malalignment, training errors, degenerative tendon TO

Haglund deformity ↑ TA rupturetrue (TO)

"Antithrombolytics have a role"the incorrect statement in the TO list (TO)

Anatomy

Achilleslargest (Orthobullets) / strongest (OB) tendon in body · confluence of soleus + medial and lateral gastrocnemius

Tendon blood supply (TO)

Fact TO answer
Three sources Musculotendinous junction, osteotendinous junction, paratenon (paratenon = most important)
Major artery Posterior tibial artery (also Orthobullets)
Minor Peroneal artery — small contribution to mid-section
Most abundant zone At the tendon insertion (✗ Wrong options: mid-section between MTJ and bone–tendon junction)
Least vascularised zone 2–6 cm above calcaneal insertion, at all ages → poor repair
Main surface of supply Anterior (deep) surface (✗ Wrong options: posterior · medial · lateral) — branches loop round / pass through to posterior surface

Sural nerve

Courselateral to the TA · accompanied by small saphenous vein, which lies just lateral to the nerve

Protectskin incision slightly medial to TA (TO, Orthobullets) · injury → heel + lateral foot numbness (TO)
✗ Wrong options: saphenous · tibial · lateral plantar nerve

2Mechanism

Mechanismsudden forced plantarflexion · violent dorsiflexion of a plantarflexed foot · push-off with weight-bearing forefoot while extending knee (TO) · sudden unexpected dorsiflexion (TO) · eccentric load (OB)

Site4–6 cm above calcaneal insertion (Orthobullets, OB) · 3–6 cm above os calcis, watershed (TO) · least vascular zone 2–6 cm (TO) — read the options

3Presentation

History"pop" · weakness, difficulty walking, heel pain · ecchymosis

Inspection↑ resting ankle dorsiflexion prone with knees bent (loss of resting tension) · calf atrophy (chronic)

Palpationpalpable gap

Motionweak plantarflexion · ↑ passive dorsiflexion · chronic: unable to toe off / toe walk

Diagnosis – Thompson test & ultrasound

Test (TO) Method Positive = rupture
Thompson (Simmonds) squeeze Prone, feet over couch edge; squeeze calf just distal to maximal girth Little / no plantarflexion vs other side · sensitivity 0.89–0.93
Matles Prone, actively flex knees to 90° Foot falls to neutral or slight dorsiflexion
O'Brien needle 25-gauge needle in midline of proximal tendon, passive ankle ROM Needle doesn't move (moves = continuity)

"Thomas test is a reliable test"TO uses "Thomas / Simmonds" for the calf squeeze (true statement, TO) · Thomas test = hip flexion contracture, Thessaly = meniscus (OB) — read the options

Movement tested against resistance (TO)options inversion + PF / dorsiflexion / plantarflexion / eversion + DF — answer key not provided by the source · Orthobullets: weakness to ankle plantarflexion

Differential – xanthomas (TO)

Bilateral swellings over Achilles (TO)options rheumatoid nodules / tophaceous gout / tendoachilles xanthomas / ganglion — answer key not provided by the source (module filed as xanthomas) · hypercholesterolaemia = rupture risk factor (TO)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Key facts
X-ray Rule out other pathology (✗ Wrong options: IOC)
Ultrasound Investigation of choice after + Thompson (TO) · complete vs partial rupture (Orthobullets) · as good as MRI for tendinopathy + full-thickness tear (TO)
MRI Highest accuracy (TO) · superior for partial tears + types of tendinopathy (TO) · equivocal exam, chronic ruptures, gauging gap size · retracted tendon edges
Complete tear US = MRI (TO)
No Venography, CT (TO)

Diagnostic criteria – ultrasound criteria for nonoperative treatment (TO)

Position Criterion
Maximal plantarflexion Gap < 5 mm
Neutral Gap < 10 mm
20° plantarflexion > 75% tendon apposition

Acute vs chronic – definition

Chronic> 3–4 wk (OB) · > 4 wk (OB, JAAOS algorithm) · > 6 wk (other OBs) · Orthobullets: acute = < 6 wk · TO: chronic 4–6 wk — read the options

Chronic sleeve avulsion – diagnosis

Chronic Achilles avulsion (sleeve) ruptureold cast-treated rupture + new fall · X-ray: calcified / ossified distal tendon moved away from insertion · MRI: chronic avulsion from insertion
✗ Wrong options: HO of proximal tendon · untreated midsubstance · gout · musculotendinous junction

Medial gastrocnemius tear (tennis leg)

Mechanismsimultaneous knee extension + ankle dorsiflexion · athletes

Presentationsudden medial proximal calf pain + ecchymosis · US / MRI confirm (often unnecessary)

Treatmentconservative first line → excellent outcomes, most return to activity within 3 months
✗ Wrong options: surgery · quarter need surgery (nonop failure rare)

Myotendinous Achilles rupturenonop boot + PT from 3 wk → complete healing (Orthobullets: more proximal injuries → nonop)

5Management

Acute Achilles rupture
  • Sedentary, frail, proximal / myotendinous, or preference→functional bracing in equinus + early rehab
  • Active, wants surgery→open end-to-end or percutaneous repair + early functional rehab
  • Deep infection after repair→debride necrotic tendon, no reconstruction, IV antibiotics 6 wk
Chronic rupture – gap after debridement
  • < 2 cm→end-to-end repair
  • 2–5 cm→V-Y advancement ± FHL transfer
  • > 5 cm→FHL transfer ± V-Y / turndown
    • Defect too big for local tissue (> 10 cm)→allograft
Chronic / neglected rupture > 4 wk (JAAOS, OB)
  • Avoid sacrificing tendons / donor morbidity→synthetics
  • Gap 3–5 cm, viable ends→V-Y or local turndown ± FHL
  • Gap > 5 cm or unhealthy tissue→FHL / FDL transfer ± dermal matrix

Operative criteria

Indication Treatment
Acute, preference for nonop · sedentary · medically frail · proximal (musculature) injuries Functional bracing / cast in resting equinus (20° PF) + early functional rehab
Acute (< ~6 wk) Open end-to-end repair
Cosmesis concern Percutaneous repair
Chronic, defect < 3 cm V-Y advancement (Orthobullets)
Chronic, defect > 3 cm FHL transfer ± V-Y advancement — requires functioning tibial nerve (Orthobullets)
Defect < 3 cm after debridement + < 3 months Direct end-to-end repair (TO, OB)

Operative vs nonoperative acute treatment

Outcome Surgery vs nonop with functional rehab
Re-rupture Lower with surgery vs cast 6 wk (classic) · equal with early functional rehab (Willits, Soroceanu) · mixed (OB)
Re-rupture rates ~2% op vs 10–40% nonop (Orthobullets) · 2.3% vs 3.9% (meta-analysis) · op 3–4% (TO) · 1–2% (OB)
Complications ↑ with surgery (~2×; 4.9% vs 1.6%) — wound, infection, sural
Strength, ROM, calf girth, SMFA at 12 mo No difference · equivalent PF strength (some ↑ PF strength with surgery; no ↑ DF strength)
DF ROM at 6 mo Not improved — some studies ↓ in op group
Functional outcomes No significant difference
DVT No difference (7–10%)
Return to work Quicker with surgery
Return to sport Quicker with surgery (one OB) · similar (another OB) — read the options · TO: ~60% after surgery
Nerve injury Higher with surgery
Cost Higher with surgery
Satisfaction, ultimate strength Same (even vs cast)

Cast 6 wk nonop vs surgeryhigher risk of re-rupture
✗ Wrong options: ↓ satisfaction · less return to sport · ↓ strength · ↑ skin problems

Re-rupture: greater in conservatively managed casestrue (TO)

↓ Re-rupture after repairearly functional rehabilitation protocol (WB in boot ~2 wk + ROM)
✗ Wrong options: delayed WB > 6 wk (stiffness) · gastrocnemius fascial flap augmentation · biological / PRP augmentation · percutaneous technique

Nonop rehabstart within 48 h · strict adherence · supervised PT · functional bracing → low re-rupture esp. > 40 yr, women

Post-op immobilisation20° plantarflexion for 4–6 wk (↓ skin tension, protects repair) · functional bracing beats casting (↓ adhesions, ↓ complications)

Open vs percutaneous / minimally invasive repair – wound complications & sural nerve

Outcome Open Percutaneous / MIS
Wound complications / infection Higher (superficial infection 6.0%) Lower (0.4%)
Overall complications Higher Lower
Local scarring More Less
Sural nerve injury Nerve seen + protected (0%) Higher (3.4%) — blind needle passage (Orthobullets, OB) · no difference (other OBs) — read the options
Re-rupture, PF strength, calf circumference Same Same
Return to sport / running, outcome scores Same Same
Return to work — More rapid (Orthobullets)
1-year function Same Same

Open techniqueincision just medial to tendon (sural) · incise paratenon · heavy non-absorbable suture

Repair techniques – eponyms (TO)

Eponym Technique
Ma and Griffith Percutaneous repair of acute rupture
Lynn Repair + fanned-out plantaris over it (injury < 10 days)
Lindholm Two flaps from proximal tendon + gastrocnemius aponeurosis turned down 180° to distal tendon

Abraham and Pankovich V-Y tendinous flap
Wapner FHL tendon transfer

Wound complications – most common complication & risk factors

Most common complication of surgical repairskin healing problems / wound complications (5–10%, poor posterior blood supply)
✗ Wrong options: infection (common, not commonest) · neurological injury (rare after open) · re-rupture (1–2%) · stiffness · loss of motion (nonop)

Risk factorstobacco (most common) · steroid use · female sex · diabetes · open technique
✗ Wrong options: ↑ BMI · immediate surgery · male · age > 40

≥ 1 of diabetes / tobacco / steroid> 40% complications vs 6% without

Infected repair – debridement

Axis of contractile force replicates Achilles

Location / harvest avoids NV bundle

Close + well-vascularised · preserves foot muscle balance

Achilles Tendonitis

Foot & Ankle · 3 / 48

1Basics

Three conditions

Condition Who Site Key feature
Insertional Achilles tendonitis Middle-aged + elderly, tight heel cord At insertion Spur, intratendinous calcification, progressive bony enlargement
Retrocalcaneal bursitis + Haglund deformity Young Bursa between anterior Achilles + posterior calcaneus · posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity Pain anterior to + 2–3 cm proximal to insertion
Noninsertional (midportion) tendinopathy Active, middle-aged men 2–6 cm proximal to insertion Thickening, fusiform swelling

Noninsertionalthought more common · insertional less common (OB)

Pathophysiology

Insertionalrepetitive trauma → inflammation → cartilaginous then bony metaplasia

Noninsertionalabnormal vascularity / poor blood supply 2–6 cm proximal + repetitive micro-tears

Risk factorsoveruse · dorsiflexor / plantarflexor imbalance · poor blood supply · genetic · fluoroquinolones · inflammatory arthropathy

Inflammation?degeneration without inflammation (tendinosis; asymptomatic degeneration from microtrauma + ageing) (OB) · "inflammation and thickening" (another OB) — read the options

Histology

Insertionaldisorganised collagen + mucoid degeneration, few inflammatory cells

Tendinosisanaerobic degeneration in poorly vascularised segment

3Presentation

Insertionalposterior heel pain, swelling, burning, stiffness · shoe pressure pain (aversion to closed-heel shoes) · midline tenderness at insertion · bony prominence

Retrocalcaneal bursitisfullness + tenderness medial and lateral to tendon · pain with dorsiflexion

Noninsertionalpain, swelling, warmth, worse with activity, difficulty running · thickening + tenderness 2–6 cm proximal · pain through whole ROM

Painful arc signtender intratendinous nodule moves with active ROM = tendinosis (vs paratenonitis — stays still)

Dorsiflexionmost have limited passive dorsiflexion

Silfverskiöld testDF improves with knee flexion → gastrocnemius contracture · no improvement → Achilles contracture

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Lateral foot X-ray Bone spur + intratendinous calcification (enthesophyte) (insertional) · Haglund deformity = enlarged posterosuperior tuberosity
MRI Intrasubstance intermediate signal (disorganised tissue) · thickened tendon · % degeneration guides surgery · rarely needed for Haglund
Ultrasound Degeneration · colour / power Doppler ↑ intratendinous blood flow (neovascularity) · chronic rupture = hypoechoic gap between ends
MRI diffuse thickening, no focal area → tendon transfer indication

Noninsertional classification

Type Feature
Achilles tendinosis Tendon thickening; anaerobic degeneration
Achilles peritendonitis Inflammation of tendon sheath
Paratenonitis Inflammation of paratenon

Brisementfor peritendinitis, not tendinosis

5Management

Achilles tendinopathy
  • First line→eccentric strengthening, NSAIDs, heel lift, shoe change
    (avoid steroid injection — rupture)
  • Failed nonop, < 50% degenerated→debridement ± Haglund resection
    • gastrocnemius contracture→+ gastrocnemius recession
  • > 50% degenerated / diffuse / > 55 yr→debridement + FHL transfer
    • Achilles contracture (no Silfverskiöld change)→+ Achilles lengthening

Operative criteria

Finding Add to debridement
Haglund deformity Calcaneal exostectomy / calcaneoplasty (prevents recurrence)
< 50% degeneration Side-to-side repair / suture anchor; no transfer
> 50% degeneration (or debrided) FHL (or FDL, PB) transfer / augmentation
DF improves with knee flexion Gastrocnemius recession
DF does not improve with knee flexion Achilles lengthening
> 55 yr, diffuse MRI thickening, subacute rupture on tendinopathy, heavier patients Tendon transfer
Chronic symptoms > 6 months without improvement Surgery considered

Noninsertional tendinopathy – eccentric loading & PRP

First lineeccentric strengthening (cornerstone, heavy-load eccentric gastrocsoleus) + rest, NSAIDs, heel lift, shoes, orthoses for overpronation, PT 3–6 months · nonop 65–90% successful

Not for chronic tendinopathystair climbing · rope jumping · concentric · isometric

Eccentric = heel dropstand on step, heels off, slowly lower below step · force remains constant as the muscle lengthens · closed-chain · enhances dorsiflexion · most helpful in later phases of rehab / after diminished activity

Exercise (✗ Wrong options: traps) Definition / example
Eccentric ✓ Force constant while muscle lengthens · heel drop
Concentric Muscle shortens, tension ∝ external load
Isometric Constant length + tension, no movement · standing calf-raise hold, pushing a wall
Isotonic Constant force through ROM
Isokinetic Constant velocity (angular) through varied resistance · Cybex
Plyometric Jump training · may aggravate
Single-leg stance Proprioception → ankle instability
Heel walk Dorsiflexor strengthening

Why eccentric works (theory)absence of concentric phase disrupts lengthening / shortening cycle → shear in tendon + injury to collagen (exact mechanism unknown)

Doppler neovascularity, intact tendon, 4 monthseccentric closed-chain exercises
✗ Wrong options: steroid (rupture) · CT chest / abdomen / pelvis · PRP + delayed arthroscopic debridement (level IV, not before eccentrics) · resection + FHL + gastrocsoleus turndown (chronic rupture)

PRPadded to eccentrics may improve outcomes in non-responders (OB, noninsertional) · listed as nonop option (Orthobullets) · no evidence for PRP in tendinosis (OB, insertional) — read the options

Orthotic + eccentricsno better than eccentrics alone

Adjuncts studiedorthotics, PRP, ESWT, topical glyceryl trinitrate, polidocanol, blood, hyaluronic acid, pulsed light, NSAIDs, steroids · GTN, prolotherapy, aprotinin = evolving, little evidence

Steroid injectionavoid → Achilles rupture (Orthobullets, OB) · one OB lists corticosteroid injection among nonop options — read the options

Severecast or removable boot

Diagnosis from first-line eccentricsAchilles tendinopathy
✗ Wrong options: Baxter nerve (stretching, PT, NSAIDs) · calcaneal stress fracture (NWB) · ATFL tear (PT + proprioception) · syndesmotic sprain (NWB cast / CAM boot)

Nonopheel sleeves + pads (mainstay) · small heel lift · eccentric PT + gastrocsoleus stretching · locked-ankle AFO 6–9 months if others fail · no steroid · Haglund: ice, external padding · high nonop failure rates

Surgery (< 50% removed)retrocalcaneal bursa excision + debridement + calcaneal prominence resection · tendon detachment → calcaneoplasty → reattachment

Surgery (> 50% removed)suture anchor repair + FHL (FDL, PB) augmentation + primary closure
✗ Wrong options: side-to-side (for < 50%) · tibialis posterior transfer · wound VAC / staged closure · closure alone

✗ Wrong options: FHL (< 50%)

FHL transfer (overweight)↑ ankle plantar flexion strength
✗ Wrong options: ↑ AOFAS · ↑ SF-36 · ↓ great-toe plantar flexion (not seen) · no difference

Ankle Arthritis

Foot & Ankle · 5 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology & etiology

Incidence30 / 100,000 / yr · prevalence ~1% · less common than hip / knee OA

Post-traumaticcommonest, 75–80% · mostly ankle fractures; rest = chronic (lateral) ligamentous laxity

Primary OA< 10%

Other causesRA / inflammatory, osteonecrosis, neuropathic, septic, gout, haemophilia

Risk factorsprior ankle fracture · chronic ligamentous laxity · inflammatory arthropathy

Pathoanatomynonanatomic fracture healing → altered contact forces + load bearing → cartilage loss on talar body + plafond → narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, eburnation

Anatomy

Jointginglymus (tibia, talus, fibula) · talar dome biconcave with central sulcus

ROMdorsiflexion 20° · plantarflexion 50°

3Presentation

Symptomspain with weight-bearing · stiffness · locking / catching

Examvariable effusion · pain + ↓ ROM vs contralateral · angular deformity (trauma) · crepitus

Localising sign (OB)pain through tibiotalar arc · painless subtalar inversion / eversion → isolated tibiotalar disease (→ no need to fuse subtalar)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Use / finding
Weight-bearing AP, lateral, mortise Diagnosis: joint space loss, subchondral sclerosis + cysts, eburnation, angular deformity
CT Surgical planning (arthrodesis + arthroplasty); quantify healing of a fusion nonunion
MRI Focal cartilage disease · ↑ sensitivity in early disease · cartilage injury, subchondral marrow oedema, ligament tears
Labelled WBC scan Infection workup in fusion nonunion
Scanograms / contralateral films Malalignment planning before revision

Takakura classification (mortise view, varus-type OA)

Stage Radiograph Image
I Osteophytes + early sclerosis, no narrowing
II Narrowing of medial joint space, no subchondral contact
IIIA Obliteration at medial malleolus, subchondral bone contact
IIIB Obliteration over roof of talar dome, subchondral contact
IV Obliteration with complete tibiotalar contact
Stage Treatment (OB)
I Conservative / symptomatic
II, IIIA Supramalleolar osteotomy (joint preserving)
IIIB SMO poor results / higher failure → TAA or arthrodesis
IV Arthrodesis or TAA (whole joint)

Talar osteonecrosis (differential)

Late talar head osteonecrosis (rare)talonavicular + subtalar pain (selective injections) · X-ray / CT = advanced degenerative change of TN + subtalar joints

MRI↓ T1, ↑ T2 with dark serpiginous line

✗ Look-alikesPVNS (erosions + hemosiderin) · chronic osteomyelitis (fluid collections, bony destruction) · talar neck / head fracture (no fracture line)

5Management

Ankle arthritis
  • Mild / first line→NSAIDs, activity change, Arizona brace, rocker sole, steroid injection
  • Anterior osteophytes, isolated impingement→arthroscopic debridement + exostectomy
  • Asymmetric (Takakura II–IIIA), malaligned, near-normal ROM→supramalleolar osteotomy
  • Young, moderate–severe PTOA, good ROM→distraction arthroplasty
  • End-stage (IIIB–IV)
    • Young high-demand labourer, obese, neuropathic→ankle arthrodesis
    • Elderly, low demand, inflammatory, contralateral fusion→total ankle arthroplasty

Nonoperative management – bracing, rocker sole & injection

First lineactivity modification, bracing to immobilise ankle, NSAIDs · intra-articular corticosteroid = mainstay injection · PRP / hyaluronic acid no consensus (PRP not proven)

Untried nonop (OB)steroid injection + cushioned rocker-bottom shoe (± cane)
✗ Wrong options: opiates + limited WB 6 wk · cast NWB 12 wk · triple / pan-talar arthrodesis

Arizona (gauntlet) braceimmobilises ankle + hindfoot → best brace for tibiotalar OA at any age · PT may worsen pain

Orthosis / shoe Indication
Single rocker sole End-stage tibiotalar (or subtalar) arthritis with limited motion, or after ankle / subtalar fusion · ↑ toe-off propulsion, ↓ heel-strike pressure, ↓ ankle motion needed
Double rocker sole Midfoot prominences (Charcot), midfoot OA
Severe angle rocker Toe-tip ulcers
Negative heel rocker Fixed ankle dorsiflexion deformity
CROW boot Charcot / midfoot
Lateral hindfoot post Cavovarus foot
Hinged AFO Foot drop — does not immobilise ankle
Rocker sole (wrong option) Fixed planovalgus

Arthroscopic debridement & distraction arthroplasty

Debridement + anterior tibial / dorsal talar exostectomyisolated anterior impingement from anterior osteophytes · joint preserving · open option (plan future approaches) · not for advanced arthritis
✗ Wrong options: won't correct alignment

Distraction arthroplastyyoung, moderate–severe post-traumatic OA · offloading → biologic repair · needs good pre-op ROM · static / hinged ex-fix or spatial frame ± microfracture, chondroplasty, orthobiologics · outcomes controversial

Indicationsnear-normal ROM · minimal talar tilt · varus heel alignment · medially focused (asymmetric) arthritis = Takakura II / IIIA · tibiotalar malalignment, eccentric wear · young active patient wanting high activity

Biggest change in ankle forcestibial osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: deltoid / lateral ligament reconstruction · calcaneal osteotomy · PL → PB transfer (adjuncts only)

Deformity Osteotomy
Varus Medial opening wedge (or lateral closing wedge)
Valgus Medial closing wedge (or lateral opening wedge) ± oblique fibular lengthening osteotomy
Dome Less translation / length change; technically hard
Multiplanar / large Gradual correction with spatial frame

✗ Wrong options: stage IV valgus → fusion · stage I → conservative · lateral narrowing + neutral alignment → look at knee / hip · IIIB → poor results

Preoperative talar tilt Five-year survival rate
4–10° 85%
> 10° 65% (higher failure; also Takakura IIIB)

✗ Wrong options: age < 50 is NOT a contraindication

Ankle arthrodesis Total ankle arthroplasty
Indications Moderate–severe PTOA or inflammatory, refractory · young, high-demand labourers · malalignment (+ osteotomy) · comorbidities PTOA or inflammatory (RA) · elderly, low demand · ? concomitant TN / subtalar fusion · contralateral ankle fusion · wants motion (hiking, uneven ground)
Relative contraindications Vascular compromise (ABI 0.4, claudication) — poor wound + fusion healing Obesity (✗ Wrong options: not absolute, BMI 35) · young labourers · severe deformity
Absolute contraindications — Active infection · inadequate bone stock / severe osteoporosis · talus osteonecrosis · Charcot / neuropathic joint · peripheral neuropathy
Other contraindications (OB) — Uncorrectable deformity · ankle instability · neurologic muscle imbalance · severe malalignment

Arthrodesis vs total ankle arthroplasty – gait, adjacent joints

Not TAA contraindicationspost-traumatic arthritis (commonest indication) · inflammatory arthritis / RA · age > 50 · reconstructible ligament damage · correctable coronal deformity (up to 20–30°) via osteotomy / soft-tissue balancing (TO: > 10–15° = contraindication — read the options) · preserved subtalar motion = favourable

Peripheral neuropathyno protective sensation → microtrauma, instability, wounds, infection, early loosening

Arthrodesisgold standard for end-stage OA · reliable pain relief + ADLs · union ~90% (Orthobullets) · 93–94% with cancellous screws, 74% overall (OB)

Arthrodesis positionneutral dorsiflexion, 5–10° external rotation (10° OB / TO), ~5° valgus (0–5° OB), talus ~5 mm posterior

Young labourer (28 yo, BMI 31, construction)ankle fusion
✗ Wrong options: low-profile TAA · bipolar allograft · interposition · arthroscopic debridement (too advanced)

Healthy 66-yo hiker, subtalar pain-freeTAA
✗ Wrong options: TTC nail (spare subtalar) · tibiotalar fusion → younger · distraction → younger, moderate

Large OCD + 5° varus, 41 yojoint / cartilage preservation first

Function (TAA vs arthrodesis) Fact
Gait TAA patients: superior gait mechanics compared to AA post-operatively — ↑ stride length, cadence, stride / gait velocity → arthrodesis = ↓ stride length (✗ Wrong options: hip abduction · leg length)
Slopes / stairs TAA higher scores walking uphill, upstairs, downstairs
Uneven surfaces at 12 mo Both improve vs pre-op
Gait function at 12 mo Arthrodesis improves it (✗ Wrong options: "loss of gait function")
Bilateral arthrodesis Bad for gait → TAA for the second ankle

TAA outcomesup to 90% good–excellent at 5–10 yr (Orthobullets) · ~90% survivorship at 10 yr (OB) · > 80% survivorship at 5 yr if < 50 yo (Orthobullets) · survivorship ↓ if < 54 yo (OB) · 70–98% at 3–6 yr, 80–95% at 8–12 yr (OB, Easley) · 5-yr up to 60%, reoperation up to 30% (another OB) — read the options · long-term data pending

Arthrodesis long-termipsilateral midfoot / hindfoot degeneration
✗ Wrong options: revision surgery · hardware failure · walking aids · knee / hip DJD

Subtalar arthrosis after arthrodesis50% at 10 yr (Orthobullets) · > 50% within 10 yr (OB) · higher after AA than TAA
✗ Wrong options: "rare after well-done fusion"

Arthrodesis & arthroplasty technique

Arthrodesis approachesanterior · transfibular (8–10 cm distal fibula resected) · mini-open (burr) · arthroscopic

Arthrodesis fixationtransarticular compression screws · bridge plate · ex-fix · hindfoot retrograde nail (TTC)

TAA approachanterior, between tibialis anterior + EHL · protect SPN, DPN, anterior tibial artery

TAA designfixed vs mobile bearing · adjuncts: TAL / gastrocnemius recession, foot osteotomies, ligament reconstruction

Failed fusion or talar AVN – revision arthrodesis

Workupexclude infection + metabolic causes · plain films · CT (bony healing) · labelled WBC scan · scanograms if malaligned

Nonunion, subtalar pain-freerevision ankle arthrodesis + bone graft with stable compression fixation (transfibular approach + compression screws) · spare subtalar (young)

✗ Nonunion trapsexternal / internal bone stimulator · dynamisation → instability · PRP · bone grafting alone · hardware removal + IM rod / hindfoot nail (TTC) when subtalar is normal

Revision union≥ 85%

Ankle Arthrodesis

Foot & Ankle · 6 / 48

1Basics

Indications & causes

Definitionfusion of the tibiotalar joint; commonest for end-stage ankle arthritis; open or arthroscopic

Commonest causepost-traumatic arthritis · > 60% of end-stage tibiotalar arthritis (OB)

Other indicationspost-infection · chronic instability · AVN of the talus · inflammatory arthropathy · primary OA · neuropathic arthropathy · tumour resection · salvage of failed ORIF · salvage of failed TAA

Talar AVNtrauma = commonest cause (75%), mainly talar neck / body fractures · early → core decompression, non-vascularised or vascularised bone graft · late (structural change) → arthrodesis

Hindfoot OA causescalcaneus / talus fractures · RA · OA · end-stage PTTD · tarsal coalition · Charcot-Marie-Tooth (cavus)

Talar neck fracturevarus malunion ~30% → abnormal ankle loading → arthritis

Effect of hindfoot fusion on motion (talonavicular)

Joint fused Effect on motion
Talonavicular Eliminates almost all hindfoot motion — > 90% ↓ (greatest cumulative effect)
Subtalar (talocalcaneal) ↓ TN motion 74% · ↓ CC motion 44%
Calcaneocuboid ↓ TN motion 33% (OB) · 67% (another OB) — read the options · ↓ subtalar 8% (little effect)
Naviculocuneiform Little effect on hindfoot
Cuboid–5th MT Limited effect
Tibiotalar Little effect on hindfoot ROM

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Decides
Weight-bearing X-rays ankle + foot End-stage tibiotalar arthritis · coronal deformity (varus) · triple malunion (residual subtalar valgus, forefoot abduction)
CT Hindfoot (subtalar) degeneration → spared = isolated tibiotalar · involved = TTC
MRI Talar AVN — broad-based → TTC
Aspiration Prior septic ankle — no growth, WBC 9,800 = no active infection → arthrodesis (✗ Wrong options: repeat I&D)
Post-op X-ray Tibial stress fracture at proximal interlocking screw of hindfoot nail

Clinical localisationpain with passive DF / PF = tibiotalar · pain with inversion / eversion + sinus tarsi pain = subtalar · Coleman block rigid hindfoot = fixed

5Management

End-stage ankle arthritis, failed bracing / NSAIDs / injections
  • Subtalar spared→TIBIOTALAR ARTHRODESIS (screws)
  • + Subtalar arthritis / broad talar AVN / bone loss→TTC ARTHRODESIS
    (lateral transfibular · retrograde IM nail · femoral head allograft if bone loss)
  • Infection / draining hardware → REMOVE HARDWARE + I&D→STAGED ARTHRODESIS
  • Isolated subtalar arthritis, ankle painless→SUBTALAR ARTHRODESIS

Operative criteria – arthrodesis vs TAA

Favours arthrodesis Favours TAA
Young, high-demand / labourer (construction worker, 36–45 yo) Elderly, less active
Peripheral neuropathy (↑ TAA failure) · insensate foot Preserved sensation
Severe PVD —
Charcot / neuropathic arthropathy —
Osteonecrosis of talus (TAA contraindicated) Good talar bone stock
Active or prior infection (↑ periprosthetic infection) No infection history
Severe deformity · soft-tissue compromise Correctable deformity
Gold standard; most reliable pain relief Keeps ROM → better cadence, ↓ adjacent joint degeneration; reasonable 10-yr survivorship

Tibiotalar fusionhighest success rate for post-ORIF tibiotalar arthritis
✗ Wrong options: osteochondral allograft · interpositional soft tissue · arthroscopic debridement + microfracture · TTC

Supramalleolar osteotomyonly for coronal deformity > 10° with mild / moderate arthritis
✗ Wrong options: end-stage

Optimal fusion position

Plane Position
Sagittal Neutral (0°) dorsiflexion / plantarflexion — plantigrade
External rotation 5–10° ER (Orthobullets, OB) · 10° ER (OB, TO) · ER ~5° (TO explanation) — read the options
Coronal 5° hindfoot valgus (Orthobullets, TO) · 0–5° valgus (OB) · 5–10° valgus (another OB) — read the options
Translation 5 mm posterior talar translation under the plafond

Why eachneutral flexion ↓ knee extension in gait + MCL laxity · slight valgus prevents lateral column overload · posterior talus ↓ lever arm of foot

Avoid (TO)extension → excess pressure + intractable heel pain (slight flexion tolerated) · any varus · anterior talar translation → "vaulting" gait + knee pain (TO)

Wrong positionsplantarflexion → equinus gait, poor swing-phase clearance ("never the answer"; goal = plantigrade) · too much DF or valgus (20°) → altered gait, ↑ knee stress · internal rotation → abnormal foot progression angle · 0° ER · varus → poor outcome, adjacent joint degeneration

Hindfoot arthrodesisaim 5° hindfoot valgus

Indications – tibiotalar vs tibiotalocalcaneal vs subtalar fusion

Scenario Answer ✗ Traps
Post-traumatic ankle OA, 36-yo labourer, CT: hindfoot spared Tibiotalar arthrodesis with screws Arthroscopic debridement + steroid (adjunct only) · TAA · TTC IM / extramedullary
Varus end-stage ankle OA, mild subtalar changes, diabetic, no neuropathy Isolated tibiotalar fusion + slight posterior talar translation > 5° PF · IR · combined ST fusion · triple
End-stage ankle OA + peripheral neuropathy, no subtalar pain Tibiotalar arthrodesis TAA (↑ failure) · arthroscopy · subtalar fusion
Prior septic arthritis + talar AVN, aspirate sterile Ankle arthrodesis Repeat I&D · TAA (contraindicated in talar AVN) · SMOT · triple (fixed adult flatfoot)
Talar neck nonunion + AVN + talar head collapse TTC arthrodesis with femoral head allograft Steroid injection · TAA · subtalar fusion alone · triple
Broad-based talar AVN + tibiotalar + subtalar arthritis TTC via lateral transfibular approach Anterior approach (no subtalar access) · ankle fusion alone · TAA · talectomy without arthrodesis
Pes cavus, sinus tarsi pain, painful inversion / eversion, rigid on Coleman block, ankle painless Subtalar arthrodesis Broström–Gould (instability) · hindfoot scope + os trigonum excision (posterior impingement) · Chrisman–Snook (advanced instability) · triple (TN + CC + ST arthritis)
Isolated hindfoot arthritis from chronic pes planus Subtalar arthrodesis —

Techniques & fixation

Arthroscopic arthrodesisonly if minimal deformity

Opentransfibular approach when deformity present · fixation = screws · plate + screws · external fixation

Staged approachclear infection before definitive internal hardware

TTC fixation optionsSteinmann pins · plates + screws · ex-fix · retrograde IM nail

Retrograde IM nailload-sharing; ↑ bending stiffness + rotational stability vs plate-and-screw · useful with distal tibial / talar bone loss or when screw fixation suboptimal

Nail entry point (TO)crossing of bimalleolar (medial malleolus) bisector (coronal) + sagittal line from tip of 2nd toe to centre of heel (TO)

Lateral transfibular approachdual joint preparation (tibiotalar + subtalar) + local autograft (talar osteonecrosis)

TTC indicationsend-stage ankle + subtalar arthritis · Charcot neuroarthropathy · hindfoot bone loss (failed TAA, failed arthrodesis) · osteonecrosis / global AVN of talus · severe acute trauma · RA · flail ankle

Contraindication – peripheral vascular disease

Retrograde nail TTC Items
Absolute contraindications Active infection · severe (profound) peripheral vascular disease · severe tibial malalignment
Relative contraindication Normal subtalar joint — may be sacrificed in non-compliant patients + diabetic Charcot for stability
Indications (✗ Wrong options: as contraindication) Osteonecrosis of talus · bone loss from failed TAA / arthrodesis · severe peripheral neuropathy with Charcot

Salvage of infection/failed TAA – staged arthrodesis

Infected TAA + varus instability + talar bone lossstage 1: explant + antibiotic cement spacer + IV antibiotics → stage 2: ankle + hindfoot (TTC) arthrodesis with structural allograft

✗ Infected TAA trapsrevision TAA ± structural allograft (allograft remodels incompletely, fails under shear) · ankle arthrodesis in situ / with allograft (talar bone loss → poor talar purchase)

Failed TAA salvageconversion to fusion or transtibial amputation

Draining wound over old hardware + post-traumatic OAremoval of hardware, I&D, staged arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: keep hardware · simultaneous arthrodesis · simultaneous arthroplasty

Infected post-traumatic OA salvagearthrodesis or amputation · aggressive debridement + antibiotics before fusion

Footwear after fusion – rocker sole

Best gait aid after ankle fusionrocker sole (heel-to-toe / rocker-bottom) → ↓ heel-strike pressure, ↑ toe-off propulsion, "roll off" in late stance, dissipates force across fusion

✗ Option Actual use
SACH heel Mimics shock absorption of heel strike; less beneficial than rocker
Extended steel shank Stiffens sole; worse unless combined with rocker
Total contact insert Cushion / offload, correct flexible deformity
Lateral sole flare Varus deformity / lateral ankle instability
Morton's extension (± carbon fibre) Forefoot pain
Medial heel wedge Not for well-aligned fusion
AFO, Arizona, double-upright drop-lock Immobilise an already fused ankle
Pantalar arthrodesis Unnecessary if hindfoot + transverse tarsal motion painless

Malunited triple arthrodesis – osteotomy

Valgus–supination triple malunionresidual subtalar valgus → lateral subfibular impingement + forefoot abduction / midfoot supination via TN joint

Treatmentmedial displacement calcaneal osteotomy + transverse tarsal (derotational) osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopy + lateral ligament reconstruction · tendon transfer + lateral column lengthening + heel cord lengthening (PTTD flatfoot) · ankle arthrodesis with IM nail · TAA + deltoid reefing (ankle normal, patient young)

Ankle Arthroscopy

Foot & Ankle · 7 / 48

1Basics

Indications

Indicationsosteochondral lesions of talus (microfracture of OCD) · post-traumatic synovitis debridement · ATFL / AITFL anterolateral impingement · anterior tibiotalar spur resection (anterior bony impingement) · os trigonum excision · loose bodies · cartilage debridement with ankle fusion

Set-up

Positionsupine, leg over padded bolster · tourniquet + exsanguinate

Distensionexternal traction device distracts tibiotalar joint (↓ cartilage injury, ↑ visualisation) · 20 ml normal saline injected via marked AM portal site (TO)

Entrynick and spread (skin nick, mosquito spreads subcutaneous tissue) → ↓ neurovascular injury

Pre-tourniquet marking (TO)dorsalis pedis, DPN, tibialis anterior, great saphenous vein, peroneus tertius, malleoli, joint line

Workhorse portals (TO)anterolateral, anteromedial, posterolateral

5Management

Portals – location & structures at risk

Portal Location Role At risk
Anteromedial (AM) Medial to tibialis anterior, lateral to medial malleolus, at joint line · between TA + saphenous vein Primary viewing portal, established first · 2.7 mm 30° scope (TO) Saphenous nerve + great saphenous vein (mean safe distance 7.4 mm / 9 mm) · tibialis anterior tendon
Anterolateral (AL) Just lateral to peroneus tertius (~4 mm lateral, OB) + SPN, medial to lateral malleolus · made under vision with 25G needle Viewing / working portal (TO) · lateral gutter SPN — dorsal intermediate cutaneous branch (commonest)
Anterocentral Medial to EDL, lateral to EHL · through extensor tendon if needed (TO) Rarely used Dorsalis pedis artery + DPN (anterior tibial NV bundle)
Medial midline Between EHL and tibialis anterior — Deep + superficial peroneal nn. (well lateral to saphenous)
Posterolateral (PL) Just lateral to Achilles, medial to peroneals · 2 cm proximal to LM tip (Orthobullets) · at level of line from LM tip parallel to sole (TO) · prone / semi-decubitus Posterior viewing (os trigonum) · vision portal in hindfoot arthroscopy, 4.0 mm 30° scope (TO) Sural nerve + short (small) saphenous vein
Posteromedial (PM) Just medial to Achilles Posterior working (os trigonum) Posterior tibial artery (+ tibial nerve, OB)
Trans-Achilles — Abandoned (TO) Achilles injury / rupture

Anterior portals – superficial peroneal nerve injury

SPNmost commonly injured nerve in ankle arthroscopy · anterolateral portal · variable anatomy · branch of common peroneal, runs in lateral compartment → motor to peroneus longus + brevis · crosses fibula (lateral → anterior compartment) ~11 cm (3–15 cm) proximal to LM tip (OB) · fascial exit 10–12 cm (OB) · 12–15 cm (Orthobullets) — read the options · terminal medial dorsal cutaneous (great toe) + intermediate dorsal cutaneous (dorsum of foot)

Protecting SPNpalpate, transilluminate (shine scope light to see nerve under skin), blunt dissection, trace before incision · 4th toe flexion used to protect nerve when making AL portal (TO; not 4th toe extension)

Most commonly injured branchdorsal intermediate cutaneous branch (TO + Orthobullets)
✗ Wrong options: dorsal medial cutaneous branch

Dorsal foot numbness after scopeSPN via anterolateral portal

✗ SPN distractorsbetween EHL + EDL = DPN (EDB/EHB motor, 1st web) · terminates as lateral dorsal cutaneous n. = sural · motor to abductor hallucis + FHB = medial plantar · terminal branch of femoral = saphenous

Anteromedial & posterior portals – saphenous & sural nerves

Saphenous nervetravels along distal medial tibia + ankle · most at risk with anteromedial portal
✗ Wrong options: medial midline (well lateral to it)

Sural nerveposterolateral portal (os trigonum resection) · permanent numbness risk

Posterior ankle impingement (os trigonum, Stieda process) (TO)

PAISmechanical pinching in terminal plantar flexion · chronic > acute · ballet (en pointe), football, soccer, downhill running · acute plantar hyperflexion or chronic microtrauma (TO)

Most common cause (TO)os trigonum
✗ Wrong options: Stieda process · sloping posterior tibial lip · capsular calcification

Osseous causes (TO) Soft-tissue causes (TO)
Os trigonum · Stieda process · downward-sloping posterior tibial lip · posterior tibial osteophyte · prominent posterior calcaneal process · OCL, loose bodies, chondromatosis, subtalar coalition Thickened posterior capsule · post-traumatic scar · post-traumatic capsular calcification · loose bodies · FHL tenosynovitis (commonest tendon involved) · abnormal muscles

Os trigonumnon-fusion of posterolateral talar secondary ossification centre · lies lateral to FHL groove · appears 7–13 yr · forms 11–13 yr boys / 8–10 yr girls · fuses within 1 yr (→ trigonal / Stieda process) · often bilateral · pain from abutment or synchondrosis disruption (TO)

Os trigonum prevalence7–14% remain separate (TO) · 7% don't fuse (TO) · present in 10–25% (OB) — read the options

Stieda process (TO)elongated posterolateral talar process → causes posterior ankle impingement
✗ Wrong options: ossification at MCL insertion (Pellegrini-Stieda) · unfused ossicle (os trigonum) · elderly head injury

Imaging (TO)lateral X-ray: os trigonum / Stieda (may be normal) · MRI best: bone marrow oedema in talus, calcaneus or os trigonum

DDx (TO)Achilles tendinosis / tear, FHL tenosynovitis, posterior talar process fracture, Haglund's, OCL, retrocalcaneal bursitis

Treatmentnonop (NSAID, activity modification, PT) → excision open lateral or posterior arthroscopy via posterolateral portal (sural at risk) · stress fracture ± FHL tenosynovitis / entrapment

Ankle Ligaments

Foot & Ankle · 8 / 48

1Basics

Osteology & biomechanics

Ankle jointtibial plafond + medial malleolus + lateral malleolus + talus · main motion plantar / dorsiflexion · secondary inversion / eversion, rotation

Distal tibiofibular jointdistal fibula in incisura fibularis (concave distal lateral tibia) · fibula rotates in incisura during gait · mortise widens from plantar → dorsiflexion · syndesmosis screws limit external rotation

Joint reaction force5× body weight walking on level ground

Ligament overview

Group Ligaments
Medial Deltoid · calcaneonavicular (spring)
Lateral Syndesmosis (AITFL, PITFL, TTFL, IOL, ITL) · ATFL · PTFL · CFL · LTCL

Lateral ligaments

ATFL CFL PTFL
Function Primary restraint to inversion in plantar flexion · resists anterolateral talar translation Primary restraint to inversion in neutral / dorsiflexion · restrains subtalar inversion → limits talar tilt Supplementary when ATFL + CFL intact · max strain in dorsiflexion · limits posterior talar displacement + ER
Strength Weakest lateral — Strongest lateral
Origin Anteroinferior fibula, 10 mm proximal to tip Anterior border fibula, 9 mm proximal to tip Posterior border fibula
Insertion Talar neck, just distal to cartilage (18 mm distal to joint line) Calcaneus 13 mm distal to subtalar joint, deep to peroneal sheaths Posterolateral tubercle of talus
Orientation 45–90° to tibial axis (Orthobullets) · perpendicular in neutral → parallel in plantar flexion (OB) Parallel to tibia in neutral Perpendicular to tibial axis
Injured by Inversion in plantar flexion → commonest, low ankle sprain Inversion with foot in neutral Complete talar dislocation / severe sprains with other two torn
Exam Anterior drawer in 20° plantar flexion (Orthobullets; 10° PF = greatest translation, OB) vs other side · > 8 mm forward shift on lateral X-ray = ATFL tear Inversion (supination) test in slight dorsiflexion · talar tilt (ATFL + CFL) No specific test

PTFL if ATFL + CFL incompetentshort fibres restrict IR + ER, talar tilt, dorsiflexion · long fibres only ER, talar tilt, dorsiflexion

LTCLlateral process of talus → lateral calcaneus · anterior + medial to CFL · stabilises talocalcaneal joint · injured with ATFL · no specific test

Syndesmosis

Functionintegrity of ankle mortise

ComponentsAITFL · PITFL (deep part = inferior transverse ligament) · TTFL · interosseous ligament (IOL)

Clinicalhigh ankle sprain / syndesmosis injury, ankle fracture · AITFL + PITFL injured by eversion + external rotation

Testsexternal rotation test · squeeze test

Deltoid ligament

Functionprimary restraint to valgus talar tilt · both layers resist hindfoot eversion · stabilises against plantar flexion, ER, pronation

Superficial Deep
Crosses Ankle + subtalar Ankle only
Origin Anterior colliculus Inferior + posterior medial malleolus
Insertion Navicular, talar neck, sustentaculum tali, posteromedial talar tubercle Medial + posteromedial talus
Key Tibiocalcaneal (sustentacular) = strongest superficial · deep posterior tibiotalar = strongest overall (TO), resists calcaneal eversion Primary medial stabiliser · prevents lateral displacement + ER of talus
Test Eversion test in neutral External rotation stress test (+ syndesmosis)

Injurypronation (eversion) → forced ER + abduction · ± medial malleolus fracture · ankle fracture, high ankle sprain

Spring ligament anatomy & flatfoot

Spring (calcaneonavicular) ligamentconnects calcaneus and navicular · sustentaculum tali → inferior navicular
✗ Wrong options: talus–navicular · calcaneus–cuboid · talus–calcaneus

Componentssuperomedial + inferior calcaneonavicular · superomedial = largest + most important stabiliser of medial longitudinal arch
✗ Wrong options: inferior

Superomedial attachmentsanteromedial sustentaculum tali → broadly along medial navicular
✗ Wrong options: to medial cuneiform · from talus

Functionstatic stabiliser of medial longitudinal arch + talar head · arch = dynamic PTT + static ligaments / capsule + tarsal interlock · closely related to deltoid

Untreated tearflatfoot deformity
✗ Wrong options: syndesmotic widening · TMT widening · hallux valgus · talar tilt

PTTDspring ligament most likely attenuated in type II flatfoot · significant disruption → reconstruction

Acute spring tearforceful landing on flat foot · tibialis posterior usually normal

Epidemiology

Commonest reasonmissed athletic participation

Dancersankle sprain = commonest injury (Orthobullets) · inversion sprain = commonest acute skeletal injury in dancers (OB)

Ligament Attachments Tight in / injured by Test Frequency · strength

PTFL Distal fibula → lateral tubercle of posterior talus Rarely Not tested by anterior drawer Least injured · strongest + deepest of lateral complex (OB, TO)

Strength orderATFL (weakest) < CFL < PTFL (strongest)

Relative peroneal weakness → inversion ankle sprain · restore full peroneal strength to prevent recurrence

3Presentation

Symptomspain on WB, swelling, ecchymosis · recurrent instability, catching / popping after recurrent sprains · "giving way"

Anterior drawertalus translates anterior to tibia · seated, knee flexed over table edge, stabilise leg, pull heel forward · 10° PF = greatest translation (OB; 20° PF in another OB stem) · 8–10 mm = positive · PF → ATFL, DF → CFL · reflects ATFL ± CFL · limited use acutely

5Management

Acute low ankle sprain (grade I–III)
  • Ottawa +→X-ray
  • All grades → RICE→early functional rehab (brace, proprioception, peroneals)
    (± ~1 wk WB boot; grade III ± 10 d cast)
  • Pain / swelling > 6–8 wk→MRI (OCD, peroneals, syndesmosis)
Chronic lateral instability
  • Untreated / under-treated→proprioception + peroneal strengthening first
  • Failed nonop, normal alignment→modified Broström-Gould ± arthroscopy
  • + cavovarus, Coleman corrects→1st MT dorsiflexion osteotomy + reconstruction
  • + fixed hindfoot varus→lateralising calcaneal osteotomy + reconstruction

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
Grade I–III, persistent pain + instability despite extensive nonop Anatomic reconstruction (Broström-Gould) or tendon transfer / tenodesis
Grade I–III with bony avulsion Reconstruction
Open ankle dislocation, gross lateral ligament disruption Acute repair (OB)
Recurrent sprains + impingement lesion (AITFL, posteromedial) Arthroscopic debridement
Syndesmosis with tibiofibular diastasis Fixation
Peroneal tear > 50–60%, irreparable, severe tendinopathy Peroneus brevis tenodesis

Acute management – functional rehabilitation & proprioception

ProtocolRICE + elastic wrap → short (≈ 1 wk / 7–10 d) WB immobilisation (boot, Aircast, walking cast) if needed → early functional rehab: ROM → strengthening → proprioception (tilt-board) → sport-specific · functional brace (controls inversion + eversion) during strengthening + prophylactically in high-risk activity

Quickest return to activityearly functional rehabilitation · supervised PT helps early, no long-term difference · chronic instability cannot be predicted by history, exam or X-ray

Chronic instability – Broström-Gould, reconstruction & rehabilitation

Chronic instability> 6 wk · repeated episodes "giving way"

Modified Broström-Gouldanatomic shortening + reinsertion (imbrication) of ATFL + CFL · reinforced with inferior extensor retinaculum + distal fibular periosteum · 90% good–excellent · commonest procedure; preferred in athletes with normal alignment
✗ Wrong options: Evans · allograft fibula → 5th MT · added osteotomy if aligned

Gould modification factsno biomechanical difference in ankle stability
✗ Wrong options: superior extensor retinaculum · adds PTFL · ↑ nerve injury · ↓ ROM at 6 wk

Primary repair works even when chronicligaments stay attached to capsule · graft / internal brace = for failed primary repair · no technique proven superior

✗ Wrong options: inversion · eversion · PF · pronation

Tenodesis (Watson-Jones, Chrisman-Snook, Colville, Evans)nonanatomic tendon transfer · subtalar stiffness · alters biomechanics → discouraged · correct any malalignment first

✗ Wrong options: subtalar fusion · peroneal debridement if no eversion pain · 1st ray / Dwyer osteotomy if aligned

Instability + anterior impingementarthroscopic debridement + ATFL + CFL reinsertion with inferior extensor retinaculum + fibular periosteum
✗ Wrong options: PTFL · superior extensor retinaculum

Anterior Tibialis Tendon Rupture

Foot & Ankle · 10 / 48

1Basics

Anatomy

Tibialis anteriorprimary ankle dorsiflexor (80%) · inserts medial cuneiform + base of 1st MT · also inverts foot with dorsiflexion

Secondary dorsiflexorsEHL + EDL → mask the rupture → delayed diagnosis common

Siterupture at level of ankle joint, proximal stump retracts (~3 cm)

Epidemiology & risk factors

Attritional (atraumatic)older patients, men > 45 yr · eccentric load against plantarflexed ankle (missed step) · degenerative

Traumaticlaceration or closed rupture · strong eccentric contraction in young

Risk factorsolder age · diabetes · fluoroquinolones · local steroid injection · inflammatory arthritis · gout

3Presentation

Diagnosis – foot drop & attritional rupture

Acute"pop" → painful anterior ankle swelling · weak dorsiflexion

Chronicpainless · difficulty clearing foot · minimal swelling

Classic triadpseudotumour (painless mass) at anteromedial ankle = retracted stump · loss of TA contour (not palpable on resisted DF) · weak DF + hyperextension of all toes (EHL / EDL over-firing)

Eversion on dorsiflexionunopposed EHL + EDL (normal foot inverts with DF via TA)

Gaitsteppage gait (↑ hip flexion in swing) · foot slap after heel strike · toe dragging

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / role
X-ray (3 views foot + ankle) Exclude osseous injury · usually unremarkable
CT Not indicated
MRI Complete vs partial tear · sagittal "empty sheath" · does not decide need for interposition graft

Differential diagnosis

Condition Distinguishing feature
Attritional TA rupture EHL + EDL normal, painless anterior mass, steppage gait, full passive ROM
L4 radiculopathy / lumbar stenosis Tendon palpable, no ankle mass, dermatomal sensory loss (medial leg), weakness of several groups incl. quadriceps, +ve lumbar MRI
Common peroneal nerve palsy EHL + EDL also weak, sensory loss, compression history
Deep peroneal nerve palsy Toe extensors weak (not in isolated TA rupture)
Acute TA laceration Clear sharp injury, abrupt onset (not progressive over months)
Anterior ankle impingement No DF weakness, steppage gait or mass

5Management

Tibialis anterior rupture
  • Low-demand / elderly→AFO
  • Partial rupture→CAST
  • Acute < 6 wk, active→DIRECT REPAIR
    (attempt up to 3 months · gastroc recession if < 5° DF knee extended)
  • Chronic > 6 wk→RECONSTRUCTION
    • gap→INTERPOSITION GRAFT (plantaris, hamstring) / EHL transfer

Operative criteria

Option Indication
AFO Low-demand patient
Casting Partial rupture
Direct (primary) repair Acute < 6 wk, active high-demand; may be attempted up to 3 months
Gastrocnemius recession (before tensioning) < 5° passive DF with knee extended
Reconstruction Chronic > 6 wk
PTT transfer Permanent foot drop only

Surgery even latefunctional DF + gait improved in 18/19 (early 3 d–6 wk and late 7 wk–5 yr repairs) · traumatic ruptures do better with surgery regardless of timing · atraumatic presenting late → bracing acceptable

Treatment – repair or reconstruction & expected outcome

Direct repairopen: through laceration · closed: longitudinal incision over defect · hemostat under extensor retinaculum to retrieve proximal stump · non-absorbable Krackow / Bunnell / Kessler · oversew frayed ends · avulsion → suture anchors / bone tunnels

Sliding grafthalf-width of TA turned down · secured to medial cuneiform / dorsal navicular distal to retinaculum

Free graftautograft (hamstring, plantaris) or allograft · also Achilles, EDL, EHB interposition

EHL transfer / tenodesisdistal EHL → EHB · proximal EHL stump used as graft to TA insertion · TA tensioned then sutured to proximal EHL

Augment withextensor tendons (EHL, EDL)
✗ Wrong options: FHL (out of phase, too short; FHL for chronic Achilles)

Expected outcomerestores active DF with some residual weakness + improved activity level · ↑ AOFAS, high satisfaction · peak torque 72–84% of other side

Commonest long-term residualdecreased dorsiflexion strength (+ ↓ inversion strength)
✗ Wrong options: persistent foot drop / AFO (chronic missed or nonop) · numbness (missed superficial nerve laceration) · persistent pain

(✗ Wrong options: Wrong treatments — VY advancement / turndown flap (Achilles rupture with gap)) · SPR repair + groove deepening (peroneal instability) · AFO in active patient (permanent gait disturbance) · chest CT + skeletal survey + oncology biopsy of the "mass" · MRI of proximal tibiofibular joint for ganglion + peroneal EMG · PTT transfer

6Complications

Listfailure of repair / reconstruction · weakness of dorsiflexion · adhesions · neuroma

Prognosisgood with treatment

EHL / EDL Normal Weak Variable
Anterior mass Yes (pseudotumour) No No
TA tendon palpable No Yes Yes
Sensation Normal Sensory abnormality Dermatomal
Acute (< 6 wk) Chronic (> 6 wk)

"Most common long-term residual after repair?"decreased dorsiflexion strength

Intrinsic causescongenital (splayfoot, brachymetatarsia) · inflammatory arthropathy · residual surgical malalignment

Parameter Normal Bunionette
4–5 IMA 6.5–8° (Orthobullets, OB) · 6–8° (OB) ↑

Symptomslateral bunion pain · plantar callus · worse with constrictive shoes · cosmetic: medial deviation of 5th toe, prominent 5th MT head · effect on work

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical: lateral 5th MT head prominence ± pain + callus

Radiographsweight-bearing dorsoplantar, lateral, oblique · ↑ 4–5 IMA · ↑ lateral deviation angle · ↑ MT head width

Type Deformity Surgery
I Enlarged 5th MT head / lateral exostosis (head > 13 mm) Lateral condylectomy
II Congenital lateral bow of 5th MT (distal half) · normal 4–5 IMA Distal chevron osteotomy (IMA < 12°)
III ↑ 4–5 IMA · most common Distal osteotomy if < 12° · oblique diaphyseal osteotomy if > 12°
IV (OB) Combination of the above —

Type definitions differone OB uses 1 = enlarged lateral condyle · 2 = 5th MT varus · 3 = combined — read the stem

  • First line, all types→NSAIDs, wide shoes, orthotics, padding, callus shaving
  • Failed nonop
    • Type I (normal IMA)→lateral condylectomy
    • Type II / III, IMA < 12°→distal chevron osteotomy
    • Type II / III, IMA > 12°→oblique diaphyseal osteotomy (+ condylectomy if head wide)

✗ Wrong options: condylectomy · osteotomy · MT head resection as first step

✗ Wrong options: lateral condylectomy · condylectomy + distal osteotomy · diaphyseal osteotomy

Claw Toe

Foot & Ankle · 13 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Distributiontypically multiple toes · often bilateral

Pathophysiology – EDL vs intrinsic imbalance, neurological causes

Primary pathologyMTP hyperextension → chronic MTP hyperextension → unopposed DIP + PIP flexion by FDL · analogous to intrinsic minus hand

MTP jointEDL overpowering relatively weak intrinsics · hyperextended MTP makes intrinsics less efficient plantarflexors → deformity progresses
✗ Wrong options: intrinsics overpowering EDL · plantar plate overpowering EDB · lumbricals overpowering intrinsics · EDL overpowering EDB

IP jointsstronger flexors overpower weaker intrinsics (intrinsics act as IP extensors)

Plantar platebecomes insufficient / attenuated → base of proximal phalanx translates dorsally

Interossei + lumbricalsmove dorsally → flexion moment arm shifts to wrong side of MTP centre of rotation

Most common causesynovitis (Orthobullets, OB) · "occurs most commonly in diabetes, alcoholism, neuromuscular conditions" (another OB) — read the options

Other causestrauma · delayed / missed compartment syndrome (deep posterior leg compartment or foot) · cavus · inflammatory arthropathy (soft-tissue attenuation → MTP instability)

Neurological causesCharcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedreich ataxia, myelodysplasia, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, stroke, diabetic neuropathy · clawing of all 4 lesser toes → neurological abnormality

3Presentation

Symptomspain at unstable MTP joint · metatarsalgia

Plantardepressed metatarsal head with callus + tenderness

Dorsal / tipflexed IP joints with dorsal callosities · tip-of-toe ulceration (neuropathic / diabetic)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical: MTP hyperextension + PIP flexion + DIP flexion of a lesser toe

Lesser toe deformities

Deformity MTP PIP DIP
Claw toe Hyperextension Flexion Flexion
Hammer toe Slight extension (Orthobullets) · neutral (OB) Flexion Extension
Mallet toe Normal / neutral Normal / neutral Flexion
Curly toe Flexed Flexed Flexed
Crossover toe Laterally deviated Flexed Neutral

5Management

Claw toe
  • First line→taping + shoe modification
  • Flexible, no contracture→Girdlestone-Taylor: EDB tenotomy, EDL lengthening, FDL flexor-to-extensor transfer
    (diabetic, tip-of-toe ulcer, no infection → isolated percutaneous FDL tenotomy)
  • Fixed contracture→Girdlestone + MTP capsulectomy + proximal phalanx head/neck resection
  • All four lesser toes→Girdlestone + Weil (distal MT shortening) osteotomy
Claw toe (TO)
  • Flexible→flexor tendon transfer
  • Fixed→MTP soft-tissue release (dorsal + medial/lateral capsule, extensor lengthening)
    • Reduced→realigned toe
    • Not reduced→Weil osteotomy + fixed hammer-toe repair

Nonoperativefirst line · plantar padding (metatarsal / crest pads, orthotics) to offload plantarly subluxed MT heads · high toe box · sling holding proximal phalanx parallel to ground

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Painful flexible deformity without contracture · shoe-wear ulcers · otherwise healthy Girdlestone(-Taylor): EDB tenotomy + EDL lengthening + FDL flexor-to-extensor transfer
Fixed contracture Girdlestone + MTP capsulectomy + proximal phalanx head + neck resection (tendon transfer + bony resection)
Claw toe of all four lesser toes Girdlestone + Weil lesser MT osteotomy
Flexible deformity, diabetic, tip-of-toe ulcer, no infection Isolated percutaneous FDL tenotomy
Rigid diabetic claw toe with ulcer Arthrodesis
Rigid mallet toe (rigid DIP flexion) Bony: DIP fusion or resection
Hammer toe (PIP flexion, DIP extension) FDL-to-EDL transfer

Flexible deformity – flexor tenotomy or flexor-to-extensor transfer

Flexible claw toe (TO)flexor-to-extensor tendon transfer with extensor lengthening · flexor split into two slings, transferred dorsally as for hammer toe · extensor lengthening may or may not be needed (TO)
✗ Wrong options: extensor lengthening + PIP arthroplasty · flexor tenotomy + MTP pinning · distal metatarsal osteotomy

Girdlestone-TaylorFDL to extensor surface → long flexor acts like intrinsics: active MTP plantarflexion + IP extension · only for flexible deformity
✗ Wrong options: PIP arthrodesis · MTP capsulotomy + PP resection arthroplasty (fixed only) · isolated Weil

Percutaneous FDL tenotomydiabetic + flexible claw toe + tip ulcer, no osteomyelitis (bone not probed) → ↓ tip pressure; minimal exposure (infection, poor healing)

Percutaneous flexor tenotomy outcome Value
Ulcer healing 98% at 4 weeks
Reoperation ~8% (✗ Wrong options: 50%)
Ulcer recurrence 0–18% (✗ Wrong options: 30%)
Transfer ulceration Reported complication (✗ Wrong options: "no risk")

✗ Diabetic tip-ulcer trapsamputation through 2nd MTP (only with infection / osteomyelitis) · repeat ulcer debridement (doesn't offload) · DIP fusion (rigid / arthritic) · Weil (all four lesser toes, non-neuropathic; floating toe + transfer metatarsalgia)

Plantar plate repair

Plantar plate repairimproves the extension deformity at the MTP joint → toe plantigrade
✗ Wrong options: MTP flexion (claw has MTP hyperextension) · PIP / DIP (addressed indirectly)

Recurrencepersistent plantar plate dysfunction

Weil osteotomy – floating toe complication

Techniqueoblique distal MT shortening osteotomy · translates head proximal + plantar · rigid internal fixation · head moved proximal to callus → axial decompression · average shortening 4 mm

Indicationsmetatarsalgia (2nd MT, high heels) · MTP subluxation · claw toe of all four lesser toes

Floating toemost common complication of Weil = dorsiflexion contracture at the MTP joint

Mechanismplantar depression of head + altered centre of rotation → interossei move dorsal to MTP axis → converted from plantarflexors to dorsiflexors (intrinsics act as MTP extensors)
✗ Wrong options: articular damage · disruption of dorsal capsular artery · lengthening (it shortens) · ligament instability

Plantar translation in distal MT osteotomy (TO)floating toe: intrinsic force shifts volar → dorsal + weak toe flexors → extension at MTP + IP joints (TO)
✗ Wrong options: claw · hammer · mallet

Cause of 2nd toe "floating" post-optechnique of surgical osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: immobilisation · CVA · extensor tethering · infection

Avoidosteotomy parallel to plantar surface of foot or resect a wafer of bone so head isn't depressed

Rare after Weilosteonecrosis / MTP arthritis (constant plantar artery to MT head + capsule) · nonunion · significant transfer lesions

Weil vs Helal (shaft) osteotomyWeil: higher satisfaction, less recurrent metatarsalgia, fewer transfer lesions
