"Percutaneous flexor tenotomy — true?"ulcer healing rates 98% at 4 weeks

"Claw toe with lateral deviation of 2nd PP — direct result of plantar plate repair?"improves the extension deformity at the MTP joint

"Claw toes of all four lesser toes?"Girdlestone + Weil osteotomy · think neurological cause

Deep Peroneal Nerve Entrapment

Foot & Ankle · 14 / 48

1Basics

Synonymanterior tarsal tunnel syndrome · rare compression neuropathy of the deep peroneal nerve (DPN)

Commonest sitefibro-osseous tunnel under the inferior extensor retinaculum

Zone of compression1 cm proximal to ankle joint → talonavicular joint

Risk factorshigh heels, compressive shoe wear (tight laces, ski boots), previous fracture

Anterior tarsal tunnel anatomy

Border Structure
Roof (superficial) Inferior extensor retinaculum
Floor (deep) Talonavicular joint capsule
Lateral Lateral malleolus
Medial Medial malleolus

ContentsEDL, EHL, tibialis anterior, peroneus tertius, DPN, dorsalis pedis artery + vein
✗ Wrong options: superficial peroneal nerve · posterior tibial artery · intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve · medial calcaneal nerve

At risk at releasedorsalis pedis artery (vascular bundle runs with the DPN)

DPN in tunneldivides into lateral (mixed motor + sensory → EDB) and medial (sensory only → 1st web space) branches · nerve lies lateral to EHL

EHBcrosses superficially over the inferior extensor retinaculum → contributor to DPN compression (OB)

2Mechanism

Intrinsicdorsal osteophytes over tibiotalar or talonavicular joints (commonest) · pes cavus, post-fracture deformity (navicular nonunion) · ganglion · tumour · hypertrophic EHL / EDL / TA belly · peripheral oedema

Extrinsictight laces / ski boots · high heels (plantar flexion) · trauma incl. recurrent ankle instability

Stretch positionankle plantar flexion + inversion

3Presentation

Symptomsvague dorsal foot pain · paraesthesia lateral hallux, medial 2nd toe, 1st web space

MotorEDB weakness / atrophy

Sensory↓ two-point discrimination

ProvocativeTinel over DPN radiating to 1st web space · worse with plantar flexion + inversion · relief with lidocaine DPN block

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
Lateral foot + ankle X-ray Dorsal osteophytes, fracture sequelae
CT Bony anatomy of canal
MRI Mass lesions (ganglion, tumour)

5Management

DPN entrapment
  • First line→shoe modification + NSAIDs (≥3 mo)
  • Failed nonop→release inferior extensor retinaculum + osteophyte / ganglion resection
    • RSD symptoms→contraindication to release

Nonoperativepadded shoe tongue, alternative lacing (skip the tender area), full-length rocker-sole steel shank, night splint (ankle drifts into plantar flexion), PT if instability, injection, diuretic for chronic oedema · ≥ 3 months (OB)

SurgeryS-shaped dorsal incision ankle → base of 1st/2nd MT · start distal, find nerve, release both branches proximally · resect osteophytes, debulk muscle bellies · no compressive shoes after

Outcome80% good–excellent · recovery prolonged; persistent symptoms = main complication

Foot drop – tendon transfer (TO)

Complete CPN palsy (anterior + lateral groups) (TO)motor of choice = tibialis posterior to dorsum of foot → removes unopposed inversion + restores dorsiflexion · ± FDL with tib post (double transfer to EDL + EHL) · or anterior transposition of lateral gastrocnemius + peroneal neurotization (TO)

Isolated DPN palsy (peronei spared) (TO)rerouting the peroneus longus (TO)
✗ Wrong options: tib post transfer (removes inversion balance against working evertors) · FDL + tib post · gastrocnemius transposition · foot drop splint

X vs Y

Deep peroneal nerve Superficial peroneal nerve
Tunnel Anterior tarsal tunnel (inferior extensor retinaculum) Not in tunnel
Sensation 1st web space Dorsum of foot
Motor in foot EDB (+ EHB, Orthobullets nerves note) —

How it's asked

"Dorsal foot pain, medial 2nd-toe tingling, worse PF + inversion — structure in same tunnel to protect?"dorsalis pedis artery
✗ Wrong options: SPN · PTA

"Commonest intrinsic cause?"dorsal talonavicular / tibiotalar osteophytes

"Muscle weak or atrophied?"EDB

"Isolated deep peroneal palsy, foot drop — ideal procedure?"reroute peroneus longus (TO)

"Complete CPN palsy — tendon transfer motor?"tibialis posterior (TO)

Diabetic Charcot Neuropathy

Foot & Ankle · 15 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitionchronic, progressive, non-infectious destructive arthropathy from loss of protective sensation (pain + proprioception) · first described by Charcot in tabes dorsalis, 1868 (TO)

Incidence0.1–1.4% of diabetics (Orthobullets) · acute Charcot 0.15–2.5% (OB) · 1% of diabetics after 12 yr of disease (TO) · 7.5% of diabetics with neuropathy — read the options

Agetype 1 DM → 5th decade (20–25 yr after diagnosis) · type 2 DM → 6th decade (5–10 yr after diagnosis)

Bilateral9–35%

Sitefoot and ankle commonest · also shoulder, elbow · knee → ligamentous instability + bone loss

Commonest causediabetic neuropathy (now) · tabes dorsalis = former commonest lower-limb cause, now 2nd (TO)

Pathophysiology, classification & upper-limb Charcot

Neurotraumatic theoryinsensate joint + repetitive microtrauma → no protective response · overuse injury (TO)

Neurovascular theoryautonomic dysfunction → ↑ blood flow (AV shunting, hyperaemia) → bone resorption, periarticular osteopenia, demineralisation (TO)

Combined (TO)both neurotraumatic + neurovascular · often initiated by trauma, frequently unrecalled · osteoclast overactivity, vascular shunting · twisting / minor injury may trigger (OB)

Cause Typical joints (TO)
Diabetes (commonest) Tarsus + tarsometatarsal (commonest) · MTP · ankle > knee + spine
Tabes dorsalis (2nd commonest) Knee (commonest) · hip · ankle · lumbar spine
Leprosy (Hansen's) IP joints (hand) · MTP (feet) · lower limbs
Syringomyelia Shoulder (commonest) · elbow · wrist · cervical spine
Myelomeningocele Ankle · intertarsal

Upper-limb Charcot (TO)syringomyelia = commonest cause (rare overall) (TO)
✗ Wrong options: Hansen's · diabetes · tabes

Other causesalcoholism / alcoholic neuropathy · leprosy · myelomeningocele / spina bifida · tertiary syphilis · syringomyelia · post-traumatic sensory deficit · stroke with residual sensory deficit · HMSN / Charcot-Marie-Tooth · congenital insensitivity to pain · amyloidosis · MS · intra-articular steroids in weight-bearing joints · RA · methotrexate toxicity · idiopathic

NOT a causeReiter's syndrome

Genes & lab markers

Marker Role
CGRP (TO) Normally antagonises RANKL synthesis at nerve terminal · non-functioning in neuropathic foot → RANKL unchecked · maintains joint capsule integrity → loss = destruction + dislocation
RANKL (TO) Drives osteoclastogenesis → excess bone turnover
OPG (TO) Decoy receptor for RANKL · RANKL–OPG balance disrupted
IL-1, TNF-α ↑ NF-κB + RANK / RANKL / OPG pathway
✗ Wrong option: transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) Not a key marker (TO)
ESR, CRP, WBC ↑ in both Charcot + infection → don't discriminate
Wound healing Absolute lymphocyte count > 1500/mm³ · albumin > 3.0 g/dL
HbA1c > 8.0% Poor control → poor surgical outcomes
Histology Synovial hypertrophy · detritic synovitis (cartilage + bone fragments in synovium)

Bisphosphonates (pamidronate)theoretical role, ↑ osteoclast activity (TO)

3Presentation

Clinical features

Charcot's triad (TO)gross joint swelling · exaggerated movements (instability) · painless presentation (TO)

Painpainless classically; absence of pain diagnostic (TO) · usually some pain, less than expected (TO) · 50% painful / 50% painless (Orthobullets) — read the options

Single joint first · swollen, deformed, subluxed, unstable ("floppy") · crepitus from loose bodies (TO)

Acuteswollen, warm, erythematous; 3.3 °C warmer (Orthobullets) · 3–7° warmer (OB) · mimics infection · intact skin + loss of protective sensation ≈ pathognomonic

Chronicstructurally deformed · bony prominences · rocker-bottom deformity · medial arch collapse · ligamentous instability

Skin rule (TO)skin intact → think Charcot · skin broken → most likely infection (TO)

Undiagnosed patient with Charcot footevaluate for diabetes mellitus

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Finding / fact
X-ray (AP + lateral foot, ankle series) Early — mimics OA · Late — joint space obliteration, fragmentation of both articular surfaces → subluxation / dislocation, bone "chunks" in fibrous tissue, soft-tissue oedema, distension, HO
X-ray (TO) Marked destruction, periarticular erosions, JSN, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, loose bodies — simulates OA, absence of pain diagnostic
Technetium bone scan Positive in both neuropathic joint + osteomyelitis (high turnover, non-specific)
Indium WBC scan Cold (negative) in neuropathic joint · hot in osteomyelitis
Sulfur colloid marrow / indium-111 Added to Tc for specificity
MRI (with + without contrast) Most sensitive for soft tissue infection + osteomyelitis · best for abscess vs soft-tissue swelling · cannot reliably separate Charcot from infection (T2 / STIR oedema in both)
Ultrasound Fluid collections; less specific
Biopsy Guides antibiotics in osteomyelitis / abscess

Diagnosis – elevation test, neuropathy & Charcot vs infection imaging

Elevation testerythema ↓ / resolves with elevation (15–30 min, pillows, overnight) = Charcot · unchanged in infection (cellulitis, osteomyelitis, abscess) = key differentiator

Dependent ruborredness only when leg dependent → Charcot

Semmes-Weinstein monofilament (5.07)confirms neuropathy · most sensitive test · sensitivity 40–95% · neuropathy has greatest effect on diabetic foot pathology
✗ Wrong options: Thompson · Cotton · syndesmosis squeeze · Babinski

Favours Charcot over infectionno ulcer / intact skin · normal WBC + normal serum glucose · no fever / sepsis · fracture without ulceration

Low-grade fever + normal CRP + erythema settlesstill neuropathic arthropathy
✗ Wrong options: navicular stress fracture · osteomyelitis · embolic ischaemia · RA

Not useful as next stepinflammatory markers (↑ in both) · MRI (low specificity) · Tc scan alone

Diagnostic criteria – Charcot vs infection

Feature Charcot Infection / osteomyelitis
Elevation Erythema decreases Unchanged
Skin Intact Broken / ulcer
WBC, glucose Normal Leukocytosis, ↑ glucose, fever
ESR / CRP ↑ ↑
Tc bone scan + +
Indium WBC Cold Hot
MRI Oedema Oedema; abscess
✗ Mimic Distinguishing point
Cellulitis Erythema persists on elevation · no radiographic destruction
CRPS Aberrant inflammation, no Charcot X-ray changes
DVT Swelling + posterior calf tenderness; erythema (if any) persists
Occult fracture Typically spinal cord injury patients
Gout Normal uric acid · no rapid bony destruction
Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Lisfranc injury, Freiberg Different history / X-ray

Brodsky classification (anatomical)

Type Joints Feature Frequency
1 (midfoot) TMT + naviculocuneiform Fixed rocker-bottom with valgus · commonest 60%
2 (hindfoot) Subtalar, TN, CC Unstable, immobilise up to 2 yr · 2nd commonest (TO) 10% (Orthobullets) · 30–35% (TO) — read the options
3A Tibiotalar (ankle) Late varus / valgus → malleolar ulcer + osteomyelitis; significant deformity + disability 20%
3B Calcaneal tuberosity fracture Distal foot changes / proximal migration of tuberosity < 10%
4 Combination — < 10%
5 Forefoot only — < 10%

Brodsky trap (TO)"Type 3A = forefoot" is FALSE → 3A = ankle · forefoot = type 5 (TO)

Eichenholtz classification (staging)

Stage Name Clinical X-ray Treatment (TO)
0 — Oedema, erythema, loss of protective sensation, instability Negative (bone scan + in all stages) Frequent follow-up + serial X-rays
1 Fragmentation (dissolution, acute) Warm, oedema, ↑ ligamentous laxity Osteopenia, periarticular fragmentation, subluxation / dislocation TCC
2 Coalescence (subacute, reparative) ↓ oedema + warmth Coalescence, absorption of fine debris, early fusion, sclerosis TCC → CROW
3 Reconstruction (Orthobullets) · consolidation (TO) — chronic No inflammation, stable, often deformed Consolidation + remodelling, arthrosis, osteophytes Plantigrade → custom inlay shoes / CROW · non-plantigrade / recurrent ulcer → debridement ± arthrodesis

Time to consolidation (TO)forefoot 6 mo · midfoot 12 mo · hindfoot 18 mo (TO)

5Management

Charcot foot — goal: stable plantigrade foot in shoewear
  • Acute (Eichenholtz 0–2), skin intact→TOTAL CONTACT CAST
    • then → CROW→depth shoes + double rocker
  • Braceable, equinus + focal prominence / ulcer→EXOSTECTOMY + TAL
  • Unbraceable / unstable deformity→REDUCTION + ARTHRODESIS
    (ring fixator if ulcer / poor bone · TTC nail for ankle + subtalar)
  • Failed surgery / recurrent infection→AMPUTATION

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
TCC (nonop) First line — acute Charcot without skin breakdown · 75% success
Exostectomy + TAL "Braceable" foot with equinus + focal bony prominence causing skin breakdown / ulcer failing TCC
Deformity correction, arthrodesis ± osteotomy Severe deformity not "braceable" · unstable deformity · persistent plantar ulcer · unstable Charcot ankle · failed orthotics
External (ring) fixation Poor bone quality or compromised soft tissues / ulcer
Amputation Failed previous surgery (unstable arthrodesis) · recurrent infection / osteomyelitis · troublesome ulcers
Avoid surgery in acute stage Not enough evidence for stage 1 surgery; avoid during inflammation (some authors propose early fixation)

Operative indications (Orthobullets)recurrent infection · deformity · severe skin breakdown

Joint replacementrelatively contraindicated (TO)

Acute stage – total contact casting

First line / gold standardtotal contact cast (TCC) + offloading for acute (Eichenholtz 1–2) Charcot without ulcer

Durationcast changed every 2–4 wk for 2–4 months (Orthobullets) · up to 4 months (OB) · weekly cast changes until erythema + swelling decrease (OB) · 2–4 months (TO) — read the options

Weight bearingNWB or limited WB = gold standard until swelling resolves + consolidation on X-ray (✓ "TCC, no weight bearing, weekly cast changes") · WB TCC effective in early stages, no harm (De Souza, OB) · NWB not conclusively necessary (OB) — read the options

Alternativepneumatic bracing

Medicationsbisphosphonates · neuropathic pain drugs · antidepressants · topical anaesthetics

Stage 1 on cast, still warm at 2 monthscontinue TCC
✗ Wrong options: gout treatment (uric acid normal) · PT (aggravates stage 1) · ORIF of navicular · biopsy + ID referral

Goal in fragmentationprevent further collapse + deformity, avoid high-contact-stress ulceration

✗ Wrong first step Why
IV antibiotics / admission No infection
I&D / emergent debridement No ulcer, negative indium scan, erythema settles
MRI, inflammatory markers, Tc scan alone Don't change management (low specificity)
Midfoot / TN + TMT / subtalar / triple arthrodesis, ORIF, ring fixator Only after failed nonop, gross deformity or ulceration
Plantar exostectomy Not in acute phase
BKA / transtibial amputation Salvage only
Shoe modification, custom orthotics (Jones bar, carbon shank, AFO leaf spring, plastizote insole) Not for acute stage

Footwear & bracing after casting or partial amputation

CROW (TO)Charcot restraint orthotic walker · used in Charcot joint (TO)
✗ Wrong options: subtalar arthritis · ankle arthritis · gout of great toe

CROW designcustom bivalved total-contact AFO · full foot enclosure · rigid rocker sole · custom insole · rigid polypropylene anterior + posterior shell · DF stop, heel lift · rocker sole counters "nutcracker effect" · Velcro (TO)

CROW useafter TCC (oedema reduced first) · controls oedema · enables ambulation · prevents deformity during coalescence · removable → hygiene, wound care, comfort

CROW drawbackshigh cost · bulky → poor compliance · knee + lumbar pain (TO)

SequenceTCC → CROW → custom shoe / depth-inlay shoe with accommodative orthoses

Eichenholtz 3 shoedouble rocker sole → ↓ ulcer risk at plantar apex / midfoot prominence

Rocker sole Use
Double rocker Plantar midfoot prominence (Charcot rocker-bottom)
Severe-angle rocker Pressure distal to ball of foot (toe-tip ulcers)
Mild rocker Mild MT head relief, propulsion
Negative heel rocker Fixed dorsiflexion, forefoot pressure → shifts load to midfoot + heel
Heel-to-toe rocker After ankle / subtalar fusion · fixed lesser toe deformities

Partial 1st ray amputation (TA intact, 10° DF)steel shank (flat 1-inch steel strip) → extends foot lever, prevents deformity at toe break ± rocker sole
✗ Wrong options: snug shoe (volume fluctuation) · custom shoe (unnecessary expense) · leather sole (no catching with 10° DF + intact TA) · lateral wedge

Chronic deformity & ulceration – exostectomy & reconstructive arthrodesis

Ulcer causemalpositioned tarsal bones after joint collapse

Recurrent midfoot ulcer, failed TCC, stable deformity, equinusexostectomy + Achilles tendon lengthening + protective brace · limb salvage up to 90%
✗ Wrong options: ex-fix · BKA (viable tissue) · observation · exostectomy alone (equinus needs lengthening)

Silfverskiöld testpositive → tight gastrocnemius (gastroc recession) vs whole Achilles complex (TAL)

Talar head ulcer (Chopart dislocation), failed 2 TCC cyclesreduction + arthrodesis of Chopart joint with ring fixator (no hardware near ulcer, soft tissue monitored)

✗ Option for talar head ulcer Why wrong
CROW / repeat offloading Failed already → contraindicated
Achilles lengthening alone Doesn't reduce talar head
In-situ TTC with IM nail TTC suits Brodsky 2–3, but in-situ fusion contraindicated — must reduce
Midfoot osteotomy + Lisfranc plates For Brodsky 1; plates contraindicated with poor bone + ulcer

Charcot ankle + subtalar, failed bracing, no wounds, activeTTC fusion with retrograde nail (small incisions)
✗ Wrong options: anterior plate tibiotalar fusion (wound complications + misses subtalar) · BKA · TCC (for ulcers) · CAM orthosis

Fixationinternal: screws, pins, plates, tibiocalcaneal nail (internal may need staging) · external fixation (poor bone / soft tissue; usually single stage)

Post-opminimal WB for 3 months

Amputation level (Chopart)

Forefoot gangrene with necrosis up to navicular (smoker, hypertensive) (TO)Chopart amputation (TO)
✗ Wrong options: Pirogoff · Syme · Lisfranc

Chopart advantages (TO)conserves heel support · technically easier · shoe + AFO instead of knee-high prosthesis · little shortening · heel skin = weight-bearing end · easier muscle balancing (TO)

Equinus (TO)common cause of foot amputation failure · Chopart → tibialis anterior transfer proximally + tendo-Achilles lengthening · Syme → only TA lengthening, slight equinus ruins ambulation (TO)

Goalpartial / limited amputation if vascularity allows · BKA for severe deformity with soft-tissue involvement or failed reconstruction

6Complications

Complication Fact
Arthrodesis complications Up to 70% — hardware failure, infection, malposition, recurrent ulceration, fracture
Overall complication rate 50–56% (Sämann)
Recurrence (secondary episodes) Type 1 DM 41.6% vs type 2 18.3%
Amputation rate 3–9% — depends on avoiding ulceration (TO)
Late complications Chronic ulceration → infection → osteomyelitis
Ankle (Brodsky 3A) Malleolar ulcer + osteomyelitis

X vs Y

Charcot Hot Cold Oedema
Osteomyelitis Hot Hot Oedema / abscess

TCC CROW

Removable No Yes (hygiene, wounds)

Diabetic Foot Ulcers

Foot & Ankle · 16 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence~12% of diabetics have foot ulcers · commonest medical complication making diabetics seek treatment

Amputationulcers cause ~85% of lower-extremity amputations · diabetes = 15–40× ↑ amputation risk · diabetic foot ulceration = most likely predictor of eventual amputation

PVD60–70% of patients with diabetes > 10 yr · > 60% of diabetic ulcers have ↓ blood flow

Diabetic foot infectioncause of amputation in 25–50% · osteomyelitis ↑ amputation risk up to 4×

Charcot7.5% of neuropathic diabetics · neuropathy in 30–50% of diabetics, neuropathic fracture only 1–2.5%

Pathophysiology

Neuropathylargest effect · sensory → loss of protective sensation = primary risk factor for ulcer · autonomic → dry skin (no glandular function) · motor → intrinsic dysfunction → dynamic toe deformity

Angiopathylesser effect than neuropathy

Mechanicalequinus → forefoot (MT head) overload · ↓ MTPJ motion → ↑ IP pressure on hallux · peroneus longus overpull → plantarflexed 1st MT → 1st MT head ulcer

Three pillars of treatmentadequate blood supply · treat infection · pressure relief

Risk factors for ulceration & amputation (neuropathy, smoking)

Most likely to ulceratecannot feel 5.07 Semmes-Weinstein monofilament — vascular + nutrition tests predict healing, not ulcer formation
✗ Wrong options: TcpO2 30 · ABI < 0.6 · albumin 3.1 · autonomic dry skin · Silfverskiöld result

Concurrent variables in amputeesulceration 84% · neuropathy 64% · infection 59% · gangrene 55% · ischaemia 46% · + ↑ HbA1c, ↓ oxygen tension, ↓ ABI

Least likely to predict amputationABI 1.07 (normal)
✗ Wrong options: ulcer · monofilament loss · infection · HbA1c 10.7

Only consistent modifiable risk factorssmoking + glycaemic control (Rossboth)

Single best programme to cut amputationssmoking cessation with counselling + pharmacotherapy
✗ Wrong options: annual plantar-pressure screening + custom footwear · mandatory TCC for all · routine arterial US · GLP-1 weight-loss clinic

Infection risk factorsulcer > 30 days · recurrent ulcer · trauma · probe to bone · PAD

Microbiology

Usually polymicrobialaerobic gram-positive cocci (S. aureus) commonest · gram-negatives ↑ in chronic wounds / recent antibiotics · obligate anaerobes with ischaemia / gangrene

Gold standarddeep cultures + bone biopsy guide management

3Presentation

Symptomsoften painless

Examdepth (probe for bone) · infection (cellulitis, pus, gangrene) · Silfverskiöld · DP + PT pulses · hair on toes (absent = poor flow)

Signs of infection blunted↓ WBC function, PAD, poor metabolic control, neuropathy · commonest signs = ↑ exudate + worsening glycaemic control · ↑ WBC / ESR / CRP / fever absent in 50%

Ulcer location Driver Treatment
Plantar MT heads (1st / 2nd) Equinus TCC + TAL / gastrocnemius recession
1st MT head Equinus + PL overpull Gastrocsoleus recession + PL → PB transfer
Plantar hallux IP joint Stiff / rigid MTPJ Keller resection arthroplasty
Toe tip (apical) Flexible claw / hammer toe Percutaneous flexor tenotomy
Plantar midfoot Charcot rocker-bottom Exostectomy + TAL
Heel Bed-bound pressure · calcaneal osteomyelitis Offloading / padding boots · partial calcanectomy + TAL
Medial malleolus Venous stasis (rarely diabetic) —
Dry toe gangrene Arterial insufficiency Toe disarticulation

Silfverskiöld test

Techniqueforefoot inverted, hindfoot subtalar neutral (locks transverse tarsal joints) · compare passive DF knee flexed vs extended

Finding Contracture Procedure
DF improves with knee flexion Isolated gastrocnemius Gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)
DF equal with knee flexed + extended Gastrocsoleus / Achilles Achilles tendon lengthening (Hoke)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnostic criteria

Condition Criterion
Neuropathy (TO) 10 g (5.07 Semmes-Weinstein) monofilament not perceived all 3 times (TO)
Osteomyelitis Bone biopsy with cultures + pathology = gold standard · exposed bone → presume osteomyelitis
Infected ulcer ↑ exudate · ↑ WBC / ESR / CRP · worsening glucose · erythema persisting despite elevation
Healing potential TcpO2 = gold standard (see labs)

Monofilament technique (TO)10 g monofilament · eyes closed · 90° to skin, pressed until it buckles 1 cm · patient says "yes" · repeat 3 times (TO)
✗ Wrong options: 1 g · 5 g · 1 g polyfilament

Monofilament accuracysensitivity 41–93% / 57–93%, specificity 68–100% / 75–100% · 3-site test: plantar great toe, 3rd MT, 5th MT (Feng)

Study Use / sign

Exposed bone Highly predictive — presume osteomyelitis
Ulcer > 2 cm² LR+ 7.2
ESR > 70 mm/h LR+ 11
Bone biopsy (culture + histology) Most accurate / most specific / gold standard
Wound / swab culture Positive at all stages → not predictive of osteomyelitis
CBC Unhelpful (immunocompromise, vascular insufficiency)
CRP / ESR Helpful, not diagnostic

No single history / exam finding excludes osteomyelitis

✗ Biopsy trapsHbA1c > 15% · ESR + CRP · probe-to-bone · cortical erosions · CBC · technetium scan · WB radiographs

Wagner classification & monofilament screening (TO)

Grade Orthobullets TO table Treatment
0 Skin intact, bony deformity — "foot at risk" No open lesion; may have deformity or cellulitis Shoe modification + serial exams
1 Superficial ulcer Superficial, partial or full thickness (not exposing ligament, deep fascia, bone) Office debridement + TCC
2 Deeper, full-thickness extension To ligament, tendon, joint capsule, deep fascia; no abscess / osteomyelitis Operative debridement + TCC
3 Deep abscess or osteomyelitis + joint sepsis Operative debridement + TCC (I&D + antibiotics before casting)
4 Partial forefoot gangrene Gangrene of portion of forefoot or heel Local vs larger amputation
5 Extensive gangrene Entire foot Amputation

Exposed tendons, no bone / abscess (TO)Wagner grade 2 (TO)
✗ Wrong options: 1 · 3 · 4

TO wording conflictTO text: ulcers "breaking through superficial fascia… with exposed bone or tendon = grade 2" · TO table + Orthobullets: abscess / osteomyelitis = grade 3 — read the options

Depth Definition Treatment
0 At-risk foot, no ulcer Education, accommodative footwear, regular exams (shoe modification)
1 Superficial, not infected Offload — TCC, walking brace, special footwear
2 Deep, exposing tendons / joints Surgical debridement, wound care, offload, culture-specific antibiotics
3 Extensive ulcer or abscess (exposed bone, osteomyelitis) Debridement / partial amputation, offload, culture-specific antibiotics
Ischaemia Definition Treatment
A Not ischaemic —
B Ischaemia, no gangrene Noninvasive vascular testing → angioplasty / bypass
C Partial forefoot gangrene Vascular reconstruction + partial foot amputation
D Complete gangrene Full vascular work-up + major amputation

Definition (TO)chronic granulomatous infection of skin + subcutaneous tissue · fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria (actinomycetoma) · bacteria ~60% (TO)

Actinomycetes (bacteria) (TO) Eumycetes (fungi) (TO)

5Management

Diabetic foot ulcer
  • Infected / abscess / osteomyelitis → I&D + bone culture→culture-specific abx
    • infection cleared→TCC ± TAL
  • Clean plantar ulcer, perfused→wound care + TCC
    • forefoot + equinus→add TAL / gastrocnemius recession
  • Ischaemic → vascular studies→revascularise
  • Gangrene→amputation (level by PT pulse + labs)
Forefoot ulcer with limited dorsiflexion
  • Pulses absent→ABI / TcpO2 first
  • DF improves with knee flexion→gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)
  • No improvement with knee flexion→Achilles tendon lengthening (Hoke)

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
I&D + antibiotics before casting Wagner ≥ 3 · deep full-thickness ulcer failing TCC
Flexor tendon tenotomy Flexible toe deformity + toe-tip ulcer (high healing if no osteomyelitis)
TAL / gastrocnemius recession Plantar forefoot ulcer + equinus (DF ≤ 5°)
Ostectomy ± TAL Bony prominence causing internal pressure (TAL if tight Achilles)
Partial calcanectomy ± TAL Large heel ulcer + calcaneal osteomyelitis
Keller resection arthroplasty Plantar hallux IPJ ulcer + stiff MTPJ, failed TCC
Deformity correction + TAL Nonplantigrade, rigid Charcot deformity with recurrent ulcers
Syme amputation Forefoot gangrene + palpable posterior tibial pulse

Total contact casting, offloading & NPWT

Wound carefirst line · moist environment · absorb exudate · barrier · offload

TCCgold standard for mechanical relief of plantar ulcers · snug below-knee · protects insensate limb, keeps patient ambulatory · lower infection, admission, lost income

TCC contraindicationsabsolute: infection · relative: marginal arterial supply, poor compliance with cast care, cast claustrophobia

TCC durationchanged every 3–4 wk, prevents daily wound care · total several months (up to 4 months) · 83% heal, 17% complications (skin irritation)
✗ Wrong options: ≤ 4 weeks

Recurrence after TCCtypically 3–4 wk after removal = greatest risk within 1 month (newly healed tissue weak to vertical + shear stress) · most within first 6 months

SequenceTCC (non-removable) → CROW (removable) → custom shoe / orthotic

Clean 3-month plantar ulcer, no bone, normal labstotal contact casting
✗ Wrong options: TCC + empiric IV antibiotics · debridement + antibiotics · CROW

Infected heel ulcer — NOT indicatedtotal contact casting · indicated: surgical debridement, tighter glycaemic control, imaging (MRI), culture-directed antibiotics

✗ TCC trapsreplace weekly with active infection · cast ≤ 4 wk · avoid in insensate feet · custom insoles equally effective (orthoses prevent, TCC treats) · orthotics > TCC (TCC heals faster, compliance)

Non-removable > removablenon-removable casts heal better than removable casts / dressings · pneumatic walker = alternative, better wound surveillance, but removable → compliance; no evidence of superiority

NPWT↓ ulcer size + time to healing · for perfused, uninfected, offloaded ulcers failing standard care / deep after debridement · granulation, ↓ oedema, removes exudate, ↑ local flow
✗ Wrong options: custom shoes · electrophysical therapy · hyperbaric oxygen (mixed) · topical PDGF

Without offloadingdebridement or NPWT alone won't heal · VAC does not reduce recurrence

Achilles / gastrocnemius lengthening for forefoot ulcers (Silfverskiöld)

Rationaleequinus → cyclic forefoot overload → MT head ulcers · percutaneous TAL ↓ forefoot peak pressure ~25%

Mueller RCT (TCC ± TAL, DF ≤ 5°)healing 100% vs 88% (no difference) · recurrence ↓ 75% at 7 mo, ↓ 52% at 2 yr · 81% vs 38% recurrence at 2 yr

Lengthening effect↓ recurrence, not faster healing of active ulcers vs TCC alone · Colen 25% vs 2% recurrence (94% RRR) — avoid over-lengthening

TAL + TCC vs TCC alonelower forefoot ulcer recurrence at 2 years (✗ Wrong options: higher / same · ↑ BKA) · ↑ heel peak pressure → more heel-pad breakdown (✗ Wrong options: lower)

Static calf stretchingno effect on ROM or plantar pressure

Gastrocnemius recession (Strayer) benefits mostchronic plantar forefoot ulcer
✗ Wrong options: peroneal tendinitis · Freiberg · retrocalcaneal bursitis · calcaneal osteomyelitis

Highest successIV antibiotics based on percutaneous bone biopsy culture sensitivity · only factor affecting remission · remission only 64% at 1 yr

FHL Tendonitis & Injuries

Foot & Ankle · 17 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Siteposterior ankle (behind talus, fibro-osseous tunnel) · great toe

Risk factorexcessive / maximal plantarflexion → ballet dancers en pointe / demi-pointe, gymnasts

DancersFHL tendinitis = common cause of posteromedial (medial-sided) ankle pain · dancers endure symptoms longer before seeking care than non-dancers

Associated conditionsposterior ankle impingement (PAIS) · os trigonum (posterolateral tubercle)

Diagnosis in dancers & FHL anatomy

Origininferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula + lower part of interosseous membrane

Coursebetween posteromedial + posterolateral tubercles of talus in a fibro-osseous tunnel → beneath sustentaculum tali → crosses dorsal to FDL at knot of Henry (FHL "higher", FDL "down") → stays dorsal to FDL + NV bundle · multiple FHL–FDL connections

Insertionplantar base of distal phalanx of great toe

Actionprimary: plantarflexion of hallux IP + MTP · secondary: ankle plantarflexion

Os trigonum linkFHL runs directly medial to lateral tubercle of posterior talar process → coexistent tendinopathy
✗ Wrong options: peroneus brevis / longus · FDL · tibialis posterior (not as close)

Os trigonumunfused secondary ossification centre of lateral tubercle of posterior talar process · or united stress fracture of that tubercle

Origin (as in the options) Muscle
Inferior 2/3 posterior fibula + lower interosseous membrane FHL ✓
Anterior fibula + adjacent interosseous membrane EHL (wrong option)
Cuboid + lateral cuneiform FHB (wrong option — doesn't cross ankle)
Fibular head + upper 1/2–2/3 lateral fibula + septa Peroneus longus (wrong option)
Inferior 2/3 lateral fibula + septa Peroneus brevis (wrong option — subfibular pain with eversion + dorsiflexion)

2Mechanism

Mechanismactivities with maximal plantarflexion → impingement of FHL along posterior ankle → tendinitis → even rupture

Pathoanatomyposterior to talus, within fibro-osseous tunnel (posteromedial ankle) · or secondary to os trigonum

Chronicnodule formation → triggering of great toe

PAISscarring + tendinopathy of FHL · Achilles in vicinity but remains normal

FHL lacerationdirect acute trauma · acute laceration = most common form of injury

3Presentation

Painposteromedial ankle · worse en pointe / demi-pointe
✗ Wrong options: posterolateral = os trigonum

Halluxtriggering, locking, clicking / catching, snapping behind medial malleolus with great-toe motion

Key signpainful crepitus of tendon with passive motion of great toe (passive hallux motion moves inflamed FHL at ankle)

Other signspain with resisted flexion of hallux IP (resisted great-toe plantarflexion) · ↓ passive extension of great toe · posteromedial tenderness, fullness, crepitus · no tenderness at 1st MT head

Forced ankle plantarflexionpainful in FHL tendinitis (Orthobullets, OB PAIS stem) · no pain on forced passive PF in a classic FHL stem; forced PF pain = posterior impingement (OB) — read the options

Tib post workingheel inverts on toe rise → excludes PTT

Lacerationloss of active IP joint flexion

Exam finding Diagnosis
Painful crepitus with passive great-toe motion FHL tendinitis ✓
Pain on percussion of posterior tibial nerve Tarsal tunnel (wrong)
Posterior ankle pain with forced passive plantarflexion Posterior impingement (wrong)
Medial pain with resisted inversion Posterior tibial tendinitis (wrong)
Foot drop, weak dorsiflexion Tibialis anterior rupture (wrong)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
MRI (axial T2) Fluid around FHL tendon at level of ankle joint = tenosynovitis of FHL sheath as it wraps posteromedial ankle · intrasubstance signal
MRI – laceration Retracted tendon ends · fluid in FHL sheath
X-ray / bone scan / MRI in ballet student Os trigonum → look for associated FHL pathology

5Management

FHL tendinitis
  • First line→rest, ice, NSAIDs, activity modification, arch support, PT
    (no steroid injection – posterior tibial nerve close)
  • Fails nonop (e.g. 6 mo)→release FHL from fibro-osseous tunnel at ankle
    (arthroscopic or open posteromedial; tenosynovectomy ± repair)
  • Acute laceration of FHL + FHB→acute surgical repair

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Recalcitrant symptoms · athletes with symptoms despite rest + nonop Release of FHL from fibro-osseous tunnel, tenosynovectomy, ± tendon repair
Lacerations of both FHL and FHB Acute surgical repair

Next step after failed 6 mo nonopdecompression of FHL at the level of the ankle
✗ Wrong options: at metatarsal (ankle level commoner than distal tarsal tunnel in midfoot) · peroneal decompression (lateral pain) · 1st MT osteotomy (hallux valgus) · gastrocnemius recession (isolated gastroc equinus)

Steroid injectioncontraindicated (posterior tibial nerve close by)

Compressioncontracture of medial retinaculum over FHL → posteromedial pain

Outcomes> 90% good / excellent in dancers · good in dancers + non-dancers · professional dancers do better than amateurs (Hamilton)

1Basics

Plantar fascia

Originmedial calcaneal tuberosity

Insertionplantar plate + bases of all 5 proximal phalanges · lateral band → 5th MT base

Facetsposterior = largest · middle = medial, on sustentaculum · anterior = continuous with talonavicular joint

Motioninversion / eversion only · no role in plantar / dorsiflexion

Componentstalonavicular + calcaneocuboid

Talonavicular supportspring ligament = superomedial + inferior calcaneonavicular ligaments

Calcaneocuboidsaddle-shaped · plantar support = superficial + deep inferior calcaneocuboid ligaments · superior support = lateral limb of bifurcate ligament

Articulations1st–3rd metatarsocuneiform + 4th–5th metatarsocuboid · naviculocuneiform + intercuneiform joints = dense ligaments, little motion

Column Bones Mobility / role
Medial 1st MT, medial cuneiform, navicular Carries most load in standing
Middle 2nd + 3rd MT, middle + lateral cuneiforms Least mobile → rigidity for push-off
Lateral 4th + 5th MT, cuboid Most mobile → uneven ground

Interosseous (contains Lisfranc ligament: plantar medial cuneiform → base of 2nd MT) Strongest
Plantar Next strongest
Dorsal Weakest

Transverse Roman archdorsal surface wider than plantar · 2nd MT base = keystone

1st MTshortest + widest · takes 50% of weight during gait (Orthobullets)

2nd MTlongest · most stress during gait → commonest MT stress fracture

Adductor hallucis conjoined tendonlateral aspect of lateral sesamoid + lateral base of proximal phalanx

2nd MTP plantar platedense phalangeosesamoidal complex · must become lax before dorsal translation of proximal phalanx · once attenuated, main deforming force = EDL · weakest at origin (metatarsal neck)

Seymour fracture (hallux distal phalanx)remove nail + interposed physeal tissue, repair nail bed, splint in extension, antibiotics

✗ Wrong options: extend MTP + flex IP · flex both · extend both

Subtalar & transverse tarsal joint axes in gait

Phase Subtalar / calcaneus Chopart axes Foot
Heel strike Eversion Parallel → unlocked Supple → shock absorption, accommodates ground
Push-off / toe-off Inversion Divergent → locked Rigid lever arm for propulsion

✗ Gait trapseversion unlocks (✗ Wrong options: locks) · calcaneus everted at heel strike (✗ Wrong options: inverted throughout stance) · tibialis anterior contracts eccentrically in stance (✗ Wrong options: concentrically) · push-off foot is rigid via inversion (✗ Wrong options: flexible via eversion)

Flexible → rigid foot at toe-off(1) tightening of plantar fascia · (2) progressive external rotation of lower extremity (pelvis → ankle → subtalar) · (3) subtalar inversion locks transverse tarsal joint

Does NOT occur at push-offloosening of the spring ligament

Muscle Antagonist / force couple Fact
Tibialis posterior Peroneus brevis = primary antagonist Inverts, secondarily plantarflexes
Tibialis anterior Peroneus longus TA secondarily inverts → only partial antagonist of TP · TA eccentrically contracts after heel strike

Tibial Tibialis posterior, long toe flexors (deep + superficial posterior compartments)

Tendon transfer requirementsadequate strength + excursion · insertion close to substituted tendon, routed in direct line · intact nerve + blood supply · functional (supple) joints · donor must be innervated

Foot drop

Definitioninability to dorsiflex ankle ± toes · commonest cause = peroneal nerve palsy

Causescentral (brain, cord, roots) · peripheral (sciatic, peroneal) · traumatic (knee dislocation, laceration, blunt) · compressive (mass, deformity correction) · systemic (diabetic polyneuropathy, mononeuropathy) · iatrogenic (casting, positioning, surgery) · mechanical (muscle debridement, tumour excision) · anterior compartment syndrome (devitalised muscle) · CMT · polio

Nerve Motor loss Sensory loss
DPN Ankle / toe dorsiflexion First dorsal web space
SPN Ankle eversion Lateral leg + dorsal foot

Gaitfoot slaps floor at heel strike = tibialis anterior weakness · toes extend in swing = extensors substituting for weak TA

Knee-level injurylateral leg sensory loss + ↓ eversion + ↓ dorsiflexion

Equinovarus after stroke

Commonest ankle–foot deformity after strokeequinovarus

Equinusoveractive gastrocnemius–soleus · Varus — overactive tibialis anterior (+ tib post, FHL, FDL)

Other featuresclonus, intrinsic-minus foot, supple claw toes, compensatory knee hyperextension, premature triceps surae firing

4Diagnosis & Classification

Silfverskiöld test & gastrocnemius recession indications

Testankle dorsiflexion with knee extended, then knee flexed (hindfoot locked)

Why it worksgastrocnemius crosses the knee (origin posterior femur) → relaxes with knee flexion · soleus does not

Diagnostic criteria

Silfverskiöld result Diagnosis Surgery
↑ DF with knee flexed (e.g. −10° ext → +10° flex; −5° → 10°; 0° → 15°; 3° → 16°) Isolated gastrocnemius contracture (positive test) Gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)
Same DF knee flexed + extended, can't pass neutral in either Achilles (gastroc–soleus) contracture Achilles lengthening (Hoke triple-cut, percutaneous, open) or gastroc + soleus recession
DF past neutral in both positions Normal —
✗ Wrong option: DF better with knee extended Opposite of positive test —

Thresholdsgastroc contracture if DF < 10° with knee extended, improving with knee flexion (OB) · difference > 10° = significant (OB) · shy of neutral → past neutral with knee flexion (OB) — read the options

Not a Silfverskiöld findingcalf squeeze ± plantarflexion = Thompson test (Achilles rupture) · resting ankle position irrelevant

Other exams (wrong options)Ober = IT band · Dial = knee posterolateral corner · Thessaly = meniscus · Thomas = hip flexion contracture · Coleman = hindfoot flexibility

Gastroc contracture causes↑ forefoot strike → ↑ plantar tension → plantar fasciitis, arch collapse, Achilles tendinopathy, metatarsalgia (plantar callus under MT heads), neuromas

Lateral head of gastrocnemiusmuscle tested by the Silfverskiöld test

Coleman block test – forefoot-driven cavovarus

Methodblock under lateral border (lateral column / hindfoot), first ray allowed to drop off

Heel corrects to neutral / slight valgusflexible subtalar / hindfoot → varus is forefoot-driven = plantarflexed first ray (valgus forefoot)
✗ Wrong options: dorsiflexed first ray · varus forefoot · rigid flatfoot

Heel stays in varushindfoot-driven (rigid hindfoot) → needs calcaneal osteotomy

Subtle cavus associationslateral column overload, recurrent ankle sprains / functional ankle instability, 5th MT stress fracture

5th MT stress fracture (esp. chronic / recurrent)look for hindfoot varus deformity
✗ Wrong options: lateral ligament instability · talocalcaneal coalition (causes flatfoot, protects 5th MT) · PB rupture · anterior process fracture

5Management

Equinus
  • Silfverskiöld positive (gastroc only)→gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)
  • Fixed in both knee positions→Achilles lengthening (TAL)
Cavovarus
  • Supple, Coleman corrects → dorsiflexion 1st MT osteotomy (± PL→PB)
  • Coleman does not correct→+ lateralising calcaneal (Dwyer) osteotomy
  • Rigid / degenerative→triple arthrodesis
Chronic flexible foot drop
  • < 6–12 mo, nerve may recover→AFO + observation + therapy
  • Acute laceration→nerve repair, graft or transfer
  • No recovery, supple joints→tib post transfer to dorsum (lateral cuneiform)
    • Equinus contracture→+ gastroc / Achilles lengthening

Foot Puncture Wounds

Foot & Ankle · 20 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Settingcommon workplace injury (construction sites) · stepping on a nail or stick through sock / sole

Commonest objectnails (TO) · also needles, glass, wood, plastic, sharp metal (TO)
✗ Wrong options: needles commonest

Infection~10% · osteomyelitis 1–2% (penetration to cartilage / periosteum) (TO)

Complications (TO)soft-tissue infection · deep abscess · pyogenic granuloma · epidermal inclusion cyst · osteomyelitis

Risk factors for infection (TO)

Wound (TO)presentation > 6 h · location · depth · contamination of object · retained foreign body

Host (TO)elderly · immunocompromised · PVD · diabetes = most significant risk factor → often osteomyelitis

Microbiology – S. aureus vs Pseudomonas (rubber-soled shoes)

Infection Commonest organism Features asked
Soft tissue (cellulitis, abscess) Staphylococcus aureus (Staph + Strep species) Coagulase positive, haemolytic gram-positive cocci · commonest in diabetics + non-diabetics · S. aureus + group A strep in children
Osteomyelitis (non-diabetic) Pseudomonas aeruginosa Gram-negative rod, single polar flagellum (motile) · secretes blue-green pigment in vitro · grape-like odour · biofilm, exotoxin, moist environments
Through rubber sole of shoe Pseudomonas (TO) Grows in moist inner layers of a used athletic shoe (not new / very old) → inoculated with rubber
Diabetic osteomyelitis S. aureus more common · polymicrobial Diabetics → more osteomyelitis, more organisms
Bodies of water (TO) Pseudomonas, Aeromonas hydrophila, Vibrio, Mycobacterium marinum —
Toothpick (TO) Eikenella (oropharyngeal flora) —

Pseudomonas ✗ trapsno flagellum · spore-forming · ferments lactose · clear colonies (colonies blue-green on nutrient agar)

✗ Distractor organism Description Classic association
Staph epidermidis Coagulase-negative, non-haemolytic GPC Periprosthetic joint infection
Salmonella GN rod, multiple (peritrichous) flagella Osteomyelitis in sickle cell
Clostridium tetani Spore-forming GP rod, multiple flagella, anaerobe Tetanospasmin blocks glycine + GABA release
Pasteurella multocida — Animal bites
Eikenella corrodens — Human bites (OB) · toothpick (TO)
Vibrio — Marine environments

3Presentation

Timingoften weeks to a month after injury · limp · fever, drainage

Examswollen, tender foot · obvious wound ± tract · well-demarcated erythema · ± lymphadenopathy

Relapse after initial improvementsuggests osteomyelitis or retained foreign body

Child, nail 1 wk ago, heel pain, tender calcaneal tuberositycalcaneal osteomyelitis (Pseudomonas)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
X-ray (AP + lateral) Normal early · bone destruction later · exclude radiopaque foreign body, fracture · multiple views for all puncture wounds except knife wounds (TO)
Ultrasound Most accurate for wood / toothpick in plantar arch (abrupt density change) · non-radiopaque organic FB + abscess · detects wooden FB ≥ 5 mm (TO)
MRI Rule out osteomyelitis (1–2%) · obtain before operative I&D · osteomyelitis: low T1 / high T2 marrow · abscess + retained FB on post-contrast T1
Bone scan not indicated when imaging shows no osteomyelitis

Missed foreign bodies~40% missed on initial examination (TO)

5Management

Foot puncture wound
  • Acute (hours), no infection→tetanus + bedside I&D ± antipseudomonal cover
  • Soft-tissue infection only→oral amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Fails oral abx / through shoe sole→add ciprofloxacin
  • Delayed deep infection, abscess, FB, osteomyelitis→surgical debridement + IV abx
    • improving→convert to PO antibiotics

Prophylaxis & tetanus (TO)

Prophylactic antibioticscontroversial · not advised for all (TO) · no standard regimen; acute injury should cover Pseudomonas (Orthobullets)

Indications (TO)highly contaminated · presentation > 6 h · at-risk host (diabetes, immunosuppression)

Agents (TO)1st-generation oral cephalosporin · antistaphylococcal penicillin · fluoroquinolone · macrolide

Through the sole of a shoeantibiotic prophylaxis against Pseudomonas: oral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) ✓ (TO)

Tetanus boosterall puncture wounds with outdated or unknown immune status

Previous tetanus toxoid doses (TO) Clean, minor: TT vaccine Clean, minor: HTIG All other wounds: TT vaccine All other wounds: HTIG
< 3 or unknown Yes No Yes Yes
> 3 Yes if last dose > 10 yr No Yes if last dose > 5 yr No

Situation Antibiotic
Soft-tissue only (S. aureus, β-haemolytic strep) Amoxicillin-clavulanate = first line

Pseudomonas, child Ceftazidime or cefepime (no fluoroquinolones in children)

Freiberg's Disease

Foot & Ankle · 21 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology & diagnosis (2nd metatarsal head, female predominance)

Definitioninfarction (infraction) + fracture of the metatarsal head · osteochondrosis · = AVN / idiopathic osteonecrosis of MT head · rare

Sexfemale > male: ~4:1 (Orthobullets, OB) · 5:1 (OB) — read the options

Ageadolescents > adults: 13–18 yr (Orthobullets, OB) · 11–17 yr (OB) · female adolescent athletes
✗ Wrong options: 30s–40s

MT head involved Rate
2nd (most common), dorsal aspect 68%
3rd (second commonest) 27%
4th 3%
4th + 5th (lateral rays) Rare
1st Rarely / not typically — concurrent 1st involvement uncommon

Pathophysiology

Causedisrupted blood supply from repetitive microtrauma / stress overloading or idiopathic osteonecrosis → collapse of 2nd MT head · multifactorial: vascular compromise, genetic predisposition, altered biomechanics

Risk factorslong 2nd metatarsal · gastrocnemius contracture (OB)

Natural historydorsal articular collapse first, plantar surface preserved until late → degenerative arthritis of 2nd MTP in adulthood · early disease may resolve spontaneously with MT head remodelling

3Presentation

Symptomsforefoot pain, swelling, stiffness at 2nd MT head / base of 2nd toe, worse with WB · plantar or dorsal forefoot pain · difficulty with push-off · insidious, no trauma

Examperi-articular swelling · ↓ (passive) ROM of 2nd MTP · pain on passive motion of 2nd toe · pain worse with distraction (early) and compaction (late)

LabsESR + CRP normal → osteomyelitis unlikely

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
X-ray AP, lateral, oblique foot Early: usually normal → subchondral sclerosis → flattening of MT head (later, not an early finding) → joint destruction (late)
X-ray site Defect in upper (dorsal) half of articular surface
MRI Early disease (stage 1): subchondral fracture, patchy oedema in MT head · confirms plantar cartilage sparing

Smillie classification

Stage Finding Treatment if nonop fails
1 Subchondral fracture visible only on MRI Nonop
2 Dorsal collapse of articular surface on X-ray Debridement + MT osteotomy / DCWO
3 Collapse of dorsal MT head, plantar articular portion intact (± medial + lateral bony spurs) Debridement + MT osteotomy / DCWO
4 Collapse of entire MT head, joint-space narrowing DuVries partial head resection / interposition arthroplasty
5 Severe arthritis, joint-space obliteration DuVries / interposition arthroplasty

Differential diagnosis\

✗ Wrong options: distractors

✗ Option Why not
Morton neuroma Normal X-ray; pain at (3rd) web space, not MT head
Osteomyelitis Normal ESR / CRP
Mucous cyst DIP joints of hand, end-stage arthritis
Post-traumatic arthritis Isolated progressive 2nd MTP OA without trauma unlikely at 17
Synovial sarcoma Young adults; commonest sarcoma of foot but commonest around knee; soft-tissue calcification
Benign bone tumour / normal X-ray X-ray abnormal

5Management

Freiberg disease
  • All stages first→NSAIDs, activity change, boot / cast, MT pad
  • Failed nonop, early–mid (Smillie I–III, plantar cartilage spared)→DCWO ± debridement
  • Late (IV–V, no plantar cartilage)→DuVries partial head resection / interposition
    (avoid MTP fusion · polyvinyl implant)

Nonoperative care – metatarsal pad

Indicationearly stage · first line for all stages

Sequenceshort-leg walking cast or boot 4–6 wk (severe / orthotics fail) → stiff-soled shoe with MT bars or pads (after casting)

Metatarsal padoffloads 2nd MT head → relieves pain
✗ Wrong options: steroid · arthrotomy · shortening osteotomy · neck dorsiflexion osteotomy (before nonop fails)

12-yo, normal ESR / CRPosteochondrosis → boot immobilisation + observation
✗ Wrong options: osteomyelitis imaging · AVN → osteotomy / resection · tumour · "normal X-ray, reassure"

Steroid injection↑ intra-articular pressure → may worsen osteonecrosis · may help adults with secondary DJD · short-term relief only, doesn't stop collapse

Early surgerynot to prevent progression; no aggressive initial osteotomy

Surgery – debridement, dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy & contraindications

Indicationsprogressive pain, joint destruction, deformity after failed nonop

1Basics

Definitions

Gait cycleheel strike → heel strike of the same limb

Stance vs swing60% / 40% (Orthobullets, OB) · 62% / 38% (another OB) — read the options

Strideconsecutive initial contacts of the same (ipsilateral) foot

Stepinitial contacts of alternating (contralateral) feet

Stance phases (5)initial contact → loading response → mid-stance → terminal stance → pre-swing

Swing phases (3)initial swing → mid-swing → terminal swing

Phase (Rancho terms) Classic term Definition % cycle
Initial contact Heel strike Foot contacts ground 0–2%
Loading response (1st double support) Foot flat Initial contact → elevation of opposite limb; weight transferred to stance limb 0–10%
Mid-stance (single support) Midstance Opposite limb elevation → both ankles aligned in coronal plane 10–30%
Terminal stance (single support) Heel off Supporting heel rises → opposite heel contacts 30–50%
Pre-swing (2nd double support) Toe off Opposite initial contact → just before ipsilateral elevation 50–60%
Initial swing Acceleration Limb elevation → maximal knee flexion 60–73%
Mid-swing Midswing Knee flexion → tibia vertical 73–87%
Terminal swing Deceleration Tibia vertical → just before initial contact 87–100%

Prerequisites of gait – Gage (TO)

Five prerequisites (TO)stability in stance · adequate step length · clearance in swing · foot prepositioning (in swing) · conservation of energy

NOT prerequisites (TO)foot clearance in stance (clearance is a swing requirement) · adequate stride length (it is step length) (TO)

Tibialis anterior – eccentric at heel strike / loading response

TA eccentricheel strike (initial contact) + loading response → lowers foot to ground, controls plantar-flexion moment, limb loading + shock absorption

TA concentricinitial swing + mid-swing (→ terminal swing) → dorsiflexion for foot clearance, prepositions foot for contact

TA inactivemid-stance, terminal stance, pre-swing
✗ Wrong options: eccentric at any of these

Gastrocsoleusdormant at heel strike → eccentric at foot flat / mid-stance (weight moves forward over foot) → concentric at toe-off (push-off) → relaxed in swing
✗ Wrong options: GS eccentric at heel strike · GS concentric at heel strike · GS concentric in swing · TA concentric at toe-off

TA weakness (peroneal nerve palsy)mild–moderate → foot slap at heel strike · in swing → steppage gait (↑ hip + knee flexion to clear foot)

Primary antagonist of TAperoneus longus (PF + everts) → superficial peroneal nerve · TA dorsiflexes + inverts

Other antagonist pairperoneus brevis vs tibialis posterior

Strengthankle plantarflexors 6× stronger than dorsiflexors

Phase Active muscles
Initial contact Hip extensors stabilise hip · quadriceps eccentric · TA eccentric
Loading response TA eccentric (controls PF moment) · quads stabilise knee vs flexion moment
Mid-stance Gluteus medius + calf eccentric

Pre-swing Hip flexors propel advancing limb
Initial swing Hip flexors concentric advance the leg · TA concentric
Mid-swing Ankle dorsiflexors → foot clearance
Terminal swing Hamstrings decelerate thigh

Hallux Rigidus (MTP joint arthritis)

Foot & Ankle · 23 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest site of OA in the foot1st MTP (Orthobullets) · 2nd commonest great-toe pathology after hallux valgus (OB)

Incidence2.5% of > 50-yr-olds · F : M = 2 : 1 · peak 5th–6th decade

Risk factorstrauma to 1st MTP (~80% of unilateral cases; e.g. old turf toe) · high-impact sport

Causes of 1st MTP arthritis (OB)trauma, hallux valgus, elevated 1st metatarsal

Etiology & associations

Primary causeunknown · acute trauma + repetitive microtrauma predispose

Pathoanatomyosteophytes + cartilage loss start dorsally → whole joint later

Anatomic variantsmetatarsus adductus · MT head morphology · long 1st MT · hallux valgus / varus

Associatedsesamoid arthritis · gout · RA · seronegative arthropathies

Anatomy & biomechanics

1st MTshortest and widest

Medial branch of medial dorsal cutaneous nerveoverlies 1st MTP → irritated by dorsal osteophytes · plantar-medial hallucal nerve also supplies joint

Load1st MTP carries ~120% body weight each step

Runningneeds 60° dorsiflexion

2Mechanism

Checkrein deformity (TO)

Cause (TO)fracture of distal third of tibia → FHL adheres to fracture callus → bowstring to hallux insertion (TO)
✗ Wrong options: FHL tear · IP joint fracture · FHL tethering at 1st MTP

Sign (TO)ankle dorsiflexion → great toe flexes · ankle plantarflexion → hallux IP extends (TO)

3Presentation

Pain1st ray / 1st MTP · worse at push-off (toe-off / heel-rise) · swelling · gait abnormality · difficulty with shoes

Inspectiondorsal prominence (osteophyte) · shoe irritation + redness · severe → hyperextension deformity

Motion↓ dorsiflexion · pain at terminal dorsiflexion early → pain through whole arc as it progresses

Neurodorsomedial paraesthesia / ↓ sensation distal medial dorsal foot (medial dorsal cutaneous nerve, ± Tinel)

Grind test +severe disease, central chondral wear

Associations & sequelae (transfer metatarsalgia)

Hallux rigidus leads torestricted dorsiflexion → forefoot internal rotation → ↓ push-off strength → inverted gait → transfer metatarsalgia
✗ Wrong options: flexor hallucis longus (FHL) rupture · everted gait · ↑ push-off · Haglund deformity

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Weight-bearing AP, lateral, sesamoid, oblique Dorsal osteophytes · joint space narrowing · subchondral sclerosis + cysts
MRI Rarely needed · osteochondral lesion with normal X-ray · characterises mild OA

Radiographic progressionmay not correlate with symptoms

Coughlin & Shurnas classification

Grade Exam Dorsiflexion Radiograph X-ray
0 Stiffness, no pain 40–60° (10–20% lost) Normal —
1 Mild pain at extremes 30–40° (20–50% lost) Mild dorsal osteophyte, normal joint space
2 Moderate pain at extremes, more constant 10–30° (50–75% lost) Moderate osteophyte, < 50% JSN
3 Significant stiffness, near-constant pain at extremes, no mid-range pain ≤ 10° (75–100% lost) Severe osteophyte, > 50% JSN
4 As grade 3 + pain at mid-range As grade 3 As grade 3

Scenario → grade (OB)stiffness + ↓ push-off, no pain = 0 · dorsal osteophyte, no stiffness, pain at terminal DF = 1 · moderate pain at extremes + mild osteophyte + < 50% JSN = 2 · JSN + stiffness + pain at end-range = 3 · large osteophyte + stiffness + mid-range pain = 3 (OB) · severe JSN + pain throughout = 4

Other staging (OB)"Stage III = end-stage, cartilage lost from phalanx + metatarsal" · "Stage 4 = severe dorsal osteophyte + > 50% JSN" — read the stem

5Management

Hallux rigidus
  • Grade 0–1→NSAIDs, activity mod, injection, Morton's extension
  • Grade 1–2, pain only at terminal DF→dorsal cheilectomy
    • < 30–40° DF after cheilectomy / runner→+ Moberg
  • Grade 3–4, mid-range pain, + grind→MTP arthrodesis
  • Elderly, low demand→Keller resection arthroplasty
Failed 1st MTP arthroplasty
  • Silastic synovitis, great-toe pain only→implant removal + synovectomy
  • Infection → antibiotic spacer→staged arthrodesis
  • Loosening / bone loss / shortening + lesser metatarsalgia→removal + structural graft + arthrodesis

Operative criteria

Grade / situation Treatment
Grade 0 (motion loss, no X-ray change) Nonop · plantar release (OB)
Grade 0–1 Nonop (NSAIDs, injections, Morton's extension) · up to 55% succeed
Grade 1–2 · select grade 3 with pain only at terminal DF Dorsal cheilectomy (± synovectomy, debridement)
Cheilectomy gives < 30–40° DF · runner + Moberg dorsal closing wedge osteotomy
Grade 3–4 · mid-range pain · + grind · failed cheilectomy · grade 3 with < 50% MT head cartilage left MTP arthrodesis (gold standard)
Grade 3–4, wishes to keep motion Prosthetic / interpositional arthroplasty
Elderly, low demand, fast rehab Keller resection arthroplasty
Mild disease + intra-articular loose bodies Dorsal synovectomy + debridement

Morton's extensionstiff insert with rigid extension under 1st ray, past the 1st MTP → limits 1st MTP dorsiflexion at push-off · ↓ plantar loading across MTP · mainstay / first line for hallux rigidus
✗ Wrong options: hallux valgus · hallux varus · Morton's neuroma · spring ligament · 2nd MTP synovitis · Jones · hammer / mallet toe (high toe box) · midfoot arthritis · Freiberg

Ideal candidatepain at terminal DF only + shoe-wear irritation from dorsal prominence · grade 1–2 · no mid-range pain

Techniquedorsal approach · complete synovectomy · resect dorsal osteophyte + up to 30% dorsal MT head (Orthobullets) · 25% (OB) · > 30% → subluxation / instability

Goal70–90% of dorsiflexion intra-op (Orthobullets) · 70–90° DF (OB)

✗ Wrong options: observation · sesamoidectomy · Keller · fusion

✗ Wrong options: Lapidus · fusion · resurfacing · chevron

Mobergdorsal closing wedge osteotomy of proximal phalanx → ↑ DF by sacrificing plantarflexion arc · with cheilectomy: 88% satisfaction at 2 yr

Moberg indicationsrunners (need 60°) · cheilectomy gives < 30–40° DF (Orthobullets) · < 30° (OB) · failed cheilectomy

Runner, 30% resected, only 20° DFMoberg procedure
✗ Wrong options: close + WBAT · FDL → EDL · Keller (high demand) · fusion

Indicationsstandard of care / gold standard for grade 3–4 · commonest procedure · pain throughout MTP motion · failed cheilectomy · failed arthroplasty

"Best cheilectomy candidate?"dorsal osteophyte, no stiffness, pain at terminal DF

"Ballet dancer, stage 2?"cheilectomy, débridement ± Moberg

"+ grind, 20° painful arc — best long-term?"fusion in neutral rotation, 15° valgus, 10° dorsiflexion

"Pain at 2nd MTP + 2nd-toe deformity after fusion?"fused in shortened position

"Lateral foot pain + calluses after fusion?"fused in plantarflexion

"Sesamoid pain under 1st MT head after surgery?"5° valgus, 30° dorsiflexion arthrodesis

"Tennis player, stage 4?"arthrodesis

"Mid-range pain, 10° DF, eroded joint?"arthrodesis

"Failed cheilectomy — best pain relief + function?"1st MTP arthrodesis

"Positive grind, 10° DF, stage III?"1st MTP arthrodesis

Hallux Valgus

Foot & Ankle · 24 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Prevalence~23% of 18–65 y · up to 30% of females · women up to 15:1 · most common toe deformity (TO)

Formsadult vs juvenile / adolescent (see 5 Management)

Shoe-wearing societiesalmost exclusively with constricting footwear (OB) · still occurs in barefoot populations → footwear contributory, not sole cause (TO)

Genes & lab markers

Family history70% (Orthobullets) · 60–70% (TO) — strongest risk factor, autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance (TO)

COL5A1 mutationEhlers-Danlos → hallux valgus → MTP arthrodesis (OB)

Connective tissueEhlers-Danlos, Marfan (ligamentous laxity) (TO)

Risk factors

Type Factors
Intrinsic (TO) Genetic (strongest) · rounded (convex) 1st MT head (flat / chevron-shaped head resists subluxation) · metatarsus primus varus (↑ IMA, primary skeletal driver) · 1st metatarsal-cuneiform hypermobility · pes planus · ligamentous laxity · long 1st MT (Egyptian foot)
Intrinsic (Orthobullets) ↑ DMAA · 1st TMT instability · 2nd toe deformity / amputation · RA · CP · metatarsus adductus
Extrinsic Narrow toe box + high heel = most significant environmental factor (TO)
Systemic (TO) RA (synovitis destroys medial capsule + collaterals) · CP, poliomyelitis (muscle imbalance) · EDS, Marfan (laxity)
Not a risk factor Pes cavus (TO) · flexible cavovarus (OB)

Pes planusassociated with progression · elevation + functional lengthening of 1st MT
✗ Wrong options: cross-over toe · tarsal coalition · hammer toe · 1st MT supination

Progression predictorsDMAA + AP talo–1st MT angle at presentation (OB)

Pathoanatomy & deforming forces (pronation, adductor, abductor hallucis, conjoined tendon)

Cascadevalgus phalanx → varus 1st MT → MT head drifts medially → sesamoid complex laterally translated relative to MT head

Sesamoidssit in the two heads of FHB; attached to proximal phalanx base by sesamoid-phalangeal ligament / plantar plate

Sesamoids don't move (TO)anchored to 2nd MT by deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament → MT head migrates medially off them = apparent "sesamoid subluxation" (TO) · Orthobullets: sesamoids displace lateral to MT head — read the options

Medialcapsule + MCL stretched, attenuated (TO) · early lesion = failure of medial sesamoid ligaments + MCL (OB)

Lateral contracturelateral capsule + adductor hallucis + lateral head FHB → lateral bowstring (TO)

Adductor hallucisprimary deforming force · inserts fibular (lateral) sesamoid + lateral base proximal phalanx
✗ Wrong options: abductor hallucis · EHB · FHB (more plantar, contributes less) · FHL (not part of sesamoid complex, not primary)

Abductor hallucisinserts with medial FHB tendon into medial base proximal phalanx · migrates plantar + lateral → flexion and pronation
✗ Wrong options: ↑ abduction · extension · pronation alone

Conjoined tendonFHB + adductor hallucis at lateral base proximal phalanx · do not release → iatrogenic hallux varus · release adductor (transverse + oblique heads) adjacent to lateral sesamoid instead

EHL + FHLbowstring lateral to MTP axis → dynamic lateral deviators, perpetuate deformity (TO) · Orthobullets: FHL + adductor = plantar-plate muscles that become deforming forces

Plantar plate muscles (Orthobullets)abductor hallucis · FHB · FHL (deforming) · adductor hallucis (deforming)

Hallux positionvalgus + pronation · nail faces laterally (TO)
✗ Wrong options: valgus + supination · varus

1st MT rotation (TO)severe HV = pronation (internal rotation) of the first metatarsal → sesamoid displacement · 87% pronated on CT (OB)
✗ Wrong options: supination / external rotation · inversion of 1st ray · pure sagittal dorsiflexion

Triplanar deformity (OB)valgus + dorsiflexion + pronation of 1st ray → offloads 1st MT head → load to lesser MTs

Bunion (TO)medial eminence = normally covered medial MT head now uncovered · not an exostosis · adventitious bursa → painful bursitis · osteophytes later

Windlass mechanismless effective → transfer metatarsalgia

HV interphalangeus (TO)laterally angled distal articular surface of proximal phalanx · persists after MTP correction unless addressed

2nd toe (TO)crossover toe · 2nd MTP instability (plantar plate attenuation, dorsal subluxation) · hammer / claw · transfer metatarsalgia · lesser-toe crowding

Associatedhammer toe · callosities · pes planus · Marfan · EDS · metatarsus adductus

3Presentation

Historyslowly progressive deformity · pain with ambulation · difficulty with shoe wear (medial eminence)

Commonest complaintpain over the bunion (TO) · bursitis, callus over medial eminence

Lateral overload (TO)transfer metatarsalgia, stress fractures, callosities of lateral MTs · long-standing → MTP OA (TO)

Digital nerve compressionsymptoms possible

Examhallux valgus + pronated · 1st MTP ROM, crepitus, grind · 1st TMT hypermobility · callus · sesamoid pain · pes planus, lesser toes, midfoot / hindfoot

Flexible vs fixed (TO)flexible = toe passively pulled to normal → nonop · fixed = cannot → operative (TO)

Ligamentous laxityBeighton (thumb to forearm, knee hyperextension) + excessive passive PF / DF of 1st TMT → Lapidus

Transfer metatarsalgia signplantar focal tenderness and keratosis under the second metatarsal head, improves with metatarsal pad
✗ Wrong options: Mulder click → Morton neuroma · insertional Achilles · fixed equinus with negative Silfverskiöld · fixed hindfoot varus on Coleman block (cavus is not a HV risk)

DDxgout · hallux rigidus (stiff 1st MTP; gout, pseudogout, OA; mostly bilateral) (TO) · RA · turf toe · HV interphalangeus

Bunionette (tailor's bunion)

Site (TO)lateral side of 5th metatarsal
✗ Wrong options: medial 1st MT · lateral 1st MTP · medial 5th MTP

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Viewsweight-bearing AP, lateral, oblique · non-weight-bearing films underestimate deformity (TO) · axial sesamoid (skyline) view — sesamoid position (TO)

Measurement Definition Normal Use
HVA 1st MT axis vs proximal phalanx axis < 15° MTP deformity; > 15° diagnostic (TO)
IMA 1st vs 2nd MT axes < 9° (normal 9°, TO) MT deformity (metatarsus primus varus) → decides distal vs proximal
DMAA 1st MT axis vs line through base of distal articular cap < 15° (Orthobullets) · < 10° (OB) · < 6° (TO) — read the options MTP congruence (TO)
HVI proximal vs distal phalanx < 10° > 10° → Akin
Metatarsus adductus angle 2nd MT vs lesser tarsus axis (4th / 5th MT-cuboid reference) < 10° Predisposes; Sgarlato, Engel, Kilmartin methods

Measure of congruenceDistal Metatarsal Articular Angle (DMAA) (TO)
✗ Wrong options: talar–1st MT angle · IMA · HVA

Round sign (TO)rounded lateral MT head on AP = pronation of the first metatarsal (TO) · squared / flat lateral border = normal rotation (OB) · positive round sign → recurrence risk (OB)
✗ Wrong options: subchondral cyst · sesamoid obliteration · AVN

Sesamoid position (TO)Hardy & Clapham grades 1–7 or tibial sesamoid position · position 1 = fully covered · 7 = completely lateral · ≥ position 4 significant

1st MC joint instability (TO)joint-line obliquity, divergence of 1st / 2nd MT bases → Lapidus · plantar-flexion sag at 1st TMT (OB)

MTP arthritisnarrowing, dorsal osteophytes (hallux rigidus component), sclerosis, cysts → arthrodesis (TO)

Diagnostic criteria

Criterion Threshold
Diagnosis HVA > 15° (TO)
Surgery (symptomatic) IMA > 10° + HVA > 20° (Orthobullets, OB)
Severe (TO) HVA > 40° · IMA > 16° · HVI > 10° · DMAA up to 6° acceptable (TO)
Significant sesamoid subluxation ≥ position 4 (TO)

Congruent vs incongruent joint

Congruent Incongruent (subluxated)
Joint surfaces Parallel, matched; hallux deviates but no subluxation Proximal phalanx subluxed laterally on MT head
Cause Bony (↑ DMAA, articular tilt) Soft-tissue imbalance (tight lateral, lax medial)
DMAA ↑ (congruent HV needs ↑ DMAA) Usually low
Treatment Osteotomy correcting DMAA (biplanar chevron, Akin, double osteotomy) Lateral release + medial imbrication (modified McBride) ± osteotomy
Trap Lateral release in congruent joint → creates incongruency → OA (TO) Akin contraindicated

Severity grading — sources disagree

Grade TO Orthobullets OB explanations
Normal HVA < 15° · IMA < 9° HVA < 15° · IMA < 9° HVA < 15° · IMA < 9°
Mild HVA 15–20° · IMA < 13° (IMA grade 9–11°) HVA < 30° · IMA < 13° HVA < 25° (chevron < 25–30°) · IMA < 13°
Moderate HVA 20–40° · IMA 13–16° (IMA grade 11–16°) HVA 30–40° · IMA 13–20° · proximal if HVA > 25°, IMA > 13° IMA > 13° → proximal
Severe HVA > 40° · IMA > 16° HVA > 40° · IMA > 20° · double osteotomy HVA 41–50°, IMA 16–20° HVA > 40–41° · IMA > 15–16° (> 20°, Robinson)

Read the optionsIMA 13° = the commonest distal vs proximal divide · HVA cut-offs vary most

5Management

Symptomatic HV, failed shoe modification
  • MTP arthritis / RA / gout / neuromuscular / EDS→1st MTP ARTHRODESIS
  • 1st TMT hypermobility or TMT arthritis→LAPIDUS + modified McBride
  • IMA < 13° (mild)→DISTAL CHEVRON
    • DMAA > 10°→BIPLANAR CHEVRON
  • IMA > 13° (moderate–severe)→PROXIMAL / SCARF + modified McBride
    • + DMAA ↑ (congruent)→DOUBLE OSTEOTOMY
Joint congruence decides the HVA correction (TO)
  • Incongruent (soft tissue)→LATERAL RELEASE + MEDIAL IMBRICATION
    • IMA still ↑→ADD BASAL (PROXIMAL) OSTEOTOMY
  • Congruent (bony)→CORRECTIVE OSTEOTOMY (Akin / Chevron)
  • Low-demand elderly, degenerate→ARTHRODESIS or KELLER
Add-ons to any correction
  • HVI > 10°→AKIN
  • Elderly / very low demand→KELLER
  • Skin breakdown only→SIMPLE BUNIONECTOMY (medial eminence)

Nonoperative (TO)

Role (TO)first-line for all · definitive for mild symptoms, unfit, early deformity · does not correct deformity — relieves symptoms, slows progression

Footwear (TO)single most important · wide toe box, adequate depth · low heel < 2.5 cm (1 inch) · soft uppers · custom / extra-depth for severe

Pads + spacers (TO)bunion pads (silicone, felt, gel) · interdigital spacers · toe wedges / spacers worn 2–3 years (TO)

Orthoseshelp with pes planus or metatarsalgia (Orthobullets, TO) · Morton's extension limits MTP motion if hallux rigidus component (TO) · don't correct HV

Night splints (TO)temporary relief only · no evidence they alter natural history

Anti-inflammatory (TO)NSAIDs, ice · steroid into bursa short-term · repeated → skin atrophy + capsule weakening

Physio (TO)intrinsic strengthening (towel curls, marble picks) · gastrocnemius-soleus stretching (tight → ↑ forefoot load)

Surgery indicationpersistent symptoms despite shoe modification · never for cosmesis alone · choice by HVA, IMA, DMAA, congruency, arthritis, MC stability, age / demand (TO) · > 150 procedures described (TO) · > 130 (OB)
✗ Wrong options: asymptomatic contralateral bunion

Operative criteria

Situation Procedure
Juvenile / adolescent, open physis First cuneiform osteotomy
Hypermobile 1st MT / 1st TMT arthritis Lapidus
Recurrence + 1st TMT pain Lapidus
DJD of 1st MTP, gout, RA MTP arthrodesis
Down's, CP, EDS, neuromuscular MTP arthrodesis
Skin breakdown Simple bunionectomy (medial eminence removal)
HVI > 10° Akin
DMAA > 10° (Orthobullets, OB) · > 15° (OB) Biplanar chevron / distal medial closing wedge
IMA > 13° Proximal / shaft osteotomy
Severe + DMAA > 15° · juvenile DMAA > 20° Double osteotomy
Elderly / very low demand, severe Keller

General principles of correction (TO)

Lateral release (TO)essential except congruent deformity · dorsal 1st web space or medial transarticular · adductor from lateral sesamoid + lateral capsulotomy + lateral metatarsosesamoid ligament

Medial eminence resection (TO)flush with medial shaft · over-resection → hallux varus

Medial capsulorrhaphy (TO)plication of attenuated medial capsule

Sesamoid reduction (TO)sesamoids back under head in crista · persistent subluxation = inadequate lateral release or MT correction

Lapidus (first TMT arthrodesis) – hypermobility indications & modified McBride

Indications1st TMT hypermobility (laxity) · 1st tarsometatarsal arthritis · severe HV (HVA 41–50°, IMA 16–20°, OB · HVA > 40°, IMA > 15°, OB · IMA > 16°, TO · IMA > 20°, Robinson) · metatarsus primus varus · recurrence with TMT pain · concomitant pes planus · adolescent bunion (physis closed)

Not indicationsIMA 12° · HVA 40° alone · age > 50 · flexible cavovarus · MTP (not TMT) hypermobility · MTP arthritis (→ MTP fusion) · spastic CP (→ MTP fusion)

Contraindications (OB)open physis · already shortened 1st MT

Typical answersHVA 37, IMA 18 + TMT joint hypermobility in young patient · HVA 42, IMA 24 + TMT hypermobility · laxity + hypermobile TMT + flexible planus → tarsometatarsal joint arthrodesis with modified McBride · large IMA + TMT laxity → first tarsometatarsal (TMT) joint arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: MTP fusion · 1st + 2nd TMT (2nd not fused) · distal / proximal osteotomy (don't fix hypermobility)

✗ Wrong options: dorsiflexion unloading of the first metatarsal → lesser MT overload

Modified McBride componentsrelease of the adductor from the lateral sesamoid · lateral capsulotomy · medial capsular imbrication
✗ Wrong options: medial capsulotomy · lateral imbrication · resect base of proximal phalanx (Keller)

Nonunion~10% (Orthobullets, with MTP fusion) · up to 12% (OB) · 3–10% (TO) · 4% (OB) — read the options · ~33% symptomatic · NWB 6–8 wk historically (TO)

Recurrence – sesamoid reduction & IMA

Risk factors↑ preop IMA + ↑ preop HVA · rounded lateral 1st MT head (round sign = pronation) · residual increased tibial sesamoid displacement (lateral) · DMAA ↑ missed (> 10°) · inadequate IMA correction · no lateral release / adductor not released · no medial capsule closure · Akin alone for moderate–severe · juvenile · noncompliance with WB

Sesamoidsunreduced sesamoids → 10× odds of recurrence (OB) · reduction under head prevents recurrence of the hallux valgus deformity
✗ Wrong options: extensor strength · sagittal correction · supination · nonunion

✗ Wrong options: varus

Revision targetadductor hallucis (label D) left unreleased
