Bilateral caseright (squared head, tibial sesamoid reduced) recurred vs left (rounded, sesamoid overlapping lateral border) → increased preoperative 1-2 intermetatarsal angle on the right compared to the left
✗ Wrong options: head rotation · sesamoid alignment (those favour left recurrence) · medial eminence resection → varus

Persistent after isolated distal osteotomypronation of the first metatarsal · rotation best corrected by fusion / proximal osteotomy (OB)
✗ Wrong options: IMA · HVA · DMAA (distal osteotomy corrects these) · HVI 9° (normal)

Scarfdouble-chevron diaphyseal osteotomy · more stable than others

Iatrogenic hallux varus – causes (fibular sesamoid excision, over-release, medial eminence)

Causesfibular (lateral) sesamoid resection = commonest · excessive medial capsular reefing (+ adductor + lateral FHB detached) = second commonest · over-resection of medial eminence · overcorrection of IMA (< 9° normal) · excessive lateral release / conjoined tendon release · medial tibial sesamoid subluxation · excessive postoperative bandaging · MTP OA · AVN collapse into varus · malunion of distal osteotomy · original McBride

Mechanismfibular sesamoidectomy releases lateral FHB slip → unopposed medial FHB + abductor hallucis → medial rotation + translation · usually with supination
✗ Wrong options: under-corrected pronation

Not a causeresection of the tibial sesamoid (never resected in HV surgery; EXCEPT) · use of chevron / Akin per se · MTP arthritis (rarely varus) · complete medial sesamoidectomy · complete abductor release · excessive lateral capsulorrhaphy (it is medial capsulorrhaphy)

Medial eminence cutsaw blade placed too lateral (cut A) → over-resection → hallux varus
✗ Wrong options: recurrence · cock-up (FHL / Keller) · transfer metatarsalgia (shortening) · AVN

"Toe too straight"complete excision of medial eminence

Iatrogenic hallux varus
  • Early, flexible→TAPING into valgus
  • Flexible, no arthritis, failed taping→MEDIAL CAPSULAR LENGTHENING + SPLIT EHL TRANSFER
    (or reverse scarf / chevron / Akin, EHB transfer)
  • Rigid or MTP arthritis→DEFORMITY CORRECTION + 1st MTP FUSION

Flexible painless varusmedial capsular lengthening and split extensor hallucis longus tendon transfer
✗ Wrong options: MTP fusion (salvage) · lateral sesamoid excision (worsens) · lateral closing wedge phalanx osteotomy (misses MTP) · soft-tissue release alone

Varus + MTP arthritis, can't fit shoesdeformity correction and first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) fusion · standard fusion without structural graft
✗ Wrong options: cheilectomy · Keller · Moberg · Lapidus

Nerve injury – dorsomedial cutaneous nerve

Nervedorsomedial (medial dorsal) cutaneous nerve of the hallux (DMCN) = terminal branch of the superficial peroneal nerve · sensation dorsal + medial half of hallux · lies directly over medial eminence · commonest nerve injured (~3%)

Injurydorsal / dorsomedial approach · medial capsular imbrication / MT osteotomy → numbness or neuritic pain medial hallux, painful neuroma against shoe · prefer direct medial / mid-medial incision · transverse vein superficial + proximal to nerve (OB)

Coursemostly neuropraxia → resolves over months · recalcitrant → resect DMCN + bury in proximal 1st MT or medial cuneiform (OB)

✗ Distractor nerve Territory per explanations
Deep peroneal (medial branch) 1st web space, lateral hallux; extensors
Dorsolateral cutaneous "Branch of deep peroneal" (OB)
Saphenous Dorsomedial hindfoot · medial ankle · medial midfoot (OB, three wordings)
Medial plantar / plantar hallucal Plantar medial foot (tibial)
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous Mid-dorsum, doesn't reach medial hallux
Sural Lateral foot + ankle
Tibial Posterior to medial malleolus → medial + lateral plantar

Complications – osteonecrosis, dorsiflexion malunion, shortening & transfer metatarsalgia

AVN — classic linkdistal Chevron osteotomy (✗ Wrong options: proximal osteotomies) · collapse → osteonecrosis of the metatarsal head and MTP arthrodesis (✗ Wrong options: PTOA dx · intra-articular osteotomy · varus / recurrence)

AVN — blood supply conflictmedial capsulotomy = primary insult; distal osteotomy + lateral release do not ↑ risk (Orthobullets, OB) · laterally based head supply → chevron + extensive lateral release ↑ risk (OB) — read the options

AVN + shortening + lesser MT overloadmetatarsophalangeal joint fusion with an autologous bone block (restores length) · AVN with bone loss = only complication needing bone block arthrodesis (OB)
✗ Wrong options: revision Lapidus · Keller (worsens overload) · Moberg · allograft MT head (experimental)

Dorsiflexion malunionfirst metatarsal proximal crescentic osteotomy · inherently unstable · smooth pins / single screw · plate stronger (OB) · presents: loss of MTP dorsiflexion, transfer metatarsalgia ("marble" under 2nd–3rd MT heads)
✗ Wrong options: AVN (distal) · cock-up · varus · neuroma

Dorsiflexion malunion treatmentplantar flexion metatarsal osteotomy · plantarflexion malunion → revision osteotomy ± MTP fusion
✗ Wrong options: capsular release (bony block) · biplanar / double (DMAA) · phalanx osteotomy (HVI)

Transfer metatarsalgia — causes1st metatarsal shortening (aggressive resection in MTP fusion, modified Lapidus procedure done incorrectly, chevron) · dorsiflexion malunion · residual pronation · functional load transfer from altered forefoot biomechanics after modified Lapidus · MTP fusion in plantarflexion (5° PF relative to floor) · long 2nd MT · equinus

✗ Transfer metatarsalgia trapsCotton osteotomy (plantarflexion medial cuneiform for forefoot varus) · Akin · lateral sesamoidectomy (→ varus) · modified McBride (no shortening) · Morton's neuroma (Mulder click, paraesthesia) · Freiberg (2nd MT head AVN, visible on X-ray) · 1st MT nonunion · recurrence · pseudoarthrosis · TMT instability · cock-up toe

Preventionminimal bone resection at 1st MT base · avoid shortening · fuse MTP in correct position

First MTbears half the forefoot weight (OB)

Weil osteotomy technique

Indication2nd MTP metatarsalgia / long 2nd MT (e.g. after MTP fusion) → second metatarsal osteotomy (Weil) with extensor tendon and dorsal capsular release
✗ Wrong options: 2nd MTP fusion · Girdlestone-Taylor · Helal (shaft, ↑ nonunion) · head resection

Weilintra-articular MT head osteotomy · longitudinal decompression by shortening

Saw cutparallel with the plantar surface of the foot → minimises plantar displacement of capital fragment · remove wafer / thicker blade also ↓ plantar shift
✗ Wrong options: perpendicular to shaft · parallel to MT inclination · 45° · 10°

Sesamoid excision – FHB preservation

Medial (tibial) sesamoidectomypreserve / repair flexor hallucis brevis tendon → prevents hallux valgus
✗ Wrong options: FHL · abductor · adductor · EHB

Complications of medial sesamoidectomystiffness · claw toe · hallux valgus · (lateral sesamoidectomy → hallux varus)

Prognosis

Recoveryreturn to work 6–12 wk · improvement up to 1 yr · patient-reported outcome not tied to degree of correction (OB)

Hallux Varus

Foot & Ankle · 25 / 48

1Basics

Definitionmedial deviation of the hallux relative to 1st metatarsal · most often iatrogenic overcorrection after bunion surgery

Incidence2–14% after hallux valgus surgery · more common in women

Three componentsmedial deviation of hallux at 1st MTP · supination of phalanx · claw-toe deformity

Causes – excessive lateral release & over-correction

Cause Examples
Congenital Metatarsal physeal bracket
Iatrogenic (commonest) Overcorrection at bunion surgery
Trauma —
Inflammatory RA, ankylosing spondylitis
Neurological CMT, post-polio

Iatrogenic pathoanatomyexcessive lateral soft-tissue / capsular release · fibular (lateral) sesamoid excision · excessive medial eminence resection · overplication of medial capsule · overcorrection of IMA (e.g. excessively large proximal medial opening-wedge osteotomy) or of hallux valgus interphalangeus · loss of osseous support · malaligned osteotomy, soft-tissue laxity

Medial releaselisted as a contributor (OB7610) · not excessive medial capsular release (OB220893 — lateral release + medial overplication cause it) — read the options

Not causestibial sesamoidectomy · inadequate medial eminence resection · 1st TMT hypermobility · inadequate IMA correction · failed pin fixation · choosing soft-tissue procedure over fusion

After fibular sesamoid resection (TO)unopposed pull of abductor hallucis → medial dislocation of tibial sesamoid → medial hallux translation · also MTP joint hyperextension + buttonholing of metatarsal head (TO)
✗ Wrong options: adductor hallucis

3Presentation

Complaintappearance (toe "too straight" → excessive medial deviation) · difficulty wearing shoes · often asymptomatic

Painsuggests joint arthritis or trauma · ↓ ROM, instability, weak push-off

Examvarus angulation · dorsal contracture of MTP ± IP contracture · EHL displaced medially → "bowstring" · tibial sesamoid displaced medially · medial blister · fixed vs flexible (passively correctable) decides treatment

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

View / finding Detail
WB AP + lateral foot Standard · + NWB oblique + sesamoid axial
Hallux valgus angle < 0° (normal 5–15°) · e.g. HVA −19°
IMA Reduced (overcorrected; e.g. 6°)
Medial eminence Excessively resected
Sesamoids Tibial sesamoid subluxed medially · lateral (fibular) sesamoid absent
Osteotomy Overcorrected
Joints Degenerative change at MTP / IP → fusion
CT / MRI Rarely needed · osteonecrosis of 1st metatarsal

5Management

Hallux varus
  • Early post-op (first weeks)→taping / splinting up to 3 months
  • Flexible, asymptomatic / mild→wide toe box, padding
  • Flexible (passively correctable), young→tendon transfer + medial release
    • bony overcorrection→lateral closing-wedge osteotomy
  • Fixed, arthritic, painful, or elderly→1st MTP arthrodesis

Treatment – reducible vs fixed deformity (tendon transfer vs MTP fusion)

Taping / splintingearly post-op varus; may correct if started within first weeks; continue up to 3 months / until soft tissues heal · not for fixed deformity

Shoe modificationwider, flexible toe box + padding · flexible, longstanding, asymptomatic · not for chronic fixed + arthritic · established varus → nonop role limited

Lateral closing-wedge osteotomyovercorrected proximal / distal MT or proximal phalangeal osteotomy · ± scar release + lateral ligament repair · not when MTP degenerative

Tendon procedure (flexible deformity) Detail
Adductor hallucis reattachment + medial release Difficult after McBride
Abductor hallucis transfer → lateral base of proximal phalanx + reattach / reef conjoined tendon in web space
EHL or EHB transfer + medial release ± IP fusion Under transverse intermetatarsal ligament → distal MT neck (lateral → medial) · split EHL + MT osteotomy + medial capsule release for young, passively correctable

Operative criteria

1st MTP arthrodesis Indication
Absolute Fixed (not passively correctable) MTP with significant deformity + non-functioning hallux · painful MTP arthritis
Relative Medial eminence resected beyond tibial sesamoid sulcus
Age Elderly — 72-yo, moderately reducible, painful → fusion (soft tissue not indicated for age)

Fusion givesmost predictable pain relief, alignment, activity, shoe fit, no recurrence

✗ Alternative Why not
MTP replacement / hemiarthroplasty Unpredictable; radiolucency, subsidence, high failure (hallux rigidus)
Keller resection arthroplasty Unpredictable pain relief, activity, recurrence
Interposition arthroplasty No realignment
Lateral MT opening-wedge osteotomy Doesn't correct arthritic, incongruent MTP
1st MT–cuneiform (Lapidus) fusion Salvage for failed hallux valgus, not varus
Cheilectomy + medial release / soft tissue alone Won't correct fixed deformity
Great-toe amputation Unreasonable in healthy patient

X vs Y

Flexible (passively correctable) Fixed / arthritic
Patient Young Elderly or degenerative MTP
Surgery Tendon transfer + medial release ± osteotomy 1st MTP arthrodesis
Splint / tape Useful early No

"Progressive varus 2 yr after bunion surgery — factor?"excessive lateral soft-tissue release

"HVA −19°, IMA 6° after bunionectomy — error?"excessively large proximal metatarsal medial opening-wedge osteotomy

"Rigid varus, pain mid-range, 70-yo?"hallux metatarsophalangeal joint fusion

"Not completely reducible, failed taping — predictable alignment + pain relief?"MTP joint arthrodesis

"72-yo, moderately reducible, painful — most predictable?"first MTP fusion

"Fixed varus + DJD after fibular sesamoidectomy?"first MTP arthrodesis

Hammer Toe

Foot & Ankle · 26 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest lesser-toe deformityhammer toe · older / middle-aged women · 2nd toe usually

Associatedpainful corn on dorsal PIP · secondary to hallux valgus or curly toe · neurogenic, degenerative, metabolic causes

Plantar plate attenuation – MTP deformity

Pathoanatomyplantar plate injury · overpull of EDL · intrinsic imbalance / weakness

Plantar plate rupture → hammer toeMT head no longer suspended → translates plantarly → MTP extension → EDL overpull → PIP flexion to keep toe plantigrade
✗ Wrong options: mallet toe · TMT arthritis · Freiberg · hallux valgus (not the direct result)

Plantar plate attenuation causesMTP joint extension
✗ Wrong options: DIP flexion · PIP extension · MTP / DIP malrotation

Plantar 2nd MTP pain"stepping on a pebble" · worse in high heels · MRI = degenerative plantar plate tear

3Presentation

Symptomsdorsal PIP pain with shoe wear · deformity · plantar 2nd MTP pain

ExamPIP flexion + DIP extension (+ slight MTP extension)

Ankle plantarflexion testflexible deformity corrects · fixed / rigid does not correct

Push-up testdorsal pressure under the MT head → flexible deformity reduces (removes extrinsic overpull)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical: rigid or flexible lesser toe with PIP flexion, DIP extension, slight MTP extension

Key radiology findings

Imagingnot required for diagnosis or treatment

Claw toe vs hammer toe vs mallet toe

Joint Claw toe Hammer toe Mallet toe
DIP Flexion Extension Flexion
PIP Flexion Flexion Normal
MTP Hyperextension Slight extension Normal
Cause — EDL overpull + intrinsic weakness FDL overpull / contracture or EDL rupture
Callus — Dorsal PIP Toe pulp (ulcers / calluses)

5Management

Hammer toe
  • Pain / dorsal PIP corn→high toe box, foam / silicone sleeves, dorsal PIP padding
  • Flexible, failed nonop → FDL→EDL transfer
  • Rigid, failed nonop→PIP resection arthroplasty (± arthrodesis)
  • MTP involved → Girdlestone (FDL→EDL)
    • Mild MTP hyperextension→EDL Z-lengthening / tenotomy
    • Moderate–severe→EDL Z-lengthening + dorsal capsular release

Operative criteria

Situation Procedure
Flexible, failed nonop FDL → EDL tendon transfer
Rigid / fixed, failed nonop PIP resection arthroplasty ± tenotomy / transfers · or PIP arthrodesis
MTP involvement Girdlestone (FDL → EDL) — as for claw toe
Mild MTP hyperextension EDL Z-lengthening or tenotomy
Moderate–severe MTP hyperextension EDL Z-lengthening + dorsal capsular release
2nd hammer toe + hallux valgus Correct hallux valgus (arthrodesis if severe) · amputation if HV touches 3rd toe in elderly / poor health / declines reconstruction

Surgery indicated forprogressive deformity · fixed contractures · dorsal toe ulceration

Flexible vs rigid deformity – padding & PIP resection arthroplasty

Fixed deformityprecludes success with soft-tissue procedures alone → indication for PIP resection arthroplasty
✗ Wrong options: pain with shoes · all lesser toes involved · no MTP deformity · no hallux valgus

Rigid 2nd hammer toe sequencedorsal PIP padding → shoe modification → PIP resection arthroplasty
✗ Wrong options: plantar padding (pain is dorsal) · MTP capsular release · MT head excision

Extensor tenotomy / lengtheningwith (not before) resection arthroplasty in severe cases → for MTP dorsiflexion contracture
✗ Wrong options: tenotomy preceding arthroplasty

Rigid hammer toe, failed nonopPIP resection arthroplasty with K-wire fixation
✗ Wrong options: Weil osteotomy (irreducible MTP subluxation / transfer metatarsalgia) · FDL transfer (flexible) · EDL lengthening (claw toe) · DIP fusion (rigid mallet toe)

Resection arthroplasty techniqueresect head + neck (distal condyle) of proximal phalanx (± middle phalanx articular surface) → fibrous joint or arthrodesis (true fusion not necessary) · K-wire 2–3 wk · then tape PIP in extension 3 wk

PIP arthrodesisoption for rigid deformity · high nonunion rate · K-wire = most cost-effective implant

GirdlestoneEDL Z-plasty lengthening · MTP capsule release · ± oblique MT shortening osteotomy · FDL → EDL transfer

X vs Y

Flexible hammer toe Rigid hammer toe
Ankle PF / push-up test Corrects Does not correct
Surgery FDL → EDL transfer PIP resection arthroplasty / arthrodesis
Procedure Treats
FDL transfer Flexible hammer toe
PIP resection arthroplasty Rigid hammer toe
EDL lengthening Claw toe / MTP hyperextension
DIP fusion Rigid mallet toe
Weil osteotomy Irreducible MTP subluxation · transfer metatarsalgia

"Commonest lesser-toe deformity?"hammer toe (2nd toe)

High Ankle Sprain & Syndesmosis Injury

Foot & Ankle · 27 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence0.5% of ankle sprains without fracture · 13% of all ankle fractures

Associated injuriesOCD 15–25% · peroneal tendon injury up to 25% · deltoid ligament · loose bodies · fractures: Weber C, Weber B, 5th MT base, anterior process calcaneus, lateral / posterior process talus

Anatomy – distal tibiofibular syndesmosis

Ligament Origin → insertion Key fact
AITFL Chaput tubercle (anterolateral tibia) → Wagstaffe tubercle (anterior fibula) Injured in isolated high ankle sprain
PITFL Volkmann tubercle (posterior tibia) → posterior lateral malleolus Strongest component
Interosseous ligament (IOL) Distal continuation of IOM Main restraint to proximal migration of talus
Interosseous membrane (IOM) — Disrupted → synostosis risk
Inferior transverse ligament (ITL) — —

Not syndesmosisATFL (anteroinferior fibula → talar neck) · CFL, PTFL (lateral complex) · bifurcate (Chopart) ligament (subtalar + midtarsal) · IPR (peroneal tendons)

Fibular incisura morphologycrescentic commonest (61.3%) · trapezoid · chevron · widow's peak · flat least (3.1%)

Biomechanics

Functionmaintains tibia–fibula integrity · resists axial, rotational, translational forces · widens 1 mm in normal gait

Ankle position Talus in mortise Distal fibula
Dorsiflexion Wider anterior talus engages External rotation + proximal, posterolateral translation
Plantarflexion Narrow posterior talus Internal rotation + distal, anteromedial translation

Inversion / eversionmainly subtalar → little effect on fibular rotation · supination (PF + inversion + adduction) → fibular IR

Deltoidindirectly stabilises medial mortise · superficial = restrains eversion · deep = prevents excessive ER

Sectioned (Massri-Pugin, cadaver) Result
Isolated AITFL or PITFL No significant instability
AITFL + PITFL + IOL Diastasis posterior incisura only
All syndesmotic + deltoid Diastasis anterior + posterior incisura

Instabilityneeds rupture of ≥ 2 ligaments (Rammelt) · instability ↑ immensely once deltoid also cut (Zalavras)

2Mechanism

Commonestexternal rotation of foot (or foot planted, body internally rotates) → talus rotates laterally, pushes fibula away from tibia

Consequences↑ tibial compressive stress · lateral fibular subluxation · mortise incongruence

Eversion injurymedial + lateral pain, positive calf squeeze

3Presentation

Symptomsanterolateral ankle pain proximal to AITFL · ± medial tenderness / swelling · difficulty bearing weight (lateral sprains usually can WB)

Cluenagging pain with dynamic moves, relieved by tight circumferential wrap above ankle → AITFL (wrap holds fibula in incisura)

Syndesmosis tendernesssingle best predictor of return to play

Test Technique Positive
Squeeze (Hopkin) Compress tibia + fibula at midcalf Pain at syndesmosis
External rotation stress Knee + hip 90°, ankle neutral; ER / dorsiflex foot Pain / widening
Cotton (lateral stress) Lateral pull on fibula Syndesmosis widening
Fibular translation AP drawer on fibula, tibia fixed ↑ translation + pain · most false positives (Beumer)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis – examination, stress radiographs & MRI; Maisonneuve

ViewsAP, lateral, mortise ankle + AP, lateral entire tibia / fibula (proximal fibula fracture = Maisonneuve)

Optionalexternal rotation stress view · gravity stress view (deltoid competence) · contralateral ankle (widening vs normal variant)

Persisting WB pain 2 wk after "sprain"ankle stress radiographs + ipsilateral tibia-fibula radiographs (bilateral comparison)
✗ Wrong options: boot WBAT · NWB boot without further films · MRI first · tib-fib films alone

Fibular fracture + syndesmotic injuryORIF fibula, then assess syndesmosis (repair may stabilise; most still need fixation)

Key radiology findings

Measurement Normal Injury
Tibiofibular overlap > 6 mm AP · > 1 mm mortise · > 10 mm AP (Orthobullets ligament note) ↓
Tibiofibular clear space < 6 mm AP + mortise · < 5 mm (Orthobullets ligament note) ↑
Medial clear space ≤ 4 mm (best on mortise) ↑ · good specificity, very poor sensitivity
Lateral tibiofibular ratio APTF ratio avg 0.94; anterior fibular cortex crosses middle of tibial shadow Most reliable plain-film measure of reduction

AP measurementslimited sensitivity, poor reliability · cannot reliably predict injury (Krähenbühl)

Study Use
CT Suspicion with normal X-rays · more sensitive than X-ray for minor injury · post-op check of reduction · Wagstaffe tubercle (AITFL insertion) on axial
MRI Suspicion with normal X-rays · > 90% sensitivity / specificity (Han) · ~100% (Krähenbühl) — diagnostic tool of choice
Lambda sign (coronal MRI) Hyperintense signal contiguous between mortise and tibiofibular articulation (OB) · > 2 mm diastasis on coronal (TO) · "highly sensitive + specific" (Orthobullets) · not an independent predictor, sensitive + specific with positive exam (Ryan)
Deltoid discontinuity on MRI Poor indicator — no deltoid ruptures in Han's 8 syndesmotic injuries

5Management

Syndesmotic injury
  • No diastasis, stable ankle→NWB CAM boot / cast 2–3 wk
  • Unstable on stress views / refractory sprain→syndesmotic fixation
  • Fracture + syndesmosis→fix fracture, then stress test
    • stable→no syndesmotic fixation
    • unstable→screw or suture button

Operative criteria

Nonoperative Operative (screw or suture button)
Sprain without diastasis or ankle instability Sprain (no fracture) unstable on stress radiographs
— Sprain refractory to conservative treatment
— Fracture still unstable after fracture fixation

Nonopdelayed WB until pain-free · PT in brace limiting ER · recovery notoriously prolonged + variable, up to 2× standard sprain

Intraoperative assessment & reduction

Best intra-op testexternal rotation stress test: fewest false positives, smallest inter-observer variance
✗ Wrong options: squeeze · fibular translation · Cotton · anterior drawer

Cotton testpreviously reported least false positives · produces greater tibiofibular clear space widening than ER test in Weber C (Stoffel) · ER stress gives 35% more medial clear space widening (Matuszewski) — read the options

Dorsiflexionexternally rotates fibula (wide anterior talus) · aids rotational reduction · maximal dorsiflexion before screw not required (Tornetta: PF fixation did not limit DF)

Clamplateral malleolar ridge of fibula → centre of AP width of tibia = most accurate reduction (Gardner)

Goalrestore fibular length, rotation, position in incisura · outcome depends on reduction, not fixation type

Persistent talar tilt after suture buttondeltoid incompetent
✗ Wrong options: interosseous (addressed by button) · bifurcate · CFL · PTFL

Reconstruction orderproximal → distal: IOL + AITFL first → repair deltoid if medial talar tilt persists (Wake)

AITFL repairrestores mortise stability · syndesmotic fixation unnecessary once repaired · reconstruct with 4th EDL autograft or suture (Nelson)

Fixation – screw vs suture button

Screw techniquetwo 3.5 or 4.5 mm screws · 3 or 4 cortices · 2–5 cm above plafond (Orthobullets) · 2–3 cm, parallel to joint, angled 30° anterior (TO) — read the options · NWB 6–12 wk

No differencestainless steel vs titanium · 3 vs 4 cortices (pullout) · bioabsorbable similar · two screws preferable

Syndesmotic screw Suture button (TightRope)
Malreduction Higher — up to 40% (39% vs 15%, Sanders RCT) Lower
Reoperation / implant removal 30% — often requires removal 4% — no removal needed
Function Same Same · early results: earlier return to activity
Mechanics Medial + anterior talar translation Closer to native
Zone 2 fibular screws ↑ malreduction —

6Complications

Complication Fact
Malreduction Commoner than believed · up to 40% with screws
Missed injury End-stage ankle arthritis
Chronic instability Inadequate reduction → instability + post-traumatic arthritis
Tibiofibular synostosis ~10% after Weber C (Orthobullets) · 15 / 230 operative ankle fractures, mostly Weber C (Albers)

Post-injury synostosis / heterotopic ossification

Causehigh ankle sprain with IOM disruption · prior tibial stress fracture (Henry) · Weber C fixation

TimingHO develops within 6–12 months

Presentationactivity-related leg / anterior shin pain for 1–2 yr · loss of ankle dorsiflexion + tib-fib motion · often asymptomatic; most return to sport

Treatmentsymptomatic first · surgical excision (anterolateral approach) only for persistent pain despite nonop + no uptake ("cold") on bone scan

Next step, synostosis with ongoing uptakeobservation + repeat bone scan → resect when no uptake

✗ Synostosis trapsindomethacin 25 mg TID 6 wk + 700 cGy = HO prophylaxis after acetabular surgery · 60 Gy (sarcoma / myeloma; wounds won't heal) · chemotherapy (only with biopsy-proven neoplasm) · excise when "hot" · instability or ↓ plantarflexion as indication

X vs Y

High ankle sprain Low (lateral) ankle sprain
Ligaments AITFL, PITFL, IOL, IOM, ITL ATFL, CFL, PTFL
Mechanism External rotation Inversion
Weight bearing Difficult Usually possible
Test Squeeze, ER stress Anterior drawer
Recovery ≈ 2× longer Shorter
ER stress test Cotton test
Manoeuvre ER foot, tibia stabilised Lateral pull on fibula
Intra-op Fewest false positives, least variance (recent) Least false positives (older) · more clear-space widening in Weber C

How it's asked

"CT arrow at Wagstaffe tubercle — structure + next step?"anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL); ORIF of the fibula with subsequent syndesmotic assessment

"Foot planted, body turned, better with a tight wrap above ankle — injured?"AITFL

"Sprain, WB pain at 2 wk, ?MCS widening — next?"ankle stress radiographs and ipsilateral tibia-fibula radiographs

"Most sensitive + specific imaging finding?"coronal MRI hyperintense signal contiguous between mortise and tibiofibular articulation (lambda sign)

"Intra-op test with fewest false positives?"external rotation stress test

"Manoeuvre that externally rotates the fibula?"ankle dorsiflexion

"Most reliable X-ray measure of syndesmotic reduction?"lateral tibiofibular ratio (measurements 4/5)

"Persistent talar tilt after suture button?"deltoid

"True of syndesmotic screws?"higher rate of malreduction with screw fixation versus flexible fixation

"Syndesmotic synostosis, pain, uptake on bone scan — next?"observation and repeat bone scan, then surgical resection if no increased uptake

"Indication + timing for synostosis excision?"persistent pain despite non-operative treatment and no uptake on bone scan

"Single best predictor of return to play?"syndesmosis tenderness

Interdigital (Morton's) Neuroma

Foot & Ankle · 28 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Demographicsmiddle-aged women · F:M 9:1 (Orthobullets) · peak 6th decade (OB)

Commonest site3rd web space (3rd + 4th interdigital nerves, between 3rd + 4th MT heads) · 2nd web space = second commonest
✗ Wrong options: 1st web space · 1st MTPJ (hallux rigidus / valgus) · 5th MT head

Other OB wording"2nd or 3rd web space" / "2nd and 3rd interdigital nerves" — read the options

Anatomy & pathophysiology

Interdigital nerveplantar to the transverse (deep) intermetatarsal ligament between MT heads
✗ Wrong options: dorsal to it

3rd web spaceconfluence of medial + lateral plantar nerves (lateral branch MPN + medial branch LPN share a common perineurium)
✗ Wrong options: anterior tarsal tunnel (deep peroneal nerve)

Naturecompressive (entrapment) neuropathy → perineural fibrosis + entrapment of the interdigital nerve

Mechanismcompression / tension around transverse intermetatarsal ligament at toe-off · repetitive microtrauma · traction from tethering between fixed medial + mobile lateral MTs

Aggravatorshigh heels, narrow toe box, wide feet

3Presentation

Diagnosis & location (third web space, Mulder's click)

Painplantar forefoot, between MT heads · worse with weight-bearing + narrow toe-box shoes · relieved by removing shoes + massaging foot · "walking on a marble"

Paraesthesiaburning / tingling into adjacent toes (3rd + 4th toes for 3rd web space) · plantar aspect of web space

Most consistent signtenderness of involved web space · positive web-space compression test · neuroma may be palpable

Mulder's clicksqueeze forefoot (MTs together) + dorsal pressure between MT heads → painful / bursal click

Drawer test at MTPJassesses MTPJ instability (differential)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical (history + exam); advanced imaging generally not required

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
WB AP / lateral / oblique X-ray Usually normal · may show bony deformity · excludes Freiberg (MT head flattening), MTP arthritis
Ultrasound Non-palpable neuroma with clear clinical picture · oval / well-circumscribed hypoechoic mass parallel to MTs · operator dependent
MRI Not required (✗ Wrong options: "needed to confirm") · rules out other pathology / stress fracture when exam non-diagnostic

Diagnostic criteria

Test Positive result
Common digital nerve block (diagnostic lidocaine) Confirms diagnosis → numbness of lateral toe surface + relief of pain
No relief after well-placed block Think MTP synovitis
Histology Perineural fibrosis + nerve entrapment, no fibrinoid necrosis

Differential – rheumatoid nodule & histology

Lesion Histology
Morton's neuroma Perineural fibrosis, entrapped interdigital nerve, no fibrinoid necrosis
Rheumatoid nodule Subcutaneous · central fibrinoid necrosis + palisading fibrous cells
Neurofibroma Hypocellular fibroblastic network, wire-like collagen, myxoid areas
Schwannoma (benign PNST) Encapsulated · Antoni A (palisading spindle cells) + Antoni B (hypocellular mucinous)
Plantar fibromatosis From plantar fascia · dense mature collagen + fibrocytes · not provoked by squeeze

Other differentialsMTP synovitis, metatarsalgia, stress fracture, MTPJ arthritis, MT head osteonecrosis (Freiberg), neoplasm, lumbar radiculopathy
✗ Wrong options: anterior tarsal tunnel (deep peroneal nerve) · tarsal tunnel

5Management

Morton's neuroma
  • First line→wide toe-box shoe + firm sole + metatarsal pad
    (± short-term steroid injection, dorsal)
  • Failed nonop→dorsal neurectomy + DTML release, bury stump
  • Recurrent / stump neuroma→revision neurectomy (plantar or dorsal) + burial

Nonoperative

First lineflat shoe with wide toe box + firm sole + metatarsal pad
✗ Wrong options: MRI · PT (limited role) · serial steroid injections · custom orthotics before shoe change

Metatarsal padoffloads MT heads by ↑ intermetatarsal space → ↓ nerve pressure

Resultsunpredictable · ~20% complete resolution (Orthobullets) · roughly half eventually need surgery (OB) · "most" need surgery (another OB) — read the options · NSAIDs rarely help

Corticosteroid injectionshort-term relief only, no long-term relief · usually dorsal · steroid + LA not superior to LA alone · ~50% still request excision · serial injections → local tissue (fat-pad) atrophy

Alcohol sclerosing injectionnot recommended (no long-term data, risk to surrounding tissue)

(✗ Wrong options: Wrong orthoses — Morton extension = hallux rigidus) · longitudinal arch support = PTT tendinitis · carbon-fibre insert = midfoot arthritis · AFO = peroneal palsy / foot drop
✗ Wrong options: "orthotics with ↑ arch height first line"

Treatment – injection & surgical excision (dorsal vs plantar)

Failed nonopneurectomy (most effective, most durable) · dorsal approach most common
✗ Wrong options: repeat steroid · isolated DTML release (less effective) · distal oblique shortening osteotomy / MTP capsular release + extensor lengthening (these are for MTP synovitis)

Percutaneous nerve ablationnot used

Dorsal neurectomy step Detail
Incision 3–4 cm just proximal to web space
Dissection Blunt → protect superficial peroneal nerve branches (✗ Wrong options: deep peroneal)
Exposure Spread MTs → tension + transect transverse intermetatarsal ligament (✗ Wrong options: "reduces success")
Resection Identify nerve proximal + distal to bifurcation → resect ≥ 3 cm proximal to ligament
Burial Bury proximal stump in intrinsic muscles
Closure Repair DTML → prevents intermetatarsal instability

Dual neuromas (2nd + 3rd web spaces)resect 2nd web space + neurolysis (DTML release) of 3rd → equal relief, protects digital arteries to 3rd + 4th toes
✗ Wrong options: resect both via two dorsal incisions (highest arterial risk) · leave 3rd untreated · FDL transfer · single plantar incision

6Complications

Complications of neurectomy

Complication Fact
Stump neuroma – inadequate resection Commonest cause of persistent / recurrent pain
Inadequate retraction (traction neuritis) Plantar branches tether nerve → no retraction (✗ Wrong options: commonest)
Painful plantar scar ~5%, with plantar incision
Intermetatarsal instability DTML not repaired
Wrong structure resected Digital artery / neurovascular bundle or lumbrical
Toe ischaemia Digital artery injury in dual web-space surgery

Recurrent neuroma – inadequate proximal resection & revision

Causeinadequate proximal resection → residual plantar-directed nerve branches tether nerve to plantar skin → no retraction out of WB zone of MT head
✗ Wrong options: painful scar · infection · Freiberg · MTP arthritis · tarsal tunnel · MTP synovitis

Presentationsame symptoms as primary + Tinel's sign at prior resection site

Resection level≥ 3 cm proximal to DTML (Orthobullets, OB) · plantar branches absent 4 cm proximal → cut there (another OB) — read the options · "5 mm proximal" = inadequate

Revisionrevision neurectomy through plantar OR dorsal approach + nerve burial
✗ Wrong options: steroid + PT · fishmouth web-space incision (poor view, wound problems) · lumbrical transection → MTP extension deformity · dual incisions

Plantar approach in revisionpreferred by most after a dorsal primary → avoids scar, direct view of nerve bifurcation, easier proximal dissection, DTML seen directly

Dorsal approach in revisionadvantage = lower risk of plantar scar tenderness + wound complications · earlier weight-bearing but recurrence not lower · needs DTML release · harder proximal dissection

Revision outcomesfunction similar · no society recommendation favouring either

X vs Y

Dorsal approach Plantar approach
Use Most common primary Preferred for revision
Complete excision Less likely · revision 8–10% More likely · revision < 5%
Sensory loss Greater Less
Scar No plantar scar · ✓ fewer wound problems Painful plantar scar (~5%)
Weight-bearing Earlier Longer NWB
DTML Must be released Seen directly
Outcomes / satisfaction / ADL limits Comparable Comparable
Morton's neuroma MTP synovitis
Site Web space, plantar MTP joint
Test Mulder's click, web-space compression Drawer test (instability)
Digital nerve block Relief No relief
Surgery Neurectomy Shortening osteotomy (long 2nd MT) · capsular release + extensor lengthening

How it's asked

"Commonest location?"third web space

"Cyclist, pain between 3rd + 4th toes, worse in shoes — next step?"shoes with a wide toe box

"Tingling into 3rd + 4th toes, Mulder's click — true?"confluence of medial + lateral plantar nerves

"Burning between 3rd + 4th toes, forefoot click — initial management image?"metatarsal pad (Figure D)

"Plantar vs dorsal approach — plantar has?"increased likelihood of complete neuroma excision

"Commonest complication of the most effective treatment?"neuroma secondary to inadequate resection

"Failed shoe change, brief relief from steroid — next?"dorsal neurectomy

"Walking on a marble — true of treatment?"corticosteroid injections do not provide long-term relief

"2nd + 3rd web-space neuromas — safest plan?"resect 2nd, neurolysis of 3rd by DTML release

"Excised 5 mm proximal to ligament, Tinel's positive — cause?"inadequate proximal resection

"Commonest cause of persistent pain after excision?"inadequate resection of an interdigital neuroma

"Recurrence after dorsal surgery — best step?"revision neurectomy through plantar or dorsal approach with nerve burial

"Primary advantage of dorsal approach for revision?"lower risk of plantar scar tenderness + wound complications

"Polyarthropathy, ANA+, perineural fibrosis without fibrinoid necrosis?"Morton's neuroma
✗ Wrong options: rheumatoid nodule

Leg Nerve Entrapment Syndromes

1Basics

Entrapment sites – overview

Nerve Site of compression Name / clue Treatment
Ilioinguinal Hypertrophied abdominal muscles (intensive training) Hyperaesthesia · pain ↑ with hip hyperextension Surgical release if nonop fails
Obturator Well-developed adductors (skaters) Chronic medial thigh pain · nerve conduction studies establish diagnosis Supportive
Lateral femoral cutaneous Tight belts, prolonged hip flexion Meralgia paresthetica (lateral thigh pain) PT, NSAIDs, posture, release compressive devices
Sciatic Ischial tuberosity · piriformis Piriformis syndrome —
Saphenous Adductor (Hunter's, subsartorial) canal Surfer's neuropathy · prolonged kneeling · pain inferomedial to knee Knee pads first line
Common peroneal Behind fibula / fibular neck — ganglion cyst, direct blow, pressure Foot drop Proximal tibiofibular joint fusion to prevent cyst recurrence
Superficial peroneal Fascial exit ~10–12 cm (OB) · 12–15 cm (Orthobullets) proximal to lateral malleolus Dorsal foot numbness ↑ with PF + inversion Observation → fascial release
Deep peroneal Inferior extensor retinaculum Anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome · 1st web space —
Posterior tibial Flexor retinaculum / tarsal tunnel Tarsal tunnel syndrome · medial + plantar foot —
1st branch lateral plantar (Baxter) Abductor hallucis deep fascia vs medial quadratus plantae Distal tarsal tunnel syndrome · runners Release abductor hallucis fascia
Medial plantar Knot of Henry (FDL × FHL) · foot orthotics Jogger's foot Discontinue orthosis
Sural 12–15 mm distal to fibular tip (equinus) · gastrocnemius–Achilles musculotendinous junction (calf) Lateral dorsum + heel Surgical release
Interdigital — Morton's neuroma —

Tarsal tunnel anatomy

Tarsal tunnelfibro-osseous tunnel directly inferior to medial malleolus · roof = flexor retinaculum · abductor hallucis = plantar border · compression by fascial septae, flexor retinaculum, abductor hallucis

Tibial nervedivides into medial plantar, lateral plantar, medial calcaneal branches · plantar nerves = terminal sensory branches → most plantar sensation

Dissection label (medial ankle) Structure
A 1st branch of lateral plantar nerve (Baxter) — most commonly entrapped
B Medial calcaneal nerve branches
C Tibial nerve
D Lateral plantar nerve
E Medial plantar nerve (jogger's foot)

Dorsal sensationSPN = dorsum except 1st web space · DPN = 1st web space · sural = lateral foot
✗ Wrong options: plantar surface

Saphenous nerve entrapment (TO)

Saphenous nerve (TO)purely sensory · longest terminal branch of posterior division of femoral nerve · L3–L4

Course (TO)from below inguinal ligament with femoral artery · deep to sartorius throughout thigh · enters subsartorial / adductor / Hunter's canal (proximal third of thigh, per TO) — fibrous band vastus medialis ↔ adductor magnus

Exit (TO)joins saphenous branch of descending genicular artery · both pierce roof of the canal just proximal to the adductor hiatus

Commonest entrapment site (TO)adductor canal
✗ Wrong options: below inguinal ligament · at adductor hiatus · below patella

Common peroneal nerve compression (TO)

Why CPN (TO)most fixed nerve, minimum tolerance to mobility · fixed at origin under biceps femoris → fixed to fibular neck as it winds around

Unconscious, lying in lateral position, bruised lateral knee (TO)CPN injury
✗ Wrong options: tibial · ulnar · trigeminal

BranchesCPN → DPN + SPN · SPN in lateral compartment → supplies peroneus longus + brevis → dorsal foot sensation

3Presentation

Baxter's nerve (first branch of lateral plantar nerve)

Whorunning athlete · normally arched or cavus foot · responsible for ~⅕ of hindfoot pain, widely missed

Symptomschronic plantar medial heel pain (often 9–12 months) · start-up pain like plantar fasciitis plus neuritic burning pain unrelated to loading · worse at end of day / prolonged activity

Signstenderness at abductor hallucis origin · Tinel's just proximal to abductor hallucis → radiates to lateral foot / 5th MT base · no Tinel's over posterior tibial nerve · chronic → abductor digiti minimi atrophy

Innervatesabductor digiti quinti (minimi) (OB) · also FDB + quadratus plantae (one OB)
✗ Wrong options: abductor hallucis · FDL · FHL · plantar fascia

Coursedeep to abductor hallucis + FDB · superficial to quadratus plantae · medial to calcaneus · just anterior to medial calcaneal tuberosity / just superior to plantar fascia insertion

Compression pointbetween deep fascia of abductor hallucis and medial caudal margin of medial head of quadratus plantae (Orthobullets writes "abductor hallucis longus")

Mechanismstretching + tethering in abductor hallucis fascial leashes · hypertrophy of small foot muscles · hindfoot microtrauma in runners

Superficial peroneal nerve entrapment

Mechanisminversion injury · fascial defect (± muscle herniation)

Sitewhere it exits deep crural fascia of anterolateral leg, ~12 cm (Orthobullets) · 10–12 cm (OB) proximal to lateral malleolus · lateral → anterior compartment

Symptomsnumbness + tingling over dorsum of foot · ↑ with passive plantarflexion + inversion · ± eversion weakness

Sridhara signs↓ dorsal sensation sparing 1st web space · soft-tissue bulge ~10 cm above lateral malleolus · Tinel's over bulge · bulge ↑ with resisted dorsiflexion / WB · tenderness over bulge or terminal branches

Variable courseSPN in lateral compartment 72%, anterior 23% (Barrett) · anterior in almost 50% (Rosson) → explore both compartments

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key diagnostic findings

Test Finding
EMG Lateral plantar nerve entrapment positive in 88% of neurogenic subcalcaneal heel pain
MRI Abductor digiti minimi atrophy → Baxter's neuropathy
Nerve conduction studies Help establish obturator entrapment
Electrical studies Confirm peroneal compression at fibular neck

5Management

Baxter's nerve entrapment
  • First→rest, ice, PT, orthotics, NSAIDs
  • Persistent > 3 months→release abductor hallucis fascia
    (good–excellent 89%)
Superficial peroneal nerve entrapment
  • Most→observation
  • Refractory / elite athlete→fascial release + SPN neurolysis
    • fascial defect→release, never close (worsens)

Operative treatment

Condition Operation ✗ Traps
Baxter's (distal tarsal tunnel) Release of abductor hallucis fascia → decompresses lateral plantar nerve branch partial plantar fasciotomy / gastrocnemius recession (= recalcitrant plantar fasciitis)
SPN Fascial release + superficial peroneal neurolysis (80% satisfied) repair herniation + close fascial defect · 4-compartment fasciotomy · neurectomy · lumbar discectomy
CPN ganglion Excision · proximal tibiofibular fusion prevents recurrence —
Medial plantar (jogger's foot) Stop orthosis —
Saphenous Knee pads first line —
Sural Surgical release —

Baxter release complicationspersistent heel pain needing more surgery · neuroma · superficial infection · RSD

6Complications

Peroneal nerve palsy – order of recovery

Short leg cast → foot dropcompression of peroneal nerve at fibular neck

Last muscle to recoverextensor hallucis longus (innervated most distally)
✗ Wrong options: EDL · peroneus longus · tibialis anterior · FDL (tibial nerve)

Lisfranc Injury

Foot & Ankle · 30 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

DefinitionTMT fracture-dislocation · disruption between medial cuneiform and base of 2nd metatarsal · purely ligamentous or fracture-dislocation (treatment implications)

Incidence0.2% of all fractures · 1 per 55,000 / yr · males > females · 3rd decade

Missedeasily missed, up to 20% at initial encounter · missed → progressive planovalgus, chronic pain

Lisfranc equivalentscontiguous proximal metatarsal fractures or tarsal fractures · may involve multiple TMT joints

Anatomy – Lisfranc & plantar ligaments

Lisfranc joint complextarsometatarsal + intermetatarsal + intertarsal (intercuneiform) articulations · 5 MTs with 3 cuneiforms + cuboid

Column Joints Mobility
Medial 1st TMT Little / none
Middle 2nd + 3rd TMT Little / none
Lateral 4th + 5th TMT Most mobile — accommodates uneven ground

✗ Mobility trap (TO)1st–3rd cuneiform–MT joints have greater mobility than 4th–5th (false — they are stable, rigid lever for push-off)

Bony stabilitytrapezoidal bases of 1st–3rd MTs → transverse "Roman arch" · 2nd TMT = keystone, 2nd MT recessed in mortise between medial and lateral (recessed middle) cuneiforms · shallow 2nd TMT mortise = risk factor (TO)

Ligament Key facts
Lisfranc ligament Plantar interosseous · lateral surface of medial cuneiform → medial base of 2nd MT (near plantar surface) · largest + strongest interosseous TMT ligament · 8–10 mm wide, 5–6 mm thick · tightens with pronation + abduction of forefoot · stabilises 1st/2nd TMT + midfoot arch (✗ Wrong options: "dorsal interosseous" (TO trap))
Plantar TMT ligaments Plantar ligament medial cuneiform → 2nd + 3rd MTs + Lisfranc ligament both needed for transverse instability
Dorsal TMT ligaments Weaker than plantar (TO ✓) → displacement usually dorsal
Intermetatarsal ligaments 2nd–5th MT bases only · no IM ligament between 1st and 2nd MTs (✗ Wrong options: "1st–2nd IM ligament is strongest" (TO trap))
Lisfranc ligament complex (TO) TMT ligaments of 1st + 2nd rays + Lisfranc ligament
1st MT base ↔ medial cuneiform Joint capsule (not Lisfranc ligament)

Point on X-rayLisfranc ligament runs base of 2nd MT → medial cuneiform
✗ Wrong options: 1st MT → 2nd MT · 2nd MT → middle cuneiform · medial → middle cuneiform

✗ Ligament distractorsspring (calcaneus → navicular, supports talar head) · plantar fascia (plantar calcaneus → MT heads) · AITFL (tibia → fibula) · bifurcate, long plantar, Chopart, CFL

2Mechanism

Indirect (commonest)rotational force + axial load through hyper-plantarflexed forefoot → hyperflexion / compression / abduction moment → MTs displaced dorsal + lateral · usually involves at least 2nd TMT

SettingsMVA, fall from height, athletes (football player fallen on, stirrup in equestrian, soccer pivot, twist under motorcycle, dancer)

Directcrush (workplace) · hockey puck to medial foot ≠ Lisfranc → occult trabecular fractures (below)

3Presentation

Symptomssevere midfoot pain · inability to bear weight · pain at push-off

Plantar ecchymosismedial plantar bruising = highly suggestive of Lisfranc (TO) · also seen in calcaneal fracture (TO)
✗ Wrong options: mycetoma · hydatid cyst of talus · vertical talus

Exammidfoot swelling, TMT tenderness · pain with pronation + abduction of forefoot · midfoot squeeze · piano key test (hypermobility)

Instability testgrasp MT heads, dorsal force while palpating TMTs → dorsal subluxation = instability · 1st + 2nd MTs displace medially + laterally → global instability → surgery · plantar ligaments intact → no dorsal subluxation → nonop possible

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Sign View
Medial base 2nd MT ↔ medial middle cuneiform discontinuity AP — diagnostic
Widening 1st–2nd ray interval ± fleck sign (avulsion of Lisfranc ligament from 2nd MT base, in 1st IM space) AP — diagnostic
Dorsal displacement of proximal base of 1st or 2nd MT Lateral
Medial 4th MT base ≠ medial cuboid Oblique
Disrupted medial column line (tangent to medial navicular + medial cuneiform) Oblique
Study Use
AP, lateral, oblique Initial study of choice
Weight-bearing (bilateral, comparison) Non-WB films normal + suspicion → next step · reveals subtle diastasis · contralateral for low-energy injuries
Physician-assisted stress exam / stress fluoroscopy Dynamic alternative · EUA reserved for equivocal cases
CT Comminution, pre-op planning, subtle fractures, fleck sign
MRI Confirms purely ligamentous injury · plantar ligament integrity · doesn't assess dynamic instability as well as WB films

Mulcahy alignment checkAP: 2nd MT–middle cuneiform, 3rd MT–lateral cuneiform, 1st MT–medial cuneiform · oblique: middle cuneiform–2nd MT, lateral cuneiform–3rd MT · lateral: talus–2nd MT axis, medial cuneiform–5th MT, dorsal TMT surfaces

Diagnosis – weight-bearing/stress radiographs, MRI & plantar ecchymosis

Midfoot pain, plantar ecchymosis, non-WB X-ray normalstanding / weight-bearing AP radiographs (✗ Wrong options: CT · MRI · bone scan (expensive, not warranted) · compartment pressures) · "of both feet" when CT shows no fracture (✗ Wrong options: MRI first · RTP stiff-soled shoe · fix · cast 6 wk before stability known)

Football player, plantar flexed foot, nonstanding films normalweight-bearing AP radiograph
✗ Wrong options: RTP · PT · orthosis · NWB cast

WB radiograph most likely showsdorsal displacement of 1st MT proximal base on lateral
✗ Wrong options: fleck lateral to 5th MT base (5th MT avulsion) · calcaneal sclerotic line (stress fracture) · proximal medial sesamoid (turf toe) · talar head directly over navicular (medial subtalar dislocation)

MRI: dorsal capsule torn, plantar ligament intact, WB films normalstable → protected WB in CAM boot
✗ Wrong options: bridge plate · strict NWB cast 6 wk · stress fluoro EUA · primary arthrodesis

Hockey puck direct blow to medial foot, X-rays normalMRI → occult fractures medial malleolus, medial talar neck, medial cuneiform, 1st MT (trabecular stress fractures + marrow oedema; medial malleolus can displace)
✗ Wrong options: bilateral WB X-rays (mechanism inconsistent with Lisfranc) · WBAT · cast without diagnosis · RTP

Diagnostic criteria – instability

Finding Meaning
> 2 mm displacement / shift between 1st + 2nd MT on WB film Unstable → ORIF / anatomic reduction
Diastasis 2nd MT base ↔ medial cuneiform Pathognomonic of Lisfranc ligament rupture
Lisfranc + plantar ligament (medial cuneiform → 2nd/3rd MT) torn Transverse instability
Plantar ligament intact on MRI Stable → nonop
Medial gapping on stress view Injury of that TMT even without frank displacement
> 5 mm diastasis, neglected pure ligamentous (TO) Medial column arthrodesis

Hardcastle & Myerson classification

Type Pattern Diagram
A Complete homolateral dislocation (all 5 TMTs, same direction)
B1 Partial, medial column dislocation
B2 Partial, lateral dislocation —
C1 Partial divergent
C2 Complete divergent —

Primary arthrodesis may give better function + reductioncomplete injuries Type A or C2

DDxMT base fracture · MT stress fracture · tarsal fracture

5Management

Suspected Lisfranc
  • Non-WB X-ray normal→bilateral WB / stress X-ray (MRI if equivocal)
    • stable, plantar ligament intact→CAM boot / cast
  • Unstable (> 2 mm) or displaced→operative
    • massive swelling→temporary pinning, definitive at 2–3 wk
    • soft tissues OK→ORIF (< 24 h) or primary arthrodesis
Operative choice
  • Bony fracture-dislocation, acute→ORIF rigid 1–3 TMT
  • Purely ligamentous→primary arthrodesis medial ± middle column
  • Delayed / chronic / arch collapse→arthrodesis
  • Lateral column (4–5) displaced→temporary K-wires
    (never fuse 4th–5th TMT)

Operative criteria

Nonoperative ORIF Primary arthrodesis (1st–3rd TMT)
Non-displaced, stable on WB · partial Lisfranc rupture, no displacement Any instability (> 2 mm shift) Purely ligamentous (controversial)
Nonambulatory, serious vascular disease, severe neuropathy (insensate diabetic) Bony fracture-dislocation, acute Delayed treatment (e.g. 8 wk, 6 mo)
Medically unfit Young active (soldier) Chronic deformity, missed injury
Cast 8 wk (Orthobullets) · NWB cast 6 wk then gradual return (OB) — Complete A / C2 · severe intra-articular comminution · failed fixation

Nonop of displaced / unstablesignificantly worse functional + radiographic outcomes · persistent midfoot instability

ORIF indications & fixation technique (medial vs lateral columns)

Goalanatomic reduction + stable fixation = the outcome predictor · open > closed reduction (see reduction, loose osteochondral fragments, soft-tissue interposition — ligament / bony avulsion may be incarcerated)

Standard constructrigid fixation 1st–3rd TMT (screws or spanning plates) + K-wires for 4th + 5th TMT (flexible, removed later) · stiff fixation of all 5 TMTs → poor function

Plate vs screw vs wirecortical screws > K-wires (more rigid) · pin fixation inferior (ligament needs prolonged fixation) · plates span TMTs when MT base comminuted · more screws = more rigid

Fix only what's injured1st + 2nd TMT ligamentous injury → ORIF of 1st and 2nd TMT (✗ Wrong options: CR + K-wires · 1–3 + K-wire 4–5 (only when all five injured, e.g. homolateral)) · no lateral instability → ORIF medial two columns alone (✗ Wrong options: add lateral column stabilisation)

Closed manipulation + percutaneous screwacceptable only if anatomic alignment achieved closed

Bridge vs transarticularacute displaced → open reduction with spanning-bridge plate or transarticular screws · acute reducible → CRPP option

Timingwithin 24 h or wait for swelling (up to 2–3 wk) · massive swelling → temporary percutaneous pinning of medial + lateral columns → delayed ORIF / arthrodesis (↓ wound infection, low-level evidence)

Approachsingle or dual longitudinal incisions · 1st–2nd web space · 1st TMT exposed between EHL and EHB · protect deep NV bundle (DPN + dorsalis pedis)

Sequencereduce intercuneiform instability first → fix 1st–3rd TMT transarticular screws · check intercuneiform + naviculocuneiform joints

Post-opearly midfoot ROM, protected WB · K-wires out 6–8 wk · screws out 3–6 mo · full WB 8–10 wk (Orthobullets) · protected WB 3–5 mo + passive midfoot ROM (OB) — read the options · asymptomatic screws across only 1st–3rd TMT may stay · no vigorous sport 9–12 mo

ORIF vs primary arthrodesis for ligamentous injuries

Purely ligamentous — preferred treatment (TO)medial tarsometatarsal joint arthrodesis (TO)
✗ Wrong options: NWB cast · anatomical screw fixation · WBAT cast

Why fuse ligamentous injuriesligament healing less reliable than bone → deformity recurs after ORIF · ligamentous injuries do worse than bony · nonop → uniformly poor (redislocation)

Ly & Coetzee RCT (purely ligamentous)primary arthrodesis 1st–3rd rays → higher AOFAS at 2 yr · 25% of ORIF → early arthritis → revised to fusion

Best result, acute purely ligamentousopen reduction + primary arthrodesis with screw fixation
✗ Wrong options: CRPP · open + pins · metallic or bioabsorbable screws alone

Alternative to ORIF (ligamentous)open reduction + arthrodesis of medial and middle columns, reduction + stabilisation of lateral column
✗ Wrong options: fuse all three columns · CRPP all · closed reduction + cast · boot

Outcome ORIF Primary arthrodesis (PA)
Hardware removal Higher (~75%, often planned) Lower (~20%) ✓
Overall reoperation Higher (driven by HW removal) Lower ✓
Reoperation excluding HW removal Equal (Buda: 163 ORIF vs 54 PA) Equal
Functional outcome Equivalent overall (level 1, meta-analyses, delayed cases) Better for purely ligamentous (Ly & Coetzee) · improved return to activity
Patient-reported outcomes No difference (OB) Higher with PA (prospective, OB) — read the options
Cost Higher overall (OB) · ORIF less expensive (another OB) — read the options —
Infection, malreduction, hardware failure, alignment, satisfaction, NWB time Equal Equal
PTOA Higher Lower
Adjacent joint stress — Greater concern

✗ PA traps"higher implant removal with PA" · "lower PTOA with ORIF" · "higher malreduction with ORIF" · "worse function with PA" · "higher wound infection with PA" · "decreased reduction quality with PA" · "medial + lateral column arthrodesis better"
✗ Wrong options: — inferior

Lateral columnnever fuse 4th + 5th TMT → inferior functional outcomes (Mulier: total arthrodesis worse than medial arthrodesis + lateral ORIF) · use temporary K-wires · medial column fusion superior to combined medial + lateral

All 5 TMT fused (B2 injury)inferior functional outcomes vs medial ray arthrodesis + temporary lateral K-wires

Homolateral fracture-dislocation (medial + lateral columns)arthrodesis of medial column + K-wire fixation of lateral column
✗ Wrong options: cast · percutaneous screw / ORIF medial column alone · fuse medial + lateral

MVC, medial pain, plantar ecchymosisopen reduction + arthrodesis of medial two TMT joints
✗ Wrong options: ex-fix + staged screws · percutaneous wires 1–3 · Morel-Lavallée debridement · screws + ligament reconstruction

Equestrian, stirrup, 1 wkarthrodesis of medial TMT joints · operative reduction mandatory whether fusion or ORIF
✗ Wrong options: aircast NWB · walking cast · Broström · delayed osteotomy

Crush at workligamentous patterns better with primary arthrodesis than ORIF
✗ Wrong options: workplace = no difference · fusion only as salvage (post-ORIF salvage fusion does worse than primary) · rigid 4th–5th TMT fixation · suture fixation alone for complete dislocations

Suture-buttonpossible role in isolated Lisfranc ligament injury · complete dislocations need rigid fixation

Fusion techniquedenude TMT cartilage → cortical screws or square plate · cast / splint 6 wk → WB in boot 6–12 wk → full WB in shoes by 12 wk

6Complications

Complication Fact
Post-traumatic midfoot arthritis Commonest complication · ↑ with delay + ORIF · up to 80% non-anatomic ORIF · 54% symptomatic OA at ~10 yr after ORIF (Orthobullets) · > 25% even with anatomic reduction (OB) → midfoot arthrodesis
Malunion Non-anatomic ORIF → shoe modification (nonsurgical) or corrective arthrodesis
Nonunion Smoking → revision arthrodesis + graft (unless elderly low-demand)
Hardware removal ~75% ORIF · ~20% arthrodesis
Deep infection 3–4% · swelling at definitive surgery → I&D ± HW removal
Planovalgus deformity Nonop or non-anatomic ORIF · missed injury → arch collapse + forefoot abduction
Dorsal foot numbness Dorsal osteophytes impinging SPN (tight shoes)

Prognosismilitary: ~70% resume occupational running at ~3 yr after ORIF or PA · missed diagnosis = poor prognosis

Chronic/missed injuries – midfoot arthritis & arthrodesis

Most common complication (10 yr after boot NWB 6 wk)midfoot arthritis
✗ Wrong options: nonunion · planovalgus · 1st TMT hypermobility ("not associated") · dorsal numbness

Untreated trauma → chronic pain + progressive deformityLisfranc injury → pes planovalgus
✗ Wrong options: navicular (no planovalgus) · calcaneus / talar neck → varus · ATFL (ankle instability)

Chronic PTOA nonopshoe inserts / modifications + NSAIDs · fail → arthrodesis of affected joints

Malunion, pain at push-off / stairsshoe modification with cushioned heel + rocker sole (unloads TMT in terminal stance)
✗ Wrong options: neutral-posted rigid orthosis · UCBL · AFO locked 90° · Arizona

2 yr after cast, push-off pain, arch lossTMT joint arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: Evans lateral column lengthening · TN fusion · Dwyer · triple

6 mo old (ICU head injury), 1st–3rd TMTarthrodesis of 1st through 3rd TMT
✗ Wrong options: orthotics · CR + screws · ORIF · add triple

> 6 mo, instability + arch collapseopen reduction + primary arthrodesis ± tricortical ipsilateral iliac crest autograft for bone loss
✗ Wrong options: RTW · PT / orthotics (only if unfit) · cast WBAT (insensate diabetic / unfit) · ORIF (late presenters fuse)

Factors favouring primary arthrodesisprimarily ligamentous injury + delay in treatment
✗ Wrong options: significant bony injury → ORIF

Midfoot arthrodesis best indicatedchronic ligamentous Lisfranc injury (ligament won't heal functionally)
✗ Wrong options: acute nutcracker cuboid (restore lateral column length) · diabetic equinus (stretching / TAL / gastroc recession) · TN nonunion (revise that joint) · ulcers under 2nd–3rd MT heads (relative plantarflexion / 1st ray dorsiflexion)

Chronic Lisfranc + progressive flatfoot (alcoholic, supple hindfoot)midfoot arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: PT / AFO (PTTI first line) · MCO + transfers + LCL (flexible flatfoot) · triple (rigid arthritic hindfoot)

Midfoot arthrodesis techniquedenude 1st–3rd TMT + bone graft · reduce with windlass mechanism · cast 6 wk → boot 6–12 wk → WBAT at 12 wk if healed

X vs Y

ORIF Primary arthrodesis
Best for Bony fracture-dislocation, acute Purely ligamentous, delayed, chronic, A / C2
Hardware removal ~75% ~20%
Function Equivalent overall Better in ligamentous (Ly & Coetzee)
Medial + middle columns (1st–3rd TMT) Lateral column (4th–5th TMT)
Motion Rigid lever for push-off Mobile — uneven ground
Fixation Rigid screws / plate or fuse Temporary K-wires
Fusion Acceptable Avoid — inferior function
Lisfranc planovalgus PTTI planovalgus
History Trauma, plantar ecchymosis Insidious
Treatment Midfoot (TMT) arthrodesis PT / AFO → MCO + transfer + LCL → triple

Lower Extremity Os

Foot & Ankle · 31 / 48

1Basics

Definitions & epidemiology

Accessory ossiclesecondary ossification centre that stays separate from parent bone · may mimic fracture

Sesamoidbone incorporated into a tendon, moves with it

Numberup to 40 accessory ossicles + multiple sesamoids in foot and ankle

Commonest ossiclesos trigonum, accessory navicular (os tibiale externum), os intermetatarseum · os trigonum = second commonest accessory bone (OB)

Commonest sesamoidsos peroneum (in peroneus longus) · hallux sesamoids (in FHB, under 1st MT head)

Os trigonum – anatomy

Originseparated posterolateral (lateral) tubercle of talus · ossifies 8–13 yr, normally fuses within 1 yr · unfused → synchondrosis with talus

Stieda processelongated lateral tubercle (unfused) that may fracture with repetitive trauma

Relationsos lies lateral to FHL, tibial nerve, PTT, posterior tibial artery · FHL runs in fibro-osseous tunnel between posterolateral (os) + posteromedial talar tubercles

2Mechanism

Os trigonum syndromerepetitive forced plantarflexion (microtrauma → stress fracture) or acute forced plantarflexion (acute fracture) · traumatic disruption of synchondrosis → pain

Impingementos squeezed between posterior tibial malleolus + calcaneal tuberosity / superior calcaneus

At riskballet dancers (en pointe), basketball, soccer, football, kicking, downhill running, push-off

Os peroneum injurydirect trauma · sudden inversion + supination → associated PL rupture

3Presentation

Os trigonum & posterior impingement – diagnosis

Symptomchronic / recurrent posterolateral ankle pain with forced plantarflexion, en pointe, push-off, jumping

Exampain with passive maximal plantarflexion · no Achilles insertion tenderness · ± FHL swelling / tenderness if FHL tenosynovitis

Feature Os trigonum syndrome FHL tendinitis / stenosing tenosynovitis
Pain site Posterolateral Posteromedial (behind medial malleolus)
Provocation Forced plantarflexion Hallux motion, push-off, deep squat
Sign Plantarflexion pain Triggering, crepitus, great toe locking
X-ray Tibio-calcaneal impingement on plantarflexion lateral May show incidental os

Inflamed structure in os trigonum + posteromedial tendernessFHL (labelled C on axial MRI)

✗ Posterolateral look-alikesperoneal pathology (instability, pain with passive DF + eversion) · subtalar arthritis / loose body (pain with inversion / eversion) · tarsal tunnel (medial heel, plantar paraesthesia) · PTT tendinitis (posteromedial; does not abut os trigonum)

FHL stenosing tenosynovitis – examination

Functional hallux rigiduslow-lying distal FHL muscle belly jams in retrotalar fibro-osseous tunnel ("cork in a bottle")

Testmaximal knee extension + ankle dorsiflexion → passive hallux dorsiflexion limited + painful
✗ Wrong options: forced plantarflexion (os trigonum) · posterolateral tenderness behind peroneals (os trigonum) · DF + eversion (anterior impingement) · calf squeeze (Achilles)

FHL origininferior fibula + interosseous membrane

Hamiltongood results after FHL release · presence of os trigonum on X-ray does not mandate excision

Os subfibulare & os peroneum – presentation

Os subfibulareoften asymptomatic · focal tenderness + swelling · chronic ankle instability, recurrent sprains · laxity on anterior drawer + inversion / eversion stress

Os peroneumpainful os peroneum syndrome · fracture · diastasis · PL rupture

4Diagnosis & Classification

Accessory ossicles and sesamoids

Accessory bone Prevalence Clinical significance Differential
Os trigonum 10–25% Posterior ankle impingement, FHL entrapment Shepherd's fracture (posterolateral process)
Type II accessory navicular 2–12% PTT dysfunction Navicular tuberosity avulsion, type I accessory navicular
Os subfibulare 2% (table) · 1–2% (text) Painful os subfibulare, instability Lateral malleolus (ATFL) avulsion fracture
Os peroneum 9–20% · bilateral 60% · bipartite 30% Painful os peroneum, fracture, diastasis, PL rupture Painful os vesalianum, bipartite os peroneum
Os vesalianum 2% Painful os vesalianum Avulsion fracture of 5th MT base
Hallux sesamoids ~100% Fracture, stress fracture Bipartite tibial sesamoid

Key radiology findings

Ossicle Study Finding
Os trigonum Lateral X-ray in plantarflexion Round / oval / triangular ossicle impinged between posterior tibia + calcaneal tuberosity
Os trigonum Axial CT Ossicle off posterior talus (✗ Wrong options: posterior malleolus (tibia) · accessory navicular (medial + distal) · coalition (distal) · anterior loose body)
Os trigonum MRI Fluid around os + marrow oedema in os, ↑ T2 signal, FHL oedema / inflammation · no talar marrow oedema (vs acute posterior process fracture)
Os subfibulare Weight-bearing AP, lateral, mortise + varus stress view Ossicle · talar tilt on varus stress → instability · ↑ separation of os from fibular tip
Os peroneum X-ray + MRI Normal os · acute fracture · proximal migration = PL rupture

Os subfibulare vs type VII transepiphyseal fracture (child)

Os subfibulare Type VII transepiphyseal fracture
X-ray Smooth-edged, short ossicle at inferior pole of epiphysis Long, irregular line in middle third of distal fibular epiphysis
Nature Anatomic variant or ossified ATFL avulsion Sleeve avulsion through secondary ossification centre into joint (ATFL, CFL, PTFL stronger than physis)
Initial treatment Protected weight-bearing (CAM boot) Protected weight-bearing (CAM boot)

Differentiates themradiographs, not clinical picture

Paediatric ankle injuries~17% of all physeal injuries

5Management

Symptomatic os trigonum
  • First→NSAIDs, rest, immobilisation (CAM), restricted WB, PT
  • Failed ≥ 3 mo→excision (open lateral or posterior arthroscopy)
    • FHL involved→± FHL tenolysis, debridement or repair

Os trigonum excision (arthroscopic vs open, sural nerve)

NonopNSAIDs, rest, immobilisation, restricted weight-bearing, activity modification, PT · PT = short-term relief only · steroid injection not recommended here

Surgeryafter ≥ 3 months failed nonop → excision, open or arthroscopic · similar return-to-play both (Orthobullets) · open excision = high RTP, low complications (OB) · arthroscopic = 80% good / excellent at 2–5 yr (Van Dijk) · RTP 2–3 months

✗ Os trigonum trapsfixation / ORIF (not indicated) · FHL debridement alone (doesn't remove culprit) · PTT debridement · peroneal debridement + SPR repair (no snapping / instability) · retrial of failed rest · Haglund excision · os naviculare excision · biopsy

Posterolateral approachsural nerve at greatest risk
✗ Wrong options: SPN (more anterior)

Ballet dancer, failed 1 mo rest + NSAIDs + PTarthroscopic os trigonum excision

Basketball player, chronic posterior painopen excision = highest success
✗ Wrong options: PT · steroid · arthroscopic fixation · ORIF

Soccer player, posterolateral pain with plantarflexion, ↑ T2 around osarthroscopic excision
✗ Wrong options: PB tubularisation · FHL debridement · EMG · subtalar loose body removal

Os subfibulare & os peroneum treatment

Os subfibulare / type VIIprotected weight-bearing first · failed nonop → excision ± ligament re-attachment
✗ Wrong options: initial MRI (only for chronic pain / instability) · acute surgery · mandatory ATFL re-attachment

Os subfibulare excision for functional instability without laxity (children)better AOFAS than rehab alone

Os peroneum situation Treatment
Painful os peroneum syndrome, minimally displaced fracture NSAIDs, rest, immobilisation, restricted WB
Refractory syndrome (minimal tendon involvement), displaced fracture Excision
With PL tendon rupture Excision + PL repair or tenodesis to peroneus brevis

X vs Y

Os trigonum Shepherd's fracture
Edges Smooth, corticated, synchondrosis Acute fracture of posterolateral process
MRI Fluid + oedema around os, no talar body oedema Talar marrow oedema
Os vesalianum 5th MT base avulsion
Edges Smooth ossicle Acute fracture line

"Basketball player, painful max plantarflexion — highest success?"open excision

"CT arrow posterior to talus?"os trigonum fragment

Metatarsal Fractures

Foot & Ankle · 32 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Adults5th MT most commonly fractured

3rd MTrarely isolated · 68% with 2nd or 4th MT fracture

Peak age2nd–5th decade

Paediatric metatarsal fractures – most common location

Young child1st MT (proximal) most common · < 4 yr (Orthobullets) · < 5 yr (OB) — read the options

Older child (> 5 yr)5th MT

Courseusually minimally displaced, rarely operative

Ossification (age clue)lateral cuneiform 1 yr · middle 3 yr · medial 4 yr

Anatomy

1st MTwidest + shortest · plantar crista articulates with sesamoids · bears 30–50% of weight in gait · 50% (Orthobullets anatomy) · TO: standing = 1st MT, walking = 2nd MT — read the options · no intermetatarsal ligament support

2nd MTlongest · commonest stress fracture site

Distal intermetatarsal ligaments (2nd–5th)maintain length + alignment in isolated fractures · implicated in Morton's neuroma · multiple fractures lose this stability → ↑ displacement

Muscle balanceextrinsic (EDL, FDL) vs intrinsic (interossei, lumbricals)

Blood supplydorsal + plantar metatarsal arteries

2Mechanism

Indirect (commonest)forefoot fixed, hindfoot / leg rotates

Direct crushsignificant soft-tissue injury

Multiple proximal MT fracturesLisfranc-equivalent injury

Stressrepetitive microstress; MTs loaded perpendicular to long axis · relatively fixed proximal 2nd + 3rd MTs → diaphyseal stress fractures

3Presentation

Symptomspain, inability to bear weight · antecedent pain suggests stress fracture

Examfoot alignment (neutral / cavovarus / planovalgus) · tenderness · soft tissues in crush · overlap / malrotation of toes · Semmes–Weinstein monofilament if neuropathy

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
AP, lateral, oblique foot Required · ± contralateral, stress / WB views
Repeat X-ray at 2 wk X-rays lag symptoms by weeks → callus / periosteal reaction appears
CT Not routine · periarticular injury, rule out Lisfranc · better shows bone when fracture visible on X-ray
MRI Occult / stress fracture · fluid sequences show endosteal marrow + periosteal oedema (earliest) · useful screening tool
Bone scan (Tc-99) Occult stress fracture when X-rays unclear · most useful (OB1095 reference) · finds noncontiguous simultaneous fractures (e.g. 2nd MT + tibia)

Classification

Descriptor Record
Location Base / shaft / neck / head
Pattern Transverse, spiral, comminuted
Displacement mm translation
Angulation Sagittal plane degrees
Articular involvement Yes / no

5Management

Acute metatarsal fracture
  • 1st MT → any displacement→ORIF / pinning
  • Central (2–4) → isolated, < 10° sagittal, < 4 mm→stiff shoe / boot, WBAT
    • > 10° sagittal, > 4 mm, multiple→fixation
  • 5th MT diaphyseal spiral (dancer's)→hard-soled shoe, WB
  • Open fracture→fixation

Operative criteria

Nonoperative (stiff-soled shoe / walking boot, WBAT) Operative (percutaneous or open)
1st MT non-displaced 1st MT any displacement (✗ Wrong options: 3 mm displaced 1st MT nonop)
Central MT isolated, non / minimally displaced Central MT sagittal deformity > 10° (✗ Wrong options: 12°)
— > 4 mm translation (✗ Wrong options: 6 mm)
— Multiple MT fractures
5th MT spiral diaphyseal (dancer's fracture) Open fractures
Stress fractures Failed nonop stress fracture / nonunion

Shaft fractures – nonoperative indications

5th MT spiral diaphyseal (dancer's) fracturehigh union, low morbidity → hard-soled shoe + WB

Fixation goalsrestore alignment for normal force transmission across MT heads · maintain length → avoid transfer metatarsalgia

Techniquesantegrade / retrograde pinning · lag screws or mini-fragment plates for length-unstable patterns

Prognosismajority of isolated MT fractures heal nonop

Stress fractures – second MT, dancers, management & metabolic work-up

March fracture2nd, 3rd, 4th MTs, 2nd commonest · diaphyseal, callus + good alignment · runners, military recruits

Ballet dancersbase of 2nd MT · amenorrhoea / delayed menarche · pain with push-off + en pointe
✗ Wrong options: Lisfranc injury · cuneiform · 1st MT base · plantar fascia strain

Commonest stress sitedistal 2nd MT shaft (length + immobility) · "2nd + 3rd most frequent", also 5th (OB)

Risk factorslong 2nd MT, hypermobile 1st ray, female, recent ↑ training, cavovarus (recurrent), metabolic bone disease

Female athlete triadrepeated stress + low BMD + dietary restraint → ↑ fracture risk

Metabolic work-upserum cortisol, TSH, vitamin D, calcium · menstrual history · DEXA when needed · (hypothyroidism, amenorrhoea) · older patient (55 yr) → fragility fracture

Treatmentprotected WB / short walking cast / fracture boot WBAT / hard-soled shoe + activity modification · rest 4–6 wk (OB1095) · return over 6–8 wk (OB218223) — read the options · base fractures sometimes limited WB

✗ Stress-fracture trapsORIF, K-wires, IM screw, calcium phosphate / BMA (only after failed nonop) · biopsy / oncology referral (no red flags) · continue running with orthotic · observation alone · NWB cast · bone stimulator (no evidence) · NSAIDs + immediate RTP · bone density in a teenager (normal, no help) · MRI / bone scan once X-ray diagnostic

MRI already shows oedema, X-ray normalfracture boot WBAT (limit miles + repeat X-ray at 2 wk only if no MRI)

Nonunion (dancer, 2nd MT base)fixation

Differentialmetatarsalgia, MTP synovitis, Freiberg's infarction, Morton's neuroma

6Complications

Maluniontransfer metatarsalgia or plantar keratosis → corrective osteotomy

Multiple fracturesloss of intermetatarsal ligament stability → displacement

Midfoot Arthritis

Foot & Ankle · 33 / 48

1Basics

Definition & etiology

Jointsnaviculocuneiform, intercuneiform, tarsometatarsal (metatarsal–cuneiform) · 2nd + 3rd TMT commonly narrowed

Commonest causeidiopathic / primary OA (Orthobullets, OB) · post-traumatic articular damage (another OB) — read the options

Post-traumaticmissed / untreated Lisfranc injury (plantar bruising, "ankle sprain") → progressive flatfoot + midfoot arthrosis

InflammatoryRA, lupus · rule out inflammatory + neuropathic causes before treating

Pathoanatomylarge forces through joints with limited motion · supporting soft tissues overloaded → midfoot collapse · over time Achilles shortens → equinus

RA footforefoot commonest (dislocations, hallux valgus) · midfoot: symmetric degeneration across talonavicular + intertarsal joints

3Presentation

Post-traumatic vs inflammatory, abduction & gait

Symptommidfoot / arch pain with toe-off (push-off) · dull, achy, worse with weight-bearing · walking distance limited

Gait phasetoe-off (load passes hindfoot → midfoot → forefoot)
✗ Wrong options: heel strike · midstance · swing

Deformity on WB Present?
Longitudinal arch collapse Yes (✗ Wrong options: arch maintained)
Midfoot collapse — looks like PTTI Yes
Forefoot abduction Yes
Hindfoot valgus Yes (✗ Wrong options: hindfoot varus)
Equinus (Achilles) contracture Yes (✗ Wrong options: peroneus brevis contracture)
Hallux valgus Yes
Dorsal midfoot prominence Large dorsal osteophyte

Palpationarch / midfoot tender

Midfoot vs PTTIsingle-limb heel rise possible, inversion strength 5+, supple hindfoot → PTT working → deformity isolated to midfoot

DifferentialPTTI · post-traumatic Lisfranc · lateral ankle instability

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

View Finding
Lateral (WB) Break in Meary's line (talus–1st MT) with apex at midfoot · longitudinal arch collapse · dorsal osteophytes · normal calcaneal pitch (vs PTTI)
AP (WB) Midfoot arthritic change · forefoot abduction · normal talar head coverage (vs PTTI)
Inflammatory Symmetric joint degeneration, minimal extra bone
Primary OA Subchondral cysts, osteophytes, asymmetric narrowing
Image-guided steroid injection Diagnostic + therapeutic
X-ray pattern Diagnosis
Symmetric degeneration Inflammatory (lupus, RA)
Subchondral cysts + osteophytes Primary OA
Isolated dorsal osteophyte at 1st MTP Hallux rigidus
Navicular sclerosis + collapse Köhler disease
1st–2nd base widening ↑ on stress Lisfranc injury

5Management

Midfoot arthritis
  • First line→NSAIDs, activity change, stiff rocker-bottom shoe, arch support, image-guided steroid
  • Failed nonop→midfoot (medial column) arthrodesis
    • Equinus→+ Achilles lengthening
    • Hindfoot valgus→+ hindfoot realignment

Nonoperative care – orthoses & bracing

Best orthosisstiff-soled rocker-bottom shoe → transfers load hindfoot → forefoot with minimal midfoot stress

Otherscushioned heel, longitudinal arch supports

Orthosis Use
Rocker-bottom shoe Midfoot (1st–2nd TMT) arthritis
Arizona brace Flexible hindfoot planovalgus; ankle + hindfoot stability
Lateral heel wedge Cavovarus with fixed forefoot pronation
Lateral wedge + 1st ray cutout Flexible cavovarus

Midfoot / medial column arthrodesis

Indicationfailed nonoperative management · midfoot joints are non-essential → fusion gives near-normal foot function, esp. push-off

Isolated midfoot flatfoot (heel rise OK, flexible hindfoot, mild heel cord contracture)medial column arthrodesis + heel cord lengthening
✗ Wrong options: PTT debridement · tendon transfer + spring ligament / LCL · triple arthrodesis (PTTI / hindfoot procedures)

✗ Wrong options: LCL + FDL · TN · subtalar · triple (hindfoot procedures)

✗ Wrong options: PRP (not studied) · 1st MT opening wedge (hallux valgus) · dorsal exostectomy — limited relief in advanced OA · double calcaneal osteotomy (planovalgus abduction)

Iliac crest autograftimproved fusion rate / ↓ nonunion
✗ Wrong options: cost · fewer implants · long-term alignment (depends on technique + fixation) · donor morbidity (significant donor pain)

Realignment arthrodesis1st ray → 1st TMT · 2nd / 3rd rays → NC + intercuneiform joints · do NOT fuse 4th / 5th TMT (lateral ray mobility accommodates stance) · select cases: interposition arthroplasty of 4th / 5th TMT (keeps lateral column length)

TechniqueTMT joints 2–3 cm deep → prepare fully · screws, staples, midfoot plates · ± Achilles lengthening, ± hindfoot realignment

Outcomeunion linked to satisfactory outcome in up to 90% (Kurup) · union 92%, few complications at 4.5 yr (Nemec) · inflammatory midfoot: primary fusion most reliable
