Plantar Fasciitis

Foot & Ankle · 39 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Demographicsmen = women · typical age 40–70 (OB) · common bilaterally · posteromedial heel

Risk factorsobesity (↑ BMI) · ↓ ankle dorsiflexion (tight calf / foot musculature) in non-athletes · weight-bearing endurance activity (running, dancing) · steep ↑ training volume

Diagnosis & anatomy

Plantar fascianonelastic multilayered connective tissue originating on the medial calcaneal tubercle → inserts on metatarsal heads · supports the arch · windlass mechanism in late stance
✗ Wrong options: abductor hallucis origin · Baxter's nerve · Achilles insertion on calcaneal tuberosity · tibialis posterior on navicular tuberosity

Shared origin on medial calcaneal tubercleabductor hallucis, FDB, quadratus plantae (may be inflamed too)

Pathologydegenerative, chronic overuse → microtears at fascia origin · recurrent inflammation + periostitis

Heel spurmay coexist · not the cause

Associated conditions

Heel pain triadplantar fasciitis + posterior tibial tendon dysfunction + tarsal tunnel syndrome

Otherscalcaneal apophysitis · gastrocnemius–soleus contracture · femoral anteversion · pes cavus · pes planus

3Presentation

"Start-up" paininsidious inferior heel pain on first steps out of bed / after rest · may walk on toes first · eases with ambulation · worse at end of day after prolonged standing

Examtender medial calcaneal tuberosity (plantar medial / anteromedial heel) · ↑ with dorsiflexion of toes + foot · ↓ ankle DF (tight Achilles · gastrocnemius contracture on Silfverskiöld)

Abductor hallucis origin tendernesssmall subset → Baxter's nerve (first branch of lateral plantar nerve = inferior calcaneal nerve) entrapment · pain persists after activity rather than improving

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical; normal radiographs
✗ Wrong options: navicular stress fracture · Freiberg · Baxter's entrapment · anterior tarsal tunnel

Key radiology findings

Study Use
Radiographs Not necessary on first visit · often normal · may show plantar heel spur · optional WB axial + lateral hindfoot
MRI Surgical planning
Bone scan Quantifies inflammation · rules out stress fracture
Labs Not routine · if inflammatory arthritis / infection suspected
EMG Rule out nerve entrapment

5Management

Plantar fasciitis
  • First line→PF-specific + Achilles stretching, prefabricated insert, NSAIDs
  • Persists > 6 wk→night splint (± steroid injection, cast)
  • > 6 mo, failed→ESWT (FDA-approved)
  • Failed 6–12 mo (9 mo)→partial plantar fasciotomy (medial ⅓)
    • + tarsal tunnel compression→open release + distal tarsal tunnel decompression

First-line treatment – stretching, night splints & orthoses

Best initialAchilles + plantar fascia stretching with prefabricated shoe insert / heel cups
✗ Wrong options: short leg cast · steroid injection · custom orthotic · surgical release

Plantar medial heel pain + calcaneal spurAchilles stretching
✗ Wrong options: walker boot · steroid · 50% release · heel spur resection

Highest satisfaction at 8 wkplantar fascia–specific stretching (recreates windlass)
✗ Wrong options: isolated Achilles stretching · steroid · ESWT · tarsal tunnel decompression + release

NWB plantar fascia–specific stretching > WB Achilles stretching · all stretching programs equal satisfaction at 2 yr

Prefabricated vs customprefabricated more effective (with stretching) + cheaper (Orthobullets, OB) · "Level III evidence supports custom orthotics" (OB) — read the options

Chronic plantar fasciitis orthosisdorsiflexion night splint = only orthosis proven effective
✗ Wrong options: gel heel cushion · full-length prefabricated / accommodative insert · Morton's extension (1st MTP pathology) · recessed first ray / cavus orthotic (cavus foot) · semi-rigid medial post insert

Plateau at 6 wk with NSAIDs + PTadd night splints, continue PT
✗ Wrong options: stop PT for custom orthotics · ESWT · endoscopic fasciotomy · bipolar radiofrequency

Second tier (> 6 wk)night splints, repeat corticosteroid injection, cast immobilisation (short leg cast 8–10 wk, Orthobullets)

Symptom durationup to 6–12 months to resolve

Shock wave therapy

ESWTsecond line · chronic heel pain > 6 months failing other treatment · FDA approved · painful · effective at 6-month follow-up · alternative to surgery once nonop exhausted

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Plantar fasciotomy (open or arthroscopic / endoscopic) Persistent pain > 9 months of failed conservative care (Orthobullets, AAOS) · 6–12 months (OB) · after 6 months of second-tier modalities (OB)
Release + distal tarsal tunnel decompression Concomitant tibial nerve compression in tarsal tunnel → open procedure · 70–90% success
Gastrocnemius recession No clear indications established
Baxter's nerve release Release deep fascia of abductor hallucis → may improve outcomes

Release extentmedial ⅓ to ⅔ of fascia only (OB: medial third) → protects medial longitudinal arch

Avoid complete releasearch destabilisation · lateral column overload · dorsolateral foot pain

Fasciotomy outcomescomplications common · protracted recovery

6Complications

Complication Fact
Lateral plantar nerve injury Surgical
Complete release Medial longitudinal arch collapse · ↑ stress dorsolateral midfoot
Chronic pain —
Heel pad (fat pad) atrophy Steroid injection → shoe padding
Plantar fascia rupture Athletes, minimalist runners, steroid injection

Plantar fascia rupture – steroid injection & immobilisation

Steroid mechanisminhibit heel pad fibroblast proliferation → fat pad atrophy
✗ Wrong options: decrease inflammation (PF is degenerative) · no rupture association · good medium / long-term relief · US guidance prolongs relief (not needed)

Steroid evidence↓ short-term pain only · no high-quality evidence · risks: fat pad atrophy, PF rupture, local reaction · used rarely / second line

Rupture presentationacute pop in runner after steroid shot → can't bear weight · loss of medial arch → pes planus
✗ Wrong options: os trigonum (posterior pain) · pes cavus + peroneal subluxation · PTTI (no heel pain) · lateral talar process (snowboarders)

Rupture treatmentcast immobilisation 3–6 wk (OB) · CAM boot sufficient (OB) · stretching after immobilisation
✗ Wrong options: urgent / delayed primary repair (no evidence) · stretching first · steroid

X vs Y

Plantar fasciitis Baxter's nerve entrapment Calcaneal stress fracture
Pain pattern Start-up, eases with walking Persists after activity Worse with WB
Tender Medial calcaneal tubercle Abductor hallucis origin Heel squeeze
Test Clinical EMG Bone scan / MRI
Orthosis Use
Dorsiflexion night splint Chronic plantar fasciitis (only proven)
Morton's extension 1st MTP pathology
Recessed first ray Cavus foot
Gel heel cushion / prefabricated insert Acute PF with stretching; not proven in chronic

How it's asked

"Start-up heel pain, BMI 35, gastrocnemius contracture, normal X-ray?"plantar fasciitis

"Structure causing morning plantar heel pain?"connective tissue originating on medial calcaneal tubercle

"Runner, anteromedial heel pain — best initial?"Achilles + plantar fascia stretching with prefabricated insert

"Plantar heel pain with calcaneal spur — initial?"Achilles stretching exercises
✗ Wrong options: spur resection

"Highest satisfaction at 8 weeks?"plantar fascia–specific stretching program

"Chronic PF, failed stretching — which orthosis?"dorsiflexion night splint

"Orthosis proven in chronic PF?"night splint

"Improved 40% then plateaued at 6 weeks?"night splints

"ESWT indicated when?"> 6 months failed nonop (FDA)

"Fasciotomy — how much to release?"medial third (avoid arch collapse)

"PF + tarsal tunnel compression — surgery?"open plantar fascia release + distal tarsal tunnel decompression

"Steroid injection — mechanism / efficacy?"inhibits heel pad fibroblast proliferation

"Pop after steroid shot in marathoner — exam / diagnosis?"pes planus, plantar fascia rupture

"First line for plantar fascia rupture?"cast immobilisation for 3–6 weeks

Poliomyelitis

Foot & Ankle · 40 / 48

1Basics

Post-polio syndrome & epidemiology

Pathologyviral destruction of anterior horn cells (spinal cord) + brain stem motor nuclei · dorsal columns spared · up to 95% of anterior horn cells may be infected in acute stage (TO)

Virusenterovirus (poliovirus) · faecal–oral spread

Household contactsseroconversion > 90% (90–100%) · 4–7 secondary infections per case

Outcome of infection~75% asymptomatic / mild flu-like · paralysis in ~1% · respiratory failure 5–15% of paralytic cases

Age at riskyounger children (< 5 yr)
✗ Wrong options: older > 5 yr

Coursetransient infection → lifelong motor dysfunction in most paralytic cases
✗ Wrong options: paralysis from active / chronic infection

Eradicated in the USA (vaccine) · late sequelae common in developing countries (TO)

3Presentation

Acute polio presentation

Acute polio (TO)flaccid paralysis, DTR absent, muscle atrophy (TO)
✗ Wrong options: spastic paralysis · DTR ++

Probable case definition (TO)acute flaccid paralysis of ≥ 1 limb + ↓ / absent tendon reflexes · no other cause · no sensory or cognitive loss (TO)

Acute stage (TO)lasts 7–10 days · malaise → encephalomyelitis · asymmetrical paralysis (TO)

Younger children (TO)listlessness, sore throat, low fever → recurrence with hyperaesthesia / paraesthesia, headache, vomiting, nuchal rigidity, back pain, limited SLR (TO)

Older children + adults (TO)low fever, flushing, apprehension, tender muscles · superficial reflexes lost first, DTRs disappear when muscle group paralysed (TO)

Paralytic polioproximal, asymmetric weakness, back pain + stiffness, no sensory deficit (after diarrhoeal / flu-like illness)

Hallmark (Orthobullets)muscle weakness with normal sensation

Polio foot deformities

Causes (TO)muscle imbalance · abnormal posture · gravity · walking on the deformed foot (TO)

Tibialis anterior (TO)one of the most frequently completely paralysed muscles → foot drop → fixed equinus (TO)

Commonest deformityequinocavovarus (OB) · TA weakness (↓ dorsiflexion), cavus, claw toes, equinus

Range (TO)equinus · calcaneus · hindfoot varus / valgus · pes cavus / planus · combinations (TO)

Neglected deformity effects (TO)abnormal gait · pressure areas + callosities · ↑ energy expenditure · arthritis (TO)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnostic criteria – post-polio syndrome (TO)

Criterion (TO) Detail
Prior paralytic polio Motor neuron loss — history, residual weakness + atrophy, EMG denervation
Recovery + stable interval Partial / complete recovery → stable function usually ≥ 15 yr
New weakness Gradual (rarely abrupt), progressive, persistent weakness or ↓ endurance ± fatigue, atrophy, muscle / joint pain · may follow trauma, surgery, inactivity
Duration Symptoms ≥ 1 year
Exclusion Other neuromuscular, medical, orthopaedic causes

5Management

Polio foot deformity — goal: painless, stable, plantigrade foot
  • First→ORTHOTICS, physio, stretching, bracing
  • Flexible, failed nonop→SOFT TISSUE: release, lengthening, tendon transfer
  • Fixed / rigid→BONY: osteotomy, wedge resection, arthrodesis
    • Adult, flail (TA + TP grade 2), rigid equinus→PANTALAR ARTHRODESIS

Operative criteria

Factor Rule (TO unless stated)
Flexible deformity Soft-tissue procedures — release, lengthening, tendon transfer
Fixed / rigid deformity Osteotomy + arthrodesis; wedge resection extra-articular where possible
Arthrodesis timing Reserved until skeletal maturity
Tendon transfer Needs supple joints + donor power grade IV–V (normal / near normal) · document manual muscle testing first
Younger child Release / lengthen contracted tendons · older child → bony surgery
Orthoses fail to give satisfactory standard of living (Orthobullets) Contracture release, tendon transfer, arthrodesis

Lightweight orthosesfirst line for polio foot deformity · keep patient functionally independent

Equinocavovarus correction

Rigid equinus, 18 yr, TA + TP grade 2 (TO)pantalar arthrodesis (TO)
✗ Wrong options: tendon transfer (rigid + weak donors) · ankle arthrodesis alone · triple (second best)

Pantalar vs triple (TO)pantalar = triple + tibiotalar arthrodesis → better stability · triple without muscle balance → late secondary ankle deformity (unbalanced forces on mobile joint proximal to fusion) · pantalar > triple (TO)

Flexible equinocavovarus, failed nonopAchilles tendon lengthening + tibialis posterior tendon transfer (to dorsum) + plantar fascia release · FDL → EDL for claw toes

Component Procedure
Equinus Achilles lengthening
↓ Dorsiflexion (TA weak) Tibialis posterior transfer to dorsum
Cavus Plantar fascia release
Claw toes FDL → EDL transfer

✗ Flexible-foot trapstriple arthrodesis / subtalar arthrodesis + medial cuneiform osteotomy (for fixed deformity) · medializing calcaneal osteotomy + FDL transfer (tibialis posterior insufficiency) · lateralizing calcaneal osteotomy + tibialis anterior transfer (TA usually weak)

Post-polio syndrome – management

Nonop (first line)limited exercise with rest periods ± lightweight orthosis · exercise to sub-exhaustion levels → tone muscle without breakdown · maintain, don't overuse

Operativetendon transfers, contracture releases, arthrodesis to optimise function

Drugs (TO)no effective treatment · lamotrigine, IVIg some success · analgesics / antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine, codeine) — may worsen fatigue (TO)

Team (TO)physio, OT, speech, respiratory, podiatry, psychology, dietetics, pain, orthotics (TO)

6Complications

Post-polio syndrome (PPS)

Natureaging phenomenon: more nerve cells inactive with time · NOT viral reactivation / chronic infection

Incidenceup to 50% of polio cases (Orthobullets, OB) · 20–85% depending on criteria (TO) — read the options

Onset≥ 15 yr after initial infection (TO) · 20–40 yr after (OB) · after middle age (Orthobullets) · not 5–10 yr after paralytic polio (TO)

Severity (TO)more severe after acute / severe initial disease; minimal initial symptoms → mild PPS (TO)

Risk factors (TO)female sex + respiratory symptoms = most important · permanent disability, severe residual weakness, aging, muscle overuse / disuse, immune reaction (TO)

Motor featuresnew weakness, ↓ endurance, atrophy, myalgia, fasciculations, fatigue, cold intolerance, dysarthria, dysphagia, respiratory compromise · ↑ difficulty with ADLs

Sensory symptoms (TO)frank sensory deficits + paraesthesias occur in PPS (sensory evoked potential changes ↔ cord atrophy on MRI) · contrast: acute polio = normal sensation (Orthobullets) (TO)

Cognitive (TO)word-finding difficulty, poor concentration, memory impairment, mood change → social isolation (TO)

Counselling a recovered childmay experience muscle weakness and fatigue as an adult
✗ Wrong options: no risk · safe after skeletal maturity · certain paralysis + avoid sport · wheelchair by 25

X vs Y

Acute polio Post-polio syndrome
Cause Active poliovirus infection Aging of depleted motor units (✗ Wrong options: reactivation)
Timing 7–10 day acute stage ≥ 15 yr (TO) / 20–40 yr (OB) later
Weakness Flaccid, asymmetric, proximal New, gradual, previously affected muscles
Reflexes Absent DTRs —
Sensation Normal Sensory symptoms possible (TO)
Flexible deformity Fixed deformity
Surgery Soft tissue — TAL, PT transfer, plantar fascia release Bony — osteotomy, triple / pantalar arthrodesis
Age Younger Older child / after maturity

How it's asked

"Post-polio syndrome — all true EXCEPT?"seen 5–10 years after the onset of paralytic polio (TO)

"Recovered child from Liberia — counselling?"may experience muscle weakness and fatigue as an adult

"Enterovirus flaccid paralysis — true?"seroconversion rate > 90% of household contacts

"Rigid equinus, 18 yr, TA + TP grade 2 — best treatment?"pantalar arthrodesis (TO)

"Flexible equinocavovarus in polio, failed nonop?"Achilles tendon lengthening, tibialis posterior tendon transfer, plantar fascia release

"Acute poliomyelitis presentation?"flaccid paralysis, DTR absent, muscle atrophy (TO)

"Polio involves which cells?"anterior horn cells + brain stem motor nuclei
✗ Wrong options: dorsal column

"Exercise advice in PPS?"sub-exhaustion levels

Posterior Tibial Tendon Insufficiency (PTTI)

Foot & Ankle · 41 / 48

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest causeadult-acquired flatfoot deformity (AAFD) · renamed progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD) (Myerson consensus) = hindfoot valgus + forefoot abduction + midfoot varus

Whowomen, 6th decade (50s–60s), obese, middle-aged

Risk factorsobesity, hypertension, diabetes, ↑ age, corticosteroid use (incl. repeated injections), seronegative inflammatory disorders

Associated conditionsinflammatory arthropathy · tarsal coalition (young, rigid pes planus ± recurrent ankle sprains) · acute onset after pronation–external rotation ankle fracture

Anatomy & biomechanics of the PTT

Muscleorigin posterior fibula, tibia + interosseous membrane · tibial nerve (L4–5)

Courseposterior to medial malleolus → divides into 3 limbs

Limb Insertion
Anterior Navicular tuberosity + 1st (medial) cuneiform
Middle 2nd + 3rd cuneiforms, cuboid, MT 2–4
Posterior Sustentaculum tali (anteriorly)

Blood supplyposterior tibial artery branches distally (Orthobullets) · branches of sural, peroneal + posterior tibial arteries (OB)

Watershed2–6 cm proximal to navicular insertion (navicular → distal medial malleolus) = main site of synovitis + rupture

Excursion2 cm (normal)

Axisposterior to tibiotalar + medial to subtalar joint axis

Functionsprimary dynamic arch support · hindfoot invertor · adducts + supinates forefoot in stance · secondary ankle plantarflexor · with FDL + FHL dynamically restrains arch

Primary antagonistperoneus brevis (evertor)
✗ Wrong options: peroneus longus (antagonist of tibialis anterior) · tibialis anterior (antagonist of PL) · gastroc-soleus (antagonised by ankle dorsiflexors) · EHL (antagonised by FHL)

Locking mechanism (TO)midstance: TP initiates subtalar inversion → locks the transverse tarsal (TN + CC) joints → rigid lever arm for toe-off · adducts + plantarflexes navicular on talar head → buttresses medial arch (TO)

Dysfunction (TO)failure of inversion of the hindfoot that locks the transverse tarsal joints → heel rise difficult, heel remains in valgus (TO)
✗ Wrong options: eversion · "unlocks"

Calf fatigueunlocked transverse tarsal joint → no rigid lever → ↓ triceps surae mechanical advantage → medial + distal calf pain, fatigue → tendinopathy primarily affects the transverse tarsal joint
✗ Wrong options: 1st TMT (dorsiflexed, not the cause) · subtalar (altered, no extra triceps work) · Lisfranc (unaffected) · tibiotalar (stage IV only)

Spring ligament & related anatomy

Spring ligament complexsuperomedial calcaneonavicular (CNL) + inferior calcaneonavicular ligaments · anterior sustentaculum tali → plantar-medial navicular · supports plantar-medial talar head · primary static stabiliser of the TN joint

Torn / attenuated in AAFDsuperomedial calcaneonavicular (most often; 18 / 22 PTT ruptures had spring injury)
✗ Wrong options: dorsal cuneonavicular · dorsal intercuneiform · dorsal calcaneocuboid · anterior tibiofibular

Deltoid linkdistal (superficial) deltoid blends with superomedial spring ligament = tibiocalcaneonavicular ligament (TCNL) · also attenuated · deltoid-spring reconstruction for advanced medial peritalar instability

Static arch stabilisersspring ligament complex, plantar fascia, plantar ligaments (long + short) · TO: long + short plantar, spring + bifurcate ligaments kept tight by TP tension → lost tension → plantar ligament failure, esp. calcaneonavicular (TO)

Failureplantar + medial migration of the talar head → arch flattens → loss of medial peritalar stability

Medial labelled figureA = spring (superomedial CN) ligament · B = joint capsule · C = plantar ligaments · D = plantar fascia · E = tibialis posterior tendon

Plantar labelled figurestructure D = spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament · A = peroneus longus · B = long plantar ligament · C = short plantar ligament · E = tibialis anterior

✗ Ligament–condition trapsLisfranc injury = Lisfranc ligament (plantar-lateral medial cuneiform → plantar-medial 2nd MT base) · peroneal dislocation = SPR · pes cavus = muscle imbalance · 2nd toe crossover = plantar plate + collateral ligament

2Mechanism

Aetiologyexact cause unknown · acute injury vs long-standing tendon degeneration

Sequencetenosynovitis → tendinosis / elongation → loss of dynamic arch stabilisation → attritional failure of static stabilisers (spring ligament, plantar fascia, plantar ligaments) → fixed degenerative joint changes

Structure orderPTT → spring + talocalcaneal ligaments → deltoid (last = stage IV)

Deformitypes planus · hindfoot valgus · forefoot abduction · forefoot varus / supination (compensatory → keeps foot plantigrade)

Equinus cyclehindfoot valgus → Achilles lateral to subtalar axis → acts as evertor · valgus shortens gastrocnemius → fixed equinus, Achilles / gastroc contracture → worse arch collapse → worse equinus

Stage IVdeltoid incompetence → valgus talar tilt in mortise → tibiotalar arthritis

3Presentation

Diagnosis & examination (too-many-toes, single-limb heel rise, equinus)

Earlymedial ankle / foot pain + weakness · tenderness + swelling just posterior to tip of medial malleolus / along PTT · ↓ endurance

Progressiveloss of arch ("lost her arch", needs shoe inserts), foot "looks wider"

Latelateral (sinus tarsi) pain from subfibular impingement (calcaneus / talus against fibula tip)

Present in AAFD Not a feature
Hindfoot valgus Hindfoot varus
Forefoot abduction ("too many toes") Forefoot adduction
Forefoot varus / supination (compensatory) Forefoot valgus / pronation (cavovarus)
Pes planus Cavus, plantarflexed 1st ray (cavovarus compensation)
Equinus / Achilles / gastrocnemius contracture Claw toes, hallux varus, plantar fasciitis
— Hallux valgus (no ↑ rate in PTTI)

Single-limb heel risehallmark · patient unable to raise the heel off the ground and stand on the toes while supported on one leg · stages II–IV can't · stage I can (TO: grossly normal single raise but fails repeated / successive raises)

Heel on double-leg heel risenormal / flexible: heel inverts, arch reconstitutes (stage II) · rigid: heel stays valgus (stage III)

Too-many-toes signviewed from behind · forefoot abduction · > 40% TN uncoverage (stage IIB)

PTT powerfoot plantarflexed + fully inverted → can't hold against examiner's eversion force · pain with resisted inversion

Forefoot varus checkhold flexible heel neutral → fixed varus = lateral border more plantarflexed than medial · flexible = MT heads perpendicular to long axis of tibia + calcaneus

Flexible vs rigidflexible = passively correctable to plantigrade (stage II) · rigid = not correctable (III, IV) → decides joint-sparing vs fusion

Equinus (must be evaluated + addressed at surgery)Silfverskiöld with hindfoot / TN held neutral: increased ankle dorsiflexion with knee flexion = gastrocnemius contracture · no change = gastroc + soleus (Achilles) · TO: equinus = < 10° DF with knee extended (TO)

✗ Exam trapsanterior drawer in 20° PF = ATFL · Coleman block = cavovarus (correction = flexible, forefoot-driven cavovarus) · piano-key = Lisfranc · Thompson = Achilles rupture · inability to flex hallux = FHL

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Views WB AP + lateral foot, ankle mortise
AP foot ↑ TN uncoverage (TN coverage angle normal < 7°) · ↑ AP talo-1st MT angle (Simmon) — stages II–IV
WB lateral ↑ lateral talo-1st MT angle (Meary) > 4° = pes planus (II–IV) · ↓ calcaneal pitch (normal 17–32°) · ↓ medial cuneiform–floor height · dorsal navicular subluxation on talus
Lateral (TO) Midfoot break at talo-MT angle, abnormal talocalcaneal angle, ↓ cuneiform height (stage 2) (TO)
Hindfoot Subtalar arthritis — stages III–IV
Mortise Talar tilt (valgus) = deltoid insufficiency — stage IV
US Stage 1 / 2a tenosynovitis — target sign · degenerating tendon hyper- → hypo-echoic · stage 2b empty groove sign = ruptured tendon gap (TO) · ↑ role
MRI Tendinosis, tenosynovitis, tearing · elongated, thinned tendon (TO) · TN, subtalar, tibiotalar arthritis

Meary in stems8°, 12°, 30° = pes planus · collapse sometimes reported as "negative" Meary angle

Diagnostic criteria

Finding Threshold / meaning
Pes planus Meary (lateral talo-1st MT) > 4°
Calcaneal pitch Normal 17–32° → ↓ = loss of arch height
Stage IIB / LCL TN uncoverage > 40% (Orthobullets, OB, Thordarson consensus) · > 30% (OB; Myerson IIa < 30% vs IIb > 30%) · "> 40% or > 30°" (OB) — read the options
Gastroc contracture DF ↑ with knee flexion (Silfverskiöld +)
Equinus (TO) < 10° DF with knee extended
Stage I vs II Can vs can't single-leg heel rise
Stage II vs III Flexible vs rigid hindfoot · rigid = stage III irrespective of arthritis on X-ray
Stage III vs IV Deltoid compromise / talar tilt / ankle arthritis
1st TMT instability Plantar gapping medial cuneiform–1st MT base

Differential

Midfoot-driven flatfootmidfoot OA / chronic Lisfranc; apex at naviculocuneiform = cuneiform subluxes dorsally, TN alignment maintained (vs PTTI = navicular subluxes dorsally on talus) → midfoot fusion + realignment

Isolated spring ligament incompetence (no PTT pathology)standard flatfoot reconstruction + adjunctive spring ligament reconstruction

Tarsal coalitionyoung, rigid pes planus, recurrent sprains

Adolescent flexible flatfootligamentous laxity → conservative

Staging (Johnson & Strom, Myerson modification)

Johnson and Strom classificationfor tibialis posterior (TO) · stage IV added later (Myerson)
✗ Wrong options: tibialis anterior · peroneus longus · FHL

Stage Deformity Exam X-ray Treatment
I Tenosynovitis, no deformity (+) single heel raise Normal Cast / boot 3–4 mo → tenosynovectomy
IIA Flexible hindfoot valgus, normal forefoot (−) single-leg heel raise, mild sinus tarsi pain Arch collapse FDL + MDCO ± TAL / gastroc
IIB Flexible + flexible forefoot abduction (too many toes, > 40% TN uncoverage) (−) heel raise, mild sinus tarsi pain Arch collapse + lateral column lengthening
IIC Flexible hindfoot + rigid forefoot abduction / varus (−) heel raise, moderate sinus tarsi pain Arch collapse, gapping of 1st TMT + Cotton or medial column fusion
III Rigid hindfoot valgus, rigid forefoot abduction (−) heel raise, severe sinus tarsi pain Subtalar arthritis Triple (hindfoot) arthrodesis
IV III + deltoid ligament compromise + ankle pain Talar tilt in ankle mortise Correctable → triple + deltoid recon · rigid + arthritis → TTC

Johnson & Strom stages (TO)

Stage TO description
1 Tenosynovitis, no deformity · tendon pain, normal function, able to repeat tiptoes
2 Flexible deformity · tendon rupture, ↓ strength, unable to repeat tiptoes
3 Rigid flat foot, valgus heel, loss of subtalar motion, forefoot varus, absent heel raise, anterolateral impingement, secondary OA
4 Ankle joint involvement — tibiotalar degeneration

Stage 1 (TO)medial pain, ↓ endurance · erythema, swelling, warmth, tenderness along TP · arch + alignment normal (TO)

Stage 2 (TO)inflammatory signs + flexible hindfoot valgus · flattened arch returns on single-leg raise · forefoot abducted + supinated · yet usually can't do an unsupported single heel rise (TO) — Orthobullets: (−) single-leg heel raise — read the options

Stage 3–4 (TO)subtalar arthropathy, deformity fixed · stage 4 = tibiotalar degeneration · X-rays diagnostic · treatment = arthrodesis (TO)

Four-stage AAFD with surgical treatment (Myerson)

Stage Deformity Surgery
I No AAFD deformity (may have pre-existing flatfoot) Tenosynovectomy, possible tendon transfer and / or medial slide osteotomy
IIa Mild / moderate flexible, < 30% TN uncoverage Tendon transfer + medial slide osteotomy ± Cotton
IIb Severe flexible, abduction through TN, > 30% TN uncoverage Transfer + medial slide ± LCL or hindfoot fusion (subtalar or TN + CC) · Cotton / TMT fusion to lower 1st ray
III Fixed (triple-joint complex) Hindfoot fusion, usually triple — all three joints
IV Foot deformity + lateral talar tilt Correct foot ± deltoid reconstruction · severe arthritis → ankle fusion or TAA + foot correction
IVa / IVb Flexible / fixed foot Foot corrected as IIb / as III

Bluman classification (detailed Myerson)

Stage Hallmark Treatment
I A / B / C Normal anatomy, PTT tenderness (A ± systemic disease · C slight HF valgus) Immobilisation, NSAIDs, cryotherapy, orthoses, tenosynovectomy
II A1 Supple HF valgus, flexible forefoot varus Orthoses · MDCO · TAL / Strayer + FDL if deformity corrects only with ankle PF
II A2 Supple HF valgus, fixed forefoot varus MDCO + FDL + Cotton
II B Forefoot abduction, TN uncovering MDCO + FDL + LCL
II C Fixed forefoot varus + medial column instability, 1st TMT plantar gapping, 1st ray dorsiflexes with HF correction MDCO + FDL + Cotton or medial column fusion
III A Rigid HF valgus, sinus tarsi pain, subtalar space loss, angle of Gissane sclerosis Custom bracing if not surgical · triple
III B + forefoot abduction Triple ± LCL
IV A Supple tibiotalar valgus Correct HF + deltoid reconstruction
IV B Rigid tibiotalar valgus TTC or pantalar fusion

RAM classification (rearfoot · ankle · midfoot)

Stage Rearfoot Ankle Midfoot
Ia PTT tenosynovitis Neutral Neutral
Ib PTT tendonitis, no deformity Mild valgus < 5° Mild flexible supination
IIa Flexible planovalgus: < 40% talar uncoverage, < 30° Meary, incongruency 20–45° Valgus + deltoid insufficiency, no arthritis Supination, no instability
IIb Flexible: > 40%, > 30° Meary, incongruency > 45° Valgus + deltoid insufficiency + tibiotalar arthritis Supination + midfoot instability, no arthritis
IIIa Fixed / arthritic, < 40% · < 30° Valgus from lateral plafond bone loss, deltoid normal Arthritis isolated to medial column (NC or 1st TMT)
IIIb Fixed, > 40% · > 30° — not correctable through triple Plafond bone loss + deltoid insufficiency Medial + middle column arthritis

5Management

PTTI — nonoperative first at every stage
  • I tenosynovitis, heel rise OK→walking cast / boot 3–4 mo
    • fails→tenosynovectomy / PTT debridement
  • II flexible→UCBL / AFO with medial post
    • fails→FDL transfer + MDCO (+ adjuncts)
  • III rigid hindfoot ± subtalar arthritis→triple arthrodesis
  • IV deltoid failure, talar tilt→decide by ankle
    • ankle valgus correctable→triple + deltoid reconstruction
    • rigid valgus + tibiotalar arthritis→TTC / pantalar
Stage II reconstruction — base FDL → navicular + MDCO
  • Forefoot abduction, TN uncoverage > 40% (IIB)→+ lateral column lengthening
  • Residual forefoot varus, stable medial column→+ Cotton osteotomy
  • 1st TMT plantar gapping / hypermobility / arthritis→+ 1st TMT fusion (Lapidus)
  • DF ↑ with knee flexion (gastroc only)→+ gastrocnemius recession
  • No change with knee flexion (gastroc + soleus)→+ TAL
Rigid flatfoot (stage III–IV)
  • Unfit / declines surgery→custom AFO (articulated if ankle normal + active)
  • Hindfoot arthritis, CC joint spared→TN + subtalar arthrodesis (medial)
  • Hindfoot + CC involved→triple arthrodesis
    • forefoot varus unmasked→derotate through transverse tarsal joints
  • + ankle arthritis / rigid tilt→TTC (hindfoot nail) or pantalar

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication Contraindication
Tenosynovectomy / PTT debridement Stage I after failed immobilisation Stage II+ alone (no deformity correction)
FDL transfer → navicular Stage II (FDL synergistic with PT) Subtalar rigidity (< 15° motion) · fixed forefoot varus > 10–12°
Stage II reconstruction Failed nonop, flexible Hypermobility · neuromuscular · severe subtalar arthritis · obesity (relative) · age > 60–70 (relative)
MDCO Flexible hindfoot valgus (IIA; all stage II) Rigid valgus
Lateral column lengthening (Evans) Forefoot abduction / TN uncoverage > 40% (IIB) Stage IIA · normal calcaneal pitch or mild valgus (Chi)
Cotton Residual forefoot varus / supination, stable medial column Medial column unstable / arthritic
1st TMT (Lapidus) / NC fusion Stage II with 1st TMT hypermobility, instability or arthritis · NC sag —
Isolated subtalar arthrodesis No fixed forefoot deformity Fixed forefoot supination / varus (→ lateral border overload) · hypermobility
Triple / hindfoot arthrodesis Stage III · stage II with severe subtalar arthritis Ankle valgus / arthritis not addressed
Triple + TAL + deltoid reconstruction Stage IV, passively correctable ankle valgus Ankle arthritis
TTC arthrodesis Stage IV: rigid hindfoot, valgus talus, tibiotalar + subtalar arthritis —

Nonoperative care – orthoses (UCBL, AFO, medial posting)

Stage Iimmobilisation in walking cast / boot 3–4 months = first line → custom-molded in-shoe orthosis after

Stage I (TO)immobilisation, ice, NSAID, rest · CAM walker boot → less muscle atrophy than plaster · orthotics eliminate forefoot pronation, rest TP · PT once inflammation settles · recalcitrant → arthroscopic or open debridement + synovectomy (TO)

AFO indicationsinitial treatment for stage II, III + IV · non-operative candidates (sedentary / low demand, age > 60–70, comorbid)

Orthosis Key facts
Custom in-shoe orthosis Stage I after immobilisation, stage II · medial heel lift + longitudinal arch support · + medial forefoot post if fixed forefoot varus / supination
UCBL with medial posting Plastic over cast in maximal manual correction · flexible deformity · first-line orthotic for stage II · not for rigid → uncomfortable, skin breakdown
AFO family (Arizona, molded, articulating) Most effective · acquired flexible flatfoot deformity · medial post supports valgus collapse
Short articulated AFO Rigid flatfoot (stage III), active patient, normal stable ankle → supports deformity, keeps ankle motion
Arizona brace Molded leather lace-up gauntlet (UCBL + laced ankle support) → stabilises tibiotalar, hindfoot + arch · significantly limits ankle motion · TO: custom rigid AFO above malleoli accommodates rigid flatfoot (TO)
Non-articulated AFO Rigid planovalgus (OB) · stage IV — deltoid incompetence + talar tilt (Elftman; stage III → articulated AFO) — read the options
Custom-molded AFO Advanced rigid AAFD, not an operative candidate (fitted in situ)
Rocker-bottom shoe No role in PTTI (OB — ankle / subtalar arthritis, calcaneal ulcers) · palliative for rigid flatfoot (TO) — read the options
PTB brace (TO) Offloads foot in severe rigid flatfoot (TO)

Medial postpromotes hindfoot inversion · elevates medial heel → ↓ lateral hindfoot impingement pressure · fits any shoe
✗ Wrong options: medial post for eversion · lateral post for inversion · lateral post for forefoot varus / adduction

Rigid flatfoot nonop (TO)palliative only, accommodates deformity · activity modification, NSAIDs, steroid injection into subtalar / TN joint · for elderly, low-demand, medically unfit or surgery-averse (TO)

Best nonop responderselderly patient with a sedentary lifestyle
✗ Wrong options: young active · inflammatory systemic disorder · balance / ambulation problems: Parkinson's, severe ipsilateral hip / knee arthritis

OutcomesAFO + PT: 83% improved at 4 mo, 89% satisfied (Alvarez) · molded AFO (rigid) / UCBL (flexible): 67% good–excellent (Chao) · ~90% satisfaction nonop stage II (Deland) · eccentric exercise group improved most (Kulig)

✗ Orthotic trapslateral hindfoot posting + 1st ray cutout = cavovarus (worsens PTTI) · full-length semi-rigid insole + 1st ray depression + lateral wedge = cavovarus · total contact cast = insensate / Charcot · Morton's extension / rigid forefoot plate limiting MTP DF = hallux rigidus · wide toe box = hallux valgus · rigid sole + rocker = midfoot arthritis · pressure-dissipating insoles + accommodative laced shoes = diabetic neuropathy · AFO = mild equinovarus · CROW = neuropathic severe deformity

Stage II, fixed forefoot supination, first visitmedial heel lift, longitudinal arch support + medial forefoot posting
✗ Wrong options: Lapidus + LCL + spring repair (1st TMT hypermobility, after failed orthosis) · short boot + lateral heel wedge (stage I) · triple · FDL + MDCO (after failed nonop)

Stage II, untreated, no abductionphysical therapy and orthotics with medial hindfoot posting
✗ Wrong options: FDL + calcaneal osteotomy + Cotton + gastroc (only after failed nonop) · triple (rigid)

Stage II, improved with 6 wk PTcustom orthotic with medial post + arch support → hindfoot inversion

Rigid stage III, avid walker, normal ankle, declines surgeryshort articulated AFO
✗ Wrong options: short leg cast NWB (early tendon "rest") · CAM boot + PTT strengthening + Achilles stretch (immobilises normal ankle) · UCBL + medial heel wedge (stage I–II flexible) · Arizona (limits ankle motion, affects gait)

Flexible deformity – FDL transfer, calcaneal osteotomy, lateral column lengthening, Cotton, gastrocnemius recession

Classic stage IImedial displacement calcaneal osteotomy + posterior tibial augmentation with flexor digitorum longus tendon transfer to navicular
✗ Wrong options: PTT debridement alone · triple · ankle fusion · Lapidus

Why MDCOcorrects hindfoot valgus (static) · shifts Achilles pull medially · offloads / protects the transferred FDL · moves heel WB axis toward tibial axis (TO) · transfer alone → early failure
✗ Wrong options: isolated FDL transfer

FDL (dynamic)synergistic with PT → augments a deficient PT · found at knot of Henry · inserted into navicular near PT insertion

Knot of Henryat ankle FDL anterior to FHL ("Tom, Dick and Harry") · in the midfoot FHL crosses dorsal (deep) to FDL → structure immediately deep to FDL at harvest = flexor hallucis longus
✗ Wrong options: Achilles (not in exposure) · FHB (anterolateral to FHL) · adductor hallucis (too distal) · abductor hallucis (never crosses FDL)

FDL vs FHLFDL is standard (Orthobullets) · FHL harder to mobilise, no better results · FHL + MDCO: arch not reconstituted, good satisfaction (OB) · TO answer = FHL transfer (FDL not offered) — read the options

Stage II (TO)bilateral planovalgus, heel valgus passively correctable non-WB, can't single heel rise → medial displacement calcaneal osteotomy, tibialis posterior tendon debridement and FHL transfer (TO)
✗ Wrong options: posterior tibial tenotomy + lengthening · PTT debridement + medial arch support orthotics · subtalar arthrodesis + MDCO + FHL (no arthritis)

OutcomeFDL + MDCO: 87% arch reconstitution, 84% normal shoes without orthotics (Myerson)

IIA (flexible, no forefoot abduction)medial calcaneus displacement osteotomy + FDL transfer to navicular alone
✗ Wrong options: lateral calcaneal displacement (worsens valgus) · peroneus longus → brevis (cavovarus) · split PTT transfer (spastic equinovarus)

IIB (too many toes)+ lateral column lengthening (Evans): opening wedge of anterior calcaneus or through CC joint · LCL corrects forefoot abduction · aims: adduct TN joint, plantarflex midfoot, derotate calcaneus out of valgus · may need MDCO too
✗ Wrong options: hindfoot valgus (MDCO) · hindfoot varus, forefoot adduction, cavus (not PTTI features)

LCL titrationoverlengthening → correct with 1st TMT fusion or medial cuneiform osteotomy · overcorrection (> 5–10 mm) → lateral column overload

IIB packagemedial calcaneal displacement osteotomy, lateral column lengthening, FDL tendon transfer and tendoachilles lengthening (or gastroc recession) ± Cotton
✗ Wrong options: tenosynovectomy + UCBL (stage I) · Dwyer closing wedge + 1st MT closing wedge + plantar fascia release (cavovarus) · triple (stage III) · lateral calcaneal displacement

Flexible planovalgus, failed AFOlateral column lengthening, medializing calcaneal osteotomy, FDL transfer to the navicular
✗ Wrong options: isolated FDL · 1st ray dorsiflexion osteotomy + PL → PB (cavus) · lateralizing calcaneal osteotomy · triple

Large talar head uncoverage, painful heel rise that corrects valgusmedializing calcaneal osteotomy + lateral column lengthening + flexor digitorum longus transfer to the medial navicular
✗ Wrong options: PTT débridement (stage I only) · FDL alone · MCO + FDL without LCL · triple (supple, no arthritis)

Equinus not correcting with knee flexed, 50% uncoverage, no arthritisstage IIB: transfer of FDL to medial navicular + MCO + lateral column lengthening + tendo-Achilles lengthening (TAL)
✗ Wrong options: stage I debridement · IIA (has abduction) · triple / TTC

Gastroc-only equinusDF −5° knee extended → +10° flexed → open gastrocnemius muscle lengthening (recession / Strayer) · gastroc + soleus both tight → TAL (open Achilles lengthening for significant deformity, percutaneous) · recession = less weakness, better cosmesis, less powerful correction
✗ Wrong options: posterior ankle capsule release (ankle can DF) · PL → PB

No equinusSilfverskiöld +5° / +5° → no lengthening needed

Forefoot varus / supinationcompensatory; unmasked once hindfoot corrected intra-op → must be corrected or residual deformity

Cotton osteotomyplantarflexion (dorsal) opening wedge medial cuneiform osteotomy = plantarflexion osteotomy to correct residual forefoot varus · requires stable medial column (navicular colinear with 1st MT)
✗ Wrong options: medial opening wedge for abduction · for forefoot valgus · for hindfoot valgus

Cotton correctsforefoot supination / varus
✗ Wrong options: forefoot abduction (LCL) · forefoot pronation (cavovarus) · hindfoot equinus (gastroc / Achilles release) · hindfoot valgus (MCO static + FDL dynamic)

After FDL + MCO + TAL, forefoot still supinatedplantarflexion opening wedge medial cuneiform osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: dorsiflexion closing wedge (worsens) · in-situ 1st–3rd TMT fusion (Lisfranc) · lateral column closing-wedge shortening · subtalar fusion (subtalar arthritis)

Cotton vs 1st MT–cuneiform fusionCotton: predictable union, preserves 1st-ray mobility, easily varied correction

Unstable medial column (plantar sag at 1st TMT and / or NC)medial column fusion: isolated 1st TMT, NC, or both

1st TMT instability + abduction, flexible hindfootfirst tarsal-metatarsal arthrodesis, medializing calcaneal osteotomy, flexor digitorum longus tendon transfer and lateral column lengthening
✗ Wrong options: Cotton + MCO + FDL (no 1st TMT instability) · triple + Achilles lengthening (rigid) · TTC + gastroc (stage IV) · 1st TMT + subtalar fusion + PTT debridement ± LCL (IIB with severe subtalar arthritis; subtalar fusion + LCL rarely combined → CC fusion instead; PTT debridement no proven benefit)

Modified Lapidusindication = plantar gapping between medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base (1st TMT instability) · = 1st TMT fusion + distal soft tissue (modified McBride) ± medial cuneiform osteotomy · also 1st TMT arthritis, hypermobility, neuromuscular
✗ Wrong options: flexible hindfoot valgus · Meary 12° · TN uncoverage 50° → LCL · + Silfverskiöld → gastroc recession

✗ Wrong options: failed heel raise · forefoot varus · forefoot abduction · pes planus (all expected in stage II)

Procedure (Chi) Indication Contraindication
Lateral column lengthening TN sag, forefoot abduction, valgus calcaneus Normal calcaneal pitch or mild valgus · can overcorrect → forefoot varus

Combined medial + lateral NC / cuneiform–1st MT sag + valgus calcaneus —

MIS vs open calcaneal osteotomytraditional open technique associated with higher wound complications + longer surgical time compared to MIS technique · MIS: smaller incision, fewer wound complications, ↓ nerve injury, shorter time, same radiographic + patient outcomes · radiation ↓ with MIS (Orthobullets) · no difference (OB) — read the options

Exam ↔ procedureflexible forefoot abduction and hindfoot valgus deformities + gastrocnemius contracture ↔ FDL + MCO + LCL + gastroc lengthening · flexible HF valgus + gastroc contracture ↔ MCO + gastroc lengthening · isolated PTT tenderness ↔ tenosynovectomy after failed immobilisation · rigid forefoot + hindfoot ↔ triple + gastroc · + tibiotalar arthritis ↔ tibiotalar fusion ± triple

✗ Wrong options: rigid → triple · + deltoid compromise → triple + deltoid / TTC · retained heel raise → stage I, maximise nonop then debridement · + forefoot abduction → IIB, needs LCL ± spring reconstruction

Rigid deformity – triple, hindfoot & TTC arthrodesis

Rigid adult flatfoot causes (TO)stage III / IV PTTD, post-traumatic deformity, inflammatory arthropathy (TO)

Surgery indication (TO)persistent pain + functional limit despite adequate nonop, fit + willing (TO)

Stage III gold standardtriple arthrodesis (talocalcaneal, talonavicular + calcaneocuboid fusion) with appropriate structural realignments (TO) (TO)
✗ Wrong options: LCL (Evans) + Cotton · isolated PTT reconstruction with FDL transfer + spring repair · isolated subtalar fusion without addressing the midtarsal complex

Triple technique (TO)one or two incisions (medial + lateral) · realign valgus, abducted, dorsiflexed hindfoot → neutral / slight valgus (5°), adducted, plantigrade · multiple cannulated screws · bone graft (resected surfaces / iliac crest) · NWB 6–8 wk → boot until union 12–16 wk (TO) · fusion 98% at 2 yr (Pell)

Principles (TO)plantigrade, braceable foot > perfect angles · correct all components (valgus + abduction + arch; subtalar alone leaves TN subluxation) · equinus → Strayer or percutaneous TAL concurrently (deforming force into pronation) · forefoot varus → Cotton (dorsal opening wedge medial cuneiform, plantarflexes 1st ray) or lateral border overload (TO)

Preferred stage III surgeryarthrodesis of calcaneocuboid, talonavicular and subtalar joints
✗ Wrong options: FDL + MDCO + TAL (flexible) · pantalar (stage IV) · FDL + LCL through anterior calcaneus · PTT debridement + tenodesis to FDL

Forefoot derotation in tripleafter subtalar realigned, forefoot varus unmasked → derotation of the forefoot through the transverse tarsal joints (TN + CC) → plantigrade, no lateral border foot pain · alternatives: Cotton, 1st TMT fusion, NC fusion
✗ Wrong options: derotation through CC alone (can't fix abduction) · dorsiflexion osteotomy medial cuneiform · isolated TN fusion (subtalar degenerate too) · no further step

Double arthrodesistalonavicular + subtalar via single medial incision when CC not substantially arthritic (OB; medial approach: no wound complications) · TO: double = TN + CC, spares subtalar when subtalar arthrosis minimal + deformity at TN (TO) — read the options

TN + subtalar caserigid hindfoot + TN not passively correctable, pain on resisted inversion, failed bracing → talonavicular and subtalar arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: CROW (neuropathic) · MCO + PTT debridement ± FDL ± LCL (joint-sparing fails in rigid: no arthritic pain relief, loss of correction)

Isolated subtalar fusionstage III with mainly subtalar symptoms / arthritis (OB) · no fixed forefoot deformity (Orthobullets) · rarely sufficient for rigid flatfoot — TN usually degenerate → isolated subtalar coalition or post-traumatic subtalar arthritis (TO) · obese elderly with Chopart arthritis → subtalar alone leaves TN + CC symptomatic → triple (OB) — read the options

Rigid = stage III examples70-year-old, hindfoot not passively correctable → triple arthrodesis (✗ Wrong options: talocalcaneal arthrodesis · FDL + calcaneal slide ± LCL through cuboid) · obese 75-year-old → triple (✗ Wrong options: double calcaneal osteotomy · subtalar alone) · obese 62-year-old, plantar-medial callus = talar head, TN dislocation, no hindfoot motion → triple (✗ Wrong options: exostectomy (destabilises) · LCL · MCO · TN arthrodesis)

Heel rise test for rigidityhindfoot valgus persisting with double-leg heel rise = rigid → triple even with only 25% TN uncoverage
✗ Wrong options: heel inverts to varus on heel rise = flexible IIA / IIB → reconstruction · 14-year-old flexible flatfoot → conservative

Hindfoot arthrodesisstage III (usually triple) · stage II with severe subtalar arthritis
✗ Wrong options: walking cast / boot 3–4 mo (stage I) · FDL + calcaneal osteotomy + TAL ± forefoot osteotomy (stage II) · 1st TMT fusion + calcaneal osteotomy + TAL ± LCL (stage II + 1st TMT hypermobility) · TTC (no tibiotalar arthritis / tilt)

Stage IVpassively correctable ankle valgus (cartilage preserved) → triple arthrodesis + deltoid ligament reconstruction (+ TAL) · rigid ankle valgus + tibiotalar arthritis → tibiotalocalcaneal (TTC) arthrodesis with retrograde hindfoot nail · end-stage ankle arthritis → pantalar (triple + ankle) fusion — eliminates all hindfoot + ankle motion (TO; OB: "stage IV → pantalar")

Stage IV, Meary 30°, ankle osteophytes, rigid subtalar + tibiotalar valgustibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: AFO (functionally limiting deformity) · MCO + FDL ± deltoid repair (rigid) · triple (ignores ankle)

TTC caveatsalvage only; tibiotalar joint provides most DF / PF

Unfit for surgerystage IV + severe symptomatic aortic stenosis → custom-molded ankle-foot orthosis (AFO)
✗ Wrong options: TTC · triple (stage III) · triple + deltoid (stage IV correctable) · in-shoe orthosis with medial forefoot post (stage I–II with forefoot varus)

Midfoot (NC) flatfootflexible hindfoot, full strength, collapse at NC joint on X-ray → navicular-cuneiform arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: lateral calcaneal slide (worsens, cavovarus) · MCO / LCL (stage II PTTI) · TN arthrodesis (part of stage III)

6Complications

Complication Cause / fact
Lateral column overload → 5th MT stress fracture, lateral column stiffness LCL (anterior calcaneal opening wedge) for stage IIb · overcorrection > 5–10 mm
CC arthritis After LCL — 14% radiographic, rarely symptomatic (Mosier-LaClair)
Lateral border foot pain Forefoot varus not corrected after hindfoot realignment / isolated subtalar fusion with fixed forefoot varus
Early transfer failure FDL transfer without hindfoot valgus correction
Lateral plantar nerve Retrograde hindfoot (TTC) nail start point (mid plantar heel, centred on talus + tibia) → numbness lateral plantar midfoot → careful dissection to bone for guidewire + nail
FHL impingement Long lateral → medial calcaneal interlocking screw by sustentaculum → ↓ hallux flexion
Loss of correction Joint-sparing surgery in rigid deformity
Progression untreated Flexible → rigid (peritalar arthritis) → deltoid failure → tibiotalar valgus, arthritis, near-total loss of ankle ROM

Lateral column overload & hindfoot-nail nerve injury

5th MT stress fracture after correction ofstage IIb PTTI (LCL)
✗ Wrong options: ligamentous Lisfranc (planovalgus malreduction, PTOA) · moderate hallux valgus (iatrogenic hallux varus, transfer metatarsalgia) · stage I (tenosynovectomy) · stage IIa (normal TN coverage, no LCL)

✗ Wrong options: lateral plantar nerve (nail start point, not screw) · tibialis anterior · saphenous vein (superficial) · tibial nerve (anterior to FHL, not by sustentaculum)

Sesamoid Injuries of the Hallux

Foot & Ankle · 42 / 48

1Basics

Spectrumfracture (hyperextension + axial load) · dislocation · sprain (turf toe) · sesamoiditis (trauma / infection) · chondromalacia · OCD · FHB tendonitis

Epidemiology

Tibial (medial) sesamoidmore commonly injured: greater weight-bearing + larger than lateral

Stress fracturecommonest sesamoid problem (OB) · medial (tibial) sesamoid · mainly females (OB)

Bipartite sesamoid10–25% · 97% tibial · 25% bilateral

Anatomy – intersesamoid ligament

Held together byintersesamoid ligament + plantar plate
✗ Wrong options: intermetatarsal ligament (bases of 2nd–5th MTs) · spring ligament (supports talar head / arch) · plantar fascia · FHL (inserts distal phalanx)

Plantar plateinserts base of proximal phalanx of hallux

Embedded intendons of FHB (short flexor); FHB attaches to both sesamoids · both lie within 1st MTP capsule, plantar to MT head (TO)

Sesamoid Muscle attached Flexor-tendon complex (TO)
Tibial (medial) Abductor hallucis Medial FHB head + abductor hallucis → medial proximal phalanx
Fibular (lateral) Adductor hallucis Lateral FHB head + adductor hallucis → lateral proximal phalanx

Functionsabsorb weight-bearing pressure · ↓ friction at MT head · protect FHL (glides between sesamoids) · fulcrum for FHB → ↑ MTP flexion power

Analogypatella: ↑ mechanical advantage of FHB

Metatarsal load distribution (TO)

Most weight during walking (TO)2nd MT · standing → 1st MT (TO) · foot anatomy note (Orthobullets): 1st MT 50% in gait — read the options

1st MTP joint (TO)carries ~119% body weight each step

Sesamoid complex (TO)transmits 50% body weight · > 300% during push-off

2Mechanism

Commonestforced dorsiflexion (hyperextension) of 1st MTP → plantar plate avulsion off base of proximal phalanx → proximal migration of sesamoids

Fracturehyperextension + axial loading

Chronic overusedancers, players: grade 3 1st MTP sprain → chronic sesamoiditis (TO)

Complete plantar plate tear (TO)may cause sesamoid fracture · separation of bipartite sesamoid · rarely proximal migration

Bilateral sesamoiditisred flag → Reiter's disease (urethritis, conjunctivitis / iritis, IBD) · psoriatic arthritis · seronegative RA

3Presentation

Symptomsgeneralised big-toe pain · worse in terminal stance / hyperextension

Exampossible plantar-flexed MTP with cavus foot

Sesamoiditis in dancers (TO)

Dancer, walks on lateral margin, painful great-toe MTP plantar flexion (TO)sesamoiditis of first MTP joint (TO)
✗ Wrong options: 1st MTP joint arthritis · stress fracture of 1st MT head · AVN of 1st MT head

Features (TO)transfer of weight-bearing to lateral surface · pain + restricted MTPJ movement · painful push-off of great toe

DDx (TO)sesamoid stress fracture · AVN · osteochondral fracture · hallux rigidus (1st MTP arthritis)

Treatment (TO)orthotics + immobilisation → sesamoidectomy if operative

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
X-ray AP + lateral foot · medial oblique (sesamoid view) · axial sesamoid view · (TO) start with radiographs incl. axial + lateromedial sesamoid views
X-ray finding Proximal migration of sesamoids → suspect intrinsic-minus hallux (plantar plate avulsion)
Early X-ray Often negative in stress fracture (OB)
Bone scan Bipartite vs fracture (↑ uptake = fracture) · 25–30% of asymptomatic show ↑ uptake → compare with uninjured side
Bone scan + CT More reliable for confirming stress fracture (OB)
MRI Confirms diagnosis · indicated if radiographs inconclusive (TO)

5Management

Sesamoid injury
  • First line→NSAIDs, ↓ WB, activity change, orthoses
    (acute fracture: SLC with toe extension — controversial)
  • Keratotic lesion, normal alignment→shave plantar half of sesamoid
  • Plantar-flexed 1st ray→dorsiflexion osteotomy
  • Failed nonop 3–12 mo→partial / complete sesamoidectomy
    • Nonunion, 2 large fragments, no osteonecrosis→ORIF / autologous bone graft

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Partial / complete sesamoidectomy Failed nonop 3–12 months (Orthobullets) · ≥ 3 months (OB)
Autologous bone grafting Nonunion or fracture
ORIF of sesamoid Two large fragments without osteonecrosis (OB)
Dorsiflexion osteotomy Plantar-flexed first ray with sesamoid injury
Sesamoid shaving Keratotic lesion ↑ pressure on sesamoid · contraindicated with plantar-flexed 1st MT
Both sesamoids Never excise both

Stress fracture/osteonecrosis – excision indications & outcomes

Initial treatmentalmost always accommodative orthosis (OB)

Medial sesamoid excision indicatedrecalcitrant medial sesamoid stress fracture with fragmentation
✗ Wrong options: with Lapidus · with 1st MTP arthrodesis (neither needs sesamoidectomy) · acute fracture (nonop first) · Morton's neuroma (neurectomy, bury in intrinsic muscle)

Excision techniqueproximal fragment in some · entire sesamoid in others

3-yr medial sesamoid pain, fragmentation + ↑ density, failed orthoticsmedial sesamoid excision
✗ Wrong options: 1st MTP arthrodesis (doesn't unload sesamoid) · ORIF (only 2 large fragments without osteonecrosis) · shoe / heel-height change (already tried) · steroid injection (no long-term relief)

Triathlete, failed nonop tibial sesamoid fracture — fastest reliable RTStibial sesamoidectomy
✗ Wrong options: ORIF + autogenous calcaneal bone graft (valid but slower RTS) · plantar plate reconstruction (turf toe) · MTP arthroscopy + debridement (mild arthritis) · chevron + Akin (bunion)

Intractable plantar keratosis – sesamoid shaving

IPK under 1st MT head, normal standing alignment, adequate passive DFplaning / excising superficial (plantar) half of medial sesamoid → preserves function, ↓ pressure

✗ IPK trapscomplete medial sesamoid excision (→ hallux valgus) · FHL transfer (no cock-up toe) · dorsiflexion osteotomy (no deformity) · gastrocnemius recession (passive DF adequate → more instability) · Keller bunionectomy

Turf toe (TO)

Definition (TO)hyperextension injury to plantar plate + sesamoid complex of hallux MTP · mechanism hyperextension + axial loading

Plantar plate (TO)fibrocartilaginous: thickened plantar capsule + medial and lateral flexor-tendon complexes · 1st MT head → proximal phalanx · stabilisers allow ~50° DF + 30° PF

Plantar plate insufficiency (TO)primary pathology of MTP instability → main focus of surgery

Clinical (TO)pain, swelling, tenderness at MTP · push-off painfully weak · negative plantar (palmar) grip · positive vertical Lachman / drawer test

Treatment (TO)mostly nonop: ice, rest, taping, stiff-sole shoe / rocker-bottom sole · plantar plate repair only in a few → "treatment is plantar plate repair" is the false statement (TO)

Surgery indications (TO)failed nonop · retraction or fracture of sesamoids with diastasis · loose fragments in joint · hallux deformity

Approaches – sesamoidectomy

Sesamoid Approach Nerve at risk
Tibial (medial) Medial-plantar, at junction of glabrous skin Proper branch of medial plantar nerve = plantar-medial cutaneous nerve of hallux (directly under incision)
Fibular (lateral) Plantar Proper branch to lateral hallux + 1st common digital branch to 1st web space

Medial sesamoidectomy — most vulnerableplantar-medial cutaneous nerve → painful neuroma, shoe-wear problems
✗ Wrong options: abductor hallucis tendon (dorsal to incision) · intermetatarsal ligament · dorsomedial cutaneous nerve · crista

6Complications

Complications of sesamoidectomy – cock-up toe, hallux malalignment & nerve injury

Excision Complication
Both sesamoids Cock-up toe deformity (commonest)
Tibial (medial) Hallux valgus
Fibular (lateral) Hallux varus
Either Pain, nerve injury (neuroma), infection, deformity

Cock-up toe↓ FHB moment arm / FHB weakening → MTP extension + relative flexor overpull → IP flexion · prevent by meticulous FHB repair; avoid excising both

Hallux valgus after tibial sesamoidectomycommonest reported deformity · from inadequate medial capsular repair / reefing (OB)

HV 1 yr after "removing a painful bone"medial (tibial) sesamoidectomy
✗ Wrong options: accessory navicular excision · dorsal cheilectomy · lateral sesamoidectomy → varus · os vesalianum excision

Synovitis of 2nd MTP

Foot & Ankle · 43 / 48

1Basics

Definitioncommonest monoarticular synovitis of the MTP joints

Risk factorselongated 2nd MT relative to 1st (Morton foot) · hallux valgus

Plantar plate anatomy

Roleweight-bearing pushes proximal phalanx dorsally · plantar plate + intrinsics (interossei, lumbricals) resist → hold phalanx neutral at MTP

Stabilisers of 2nd MTPplantar plate + collateral ligaments

2Mechanism

Cascadesynovitis → capsuloligamentous stretch → instability → deformity

Plantar plate attenuationMTP extension · sagittal-plane deformity · → crossover toe

MTP instability→ dorsal dislocation of MTP · predisposes to hammer toe

Plantar plate deficiency – crossover toe deformity

Plantar plate deficiency — commonest associationcrossover toe deformity
✗ Wrong options: Freiberg's infraction (no plantar plate pathology) · Lisfranc injury (acute trauma) · claw toe (weak intrinsics vs stronger EDL on extensor sling) · curly toe (FDL + FDB contracture, unknown cause)

High-grade 2nd MTP plantar plate rupture — greatest risksecond toe crossover
✗ Wrong options: hallux varus · hallux valgus (may contribute to or follow crossover but not from rupture) · Freiberg's (microtrauma → blood supply loss → 2nd MT head collapse) · 2nd mallet toe (DIP flexion + lateral deviation, FDL contracture)

Crossover toe2nd toe crosses over or under the hallux · requires plantar plate + collateral ligament failure

Order of failureLCL fails first → medial deviation, plantar plate second → dorsal displacement of proximal phalanx (OB) · (Orthobullets, MTP dislocations): plantar plate first (stage 1), LCL second (stage 2) — read the options

3Presentation

Symptomspain · warm joint · fullness of joint · "walking on marbles" (OB)

Tendernessplantar over plantar plate or over dorsal capsule · may be in 2nd web space (inflammation or pressure on interdigital nerve)

Motionpain with ROM, ↓ with traction · ↓ plantar flexion · global MTP swelling

Deformitypassively correctable in predislocation stages · progresses to crossover (varus or valgus) when collateral + plantar plate disrupted

Dorsal drawer testdemonstrates instability · dorsal subluxation possible = plantar plate attenuated

Diagnosis – pain worse barefoot

Synovitis findingmore pain when barefoot (✗ Wrong options: less pain barefoot (neuroma)) · toe ROM painful (✗ Wrong options: painless ROM (neuroma))

✗ Wrong options (these are neuroma signs)pain + click with medial–lateral forefoot compression (Mulder) · pain with 2nd–3rd web-space compression

SiteMorton's neuroma usually 3rd interspace · pain in 2nd interspace → think 2nd MTP synovitis / metatarsalgia

Why it matterssteroid injection helps neuroma but weakens capsuloligamentous structures → instability → dorsal subluxation, crossover toe

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Weight-bearing AP + lateral foot Widening / medial–lateral joint-space imbalance of 2nd MTP
X-ray Dorsal subluxation — looks like joint-space narrowing or proximal phalanx overlapping MT head
X-ray Varus or valgus toe deformity
MRI If diagnosis unclear · quantifies plantar plate / ligament disruption

Causes of metatarsalgia (TO)

Metatarsalgia (TO)pain in forefoot under one or more MT heads · groups: primary, secondary, iatrogenic (after forefoot surgery)

Primary (TO) Secondary (TO)
Plantar soft-tissue lesions Iatrogenic — 1st ray shortening, MT head resection
Abnormal metatarsal parabola Neurogenic — referred pain, tarsal tunnel syndrome
Morton's foot OA · RA
Neuroma Atrophied plantar fat pad · stress fracture
Trauma · brachymetatarsia Capsulitis / bursitis / tendinitis · Freiberg's infraction
Bone tumours Pes cavus / planus · inappropriate shoegear
Rocker (TO) Phase Metatarsalgia from
1st Heel contact → foot flat Congenital deformity, tight heel cord, severe cavus
2nd Tibia over talus; triceps surae activated at end Limited ankle DF, plantarflexed metatarsals
3rd Foot turns over dorsiflexed MTP joints MTP joint deformities

Work-up (TO)exam of plantar foot + weight-bearing radiographs

5Management

2nd MTP synovitis
  • First line→shoe / activity change, NSAIDs, taping 10–12 wk
  • No deformity, failed nonop→synovectomy
  • Fixed deformity
    • Long 2nd MT→Weil distal oblique shortening osteotomy
    • No long 2nd MT, sagittal → Girdlestone-Taylor FDL→EDL / capsular release + EDL lengthening

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
First line Activity / shoe change, NSAIDs, external MTP support (crossover taping, Budin-type splint) for 10–12 weeks
No deformity + failed nonop Synovectomy
Fixed deformity + long 2nd MT Weil (distal oblique shortening MT osteotomy)
Fixed deformity, NO long 2nd MT, sagittal deformity FDL → EDL transfer (Girdlestone-Taylor) or MTP capsular release + extensor lengthening
No Steroid injection — contraindicated (weakens capsule)

Weil osteotomy technique

Weil used for (TO)metatarsalgia (TO)
✗ Wrong options: Perthes · SCFE · genu valgum

Nonop metatarsalgia first (TO)physio, orthotics, shoe modification, injections

Definition (TO)distal oblique osteotomy of MT head · corrects transverse + sagittal MTP pathology · decompresses MTP joint → relaxes soft tissues

Orthobulletspreserves joint · rebalances MT cascade · relaxes plantar plate

Indications (TO)long or plantarflexed metatarsal · transverse-plane MTP deformity · MTP subluxation / dislocation · recalcitrant generalised metatarsalgia

Technique (TO)start at dorsal articular surface of MT head · cut dorsal-distal → proximal-plantar, 30° to shaft, parallel to weight-bearing surface · screw fixation

Long 2nd MT + fixed dorsiflexion deformity, "walking on marbles" after 4 mo orthoticsWeil · avoid commonest complication (floating toe) by osteotomy parallel to plantar surface of foot (✓)

✗ Weil trapsprotect collateral ligaments (prevents AVN — much rarer than floating toe) · inject plantar to intermetatarsal ligament (steroid ↑ instability) · shorten ≥ 4–7 mm (over-shortening → plantar displacement → floating toe; shorten ≤ 3 mm) · strict immobilisation 4 wk (↑ stiffness; use protected WB in surgical shoe + aggressive ROM)

Other floating-toe preventionremove a wafer of bone (shorten without plantar migration) · combine soft-tissue procedures

6Complications

Complication Fact
Floating toe Commonest after Weil (OB) — plantar shift of MT head centre of rotation → intrinsics pass dorsal to axis → act as MTP dorsiflexors
Weil (TO) Dorsiflexed toe · pain on MTP DF · ↓ MTP ROM · PIP contracture (TO)
AVN Collateral ligament injury · uncommon
Stiffness Prolonged immobilisation
Vascular compromise Correcting chronic dislocation → contracted vessels stretched → may need to reverse procedure to save digit

2nd MTP synovitis Morton's neuroma
Interspace 2nd 3rd (usually)
Barefoot Worse Less pain
Toe ROM Painful (↓ with traction) Painless
Compression — Click (medial–lateral), web-space pain
Drawer + if unstable —
Steroid worsens instability Appropriate
Deformity Cause
Crossover toe Plantar plate + collateral ligament failure
Claw toe Weak intrinsics, EDL overpull on extensor sling
Curly toe FDL + FDB contracture
Mallet toe FDL contracture — DIP flexion
Freiberg's 2nd MT head collapse (blood supply)

"Finding most likely in 2nd MTP synovitis?"more pain when barefoot

"Click on medial–lateral forefoot compression?"Morton's neuroma
✗ Wrong options: synovitis

"Plantar plate deficiency most associated with?"crossover toe deformity

"Commonest complication of Weil?"floating toe

✗ Wrong options: 4–7 mm

Tarsal Navicular Fractures

Foot & Ankle · 44 / 48

1Basics

Rare midfoot fracturetraumatic (avulsion, tuberosity, body) or stress (repetitive microstress)

Articulationstalus, calcaneus, cuboid, cuneiforms · key to inversion–eversion motion

Medial columnnavicular supports medial longitudinal arch · only displaced fracture / navicular dislocation → arch instability (OB)

PTTinserts on navicular (tuberosity)

Stress fracture epidemiology

Whoathletes running on hard surfaces · baseball players (predilection; e.g. catcher jumping from crouch) · gymnasts, soccer, marathon runners (OB stems)

High-risk stress fracturerisk of AVN · commonest complications delayed union + nonunion

At presentation~83% incomplete · complete ones usually nondisplaced (OB)

2Mechanism

Type Mechanism
Avulsion Plantarflexion or eversion / inversion · TN or naviculocuneiform ligaments
Tuberosity Eversion + simultaneous PTT contraction · may be acute diastasis of an accessory navicular
Body Axial loading
Stress Chronic overuse · hard surfaces
Mueller-Weiss Spontaneous adult navicular AVN

3Presentation

Symptomsvague midfoot pain + swelling · insidious in stress fracture → high index of suspicion

Exammidfoot (dorsomedial / medial) swelling + tenderness · ankle + subtalar ROM usually full · full DF / PF / inversion strength

Notanterior tibial tendinitis (no evidence → no cortisone injection into tibialis anterior sheath)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / role
X-ray AP, lateral, oblique 45° · often missed / read as normal · 45° oblique best for tuberosity fractures
CT More sensitive than X-ray · shows nondisplaced fracture line through navicular · may be false-negative without frank cortical disruption
MRI T2 high signal (oedema / inflammation) · best test to confirm when X-ray negative + high suspicion or failed restricted WB (OB) · stress reaction = oedema, no fracture line
Mueller-Weiss X-ray Narrow navicular + lateral sclerosis · "double navicular sign" (split navicular) (OB)

Best imagingCT more sensitive than X-ray (Orthobullets, OB) · MRI best to confirm (OB, CT false negatives) — read the options

Sangeorzan classification (navicular body)

Type Fracture Deformity
I Transverse, dorsal fragment < 50% of bone None
II Oblique, usually dorsolateral → plantar-medial Forefoot ADduction
III Central or lateral comminution Forefoot ABduction

5Management

Navicular stress fracture
  • Any type, first presentation→NWB short-leg cast 6–8 wk
  • Stress reaction (oedema, no line)→restricted WB short-leg cast
  • Failed cast / nonunion / recurrence→ORIF + autologous bone graft
    • High-level / pro athlete→ORIF (OB, Orthobullets)
Traumatic navicular fracture
  • Avulsion, most tuberosity, undisplaced type I–II→NWB cast
    • Failed avulsion / symptomatic tuberosity nonunion→fragment excision
  • Displaced / intra-articular type I–II→ORIF (medial approach), lag screws
  • Type III or AVN→ORIF + ex-fix vs primary fusion

Operative criteria

Injury Operate when
Avulsion > 25% of articular surface → ORIF · failed nonop → excision
Tuberosity > 5 mm diastasis or large intra-articular fragment → ORIF · symptomatic nonunion → excision
Body type I–II Displaced or intra-articular → ORIF (medial approach)
Body type III ORIF + ex-fix vs primary fusion · maintain lateral column length
Stress fracture Fracture line across 2 cortices, or 1 cortex + displacement or cystic change (OB) · failed NWB cast · nonunion · high-level athletes
Navicular AVN TN + naviculocuneiform fusion

Stress fractures – non-weight-bearing cast first-line

First line (any type)short-leg cast + NWB 6–8 weeks (± walking boot + crutches) → high success

Acute fracture fixation

✗ Acute trapsNWB cast 6–8 wk (nondisplaced body fracture / stress reaction only) · CRPP (insufficient for displacement) · ex-fix (highly comminuted / substantial medial column shortening) · primary TN fusion (pre-existing TN arthritis or non-reconstructable)

Column lengthType III: maintain lateral column length (Orthobullets) · ex-fix for medial column shortening (OB) — read the options

Navicular arthrosis – talonavicular & naviculocuneiform fusion

✗ Wrong options: TN only (misses NC joint) · any fusion including subtalar — spared in this disease

Pain sourceabnormal motion at TN + NC joints

Mueller-Weiss syndrome (adult navicular osteonecrosis)

Definition (TO)spontaneous adult-onset tarsal navicular osteonecrosis · aka Brailsford disease (TO) · related to Köhler's (Köhler = paediatric) (OB)

Who (TO)40–60 yr · women · frequently bilateral (TO) · 4th–5th decade (OB) · middle-aged (Orthobullets)

Aetiology (TO)uneven load → compression of lateral half of navicular · preconditions: subtalar varus, 1st ray brachymetatarsia, mild clubfoot → lateral shift of force, lateral incompetence of acetabulum pedis

Clinical (TO)chronic mid + hindfoot pain · navicular collapse → secondary OA → pes planovarus · tibia forced into external rotation → knee OA

Exam (TO)dorsomedial midfoot swelling + tenderness · heel varus · prominent navicular tuberosity → pseudo hindfoot valgus · flattened medial arch

Paradoxical pes planovarus (TO)pseudo hindfoot valgus + pes planus · "pseudo hindfoot varus" = the false option (TO)

Treatmentsemirigid insoles first, fusion if failed (OB) · mostly surgical (TO) — read the options · fuse symptomatic joints + restore arches by correcting Meary-Tomeno line · talonavicular-cuneiform arthrodesis with bone grafting = best results (TO)

Foot & Ankle · 45 / 48

1Basics

Definitioncompressive neuropathy of the tibial nerve at the tarsal tunnel → pain + paraesthesia of the plantar foot

Diagnosisclinical: burning plantar pain + Tinel's over tibial nerve · EMG / NCS can help confirm · history = most useful diagnostic aid

Tarsal tunnel – anatomy, causes (flatfoot, space-occupying lesion) & symptoms

Posterior tarsal tunnel Structure
Roof (superficial) Flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament)
Medial wall (deep) Calcaneus + talus
Inferior Abductor hallucis
Contents Tibial nerve · posterior tibial artery · FHL · FDL · tibialis posterior

Tibial nerve coursealong fascia of tibialis posterior in deep posterior compartment → gives off medial calcaneal nerve just proximal to ankle → dives deep to flexor retinaculum → most often bifurcates in the tunnel into medial + lateral plantar nerves

3 distal branchesmedial plantar · lateral plantar · medial calcaneal · bifurcation proximal to tunnel in 5%

Plantar nervespass through two separate tunnels within and deep to abductor hallucis (superficial + deep fascial layers) · can be compressed in their own sheath distal to the tarsal tunnel

Intrinsic causes Extrinsic causes
Ganglion cyst (classic) Shoes
Tendinopathy, tenosynovitis Trauma
Lipoma / tumour Deformity — tarsal coalition, valgus hindfoot
Perineural fibrosis Post-surgical scarring
Osteophytes Systemic inflammatory disease, lower-limb oedema

Identifiable cause80% of cases · commonest = space-occupying lesion in the tunnel proper (OB)

Heel pain triadposterior tibial tendon deficiency (adult-acquired flatfoot) + plantar fasciitis + tarsal tunnel syndrome · loss of static + dynamic stabilisers of medial arch → traction neuropathy of tibial nerve · 86% improvement after surgery (Labib)

Not associated with TTSinsertional Achilles tendinitis · hypermobile first ray · metatarsal stress fracture · gastrocnemius contracture

Baxter's nerve (heel pain) (TO)

Tibial nerve divisions (TO)medial calcaneal nerve (MCN) · medial plantar nerve (MPN) · lateral plantar nerve (LPN) · first branch of LPN · tibial = larger of the two sciatic divisions

Nerve in heel pain syndrome (TO)1st branch of lateral plantar nerve
✗ Wrong options: medial plantar nerve · medial calcaneal nerve · 2nd branch of sural nerve

First branch of LPN (TO)= nerve to abductor digiti minimi · sensory branches to calcaneal periosteum · supplies no skin

Commonest neural cause of plantar heel pain (TO)entrapment of first branch of LPN

Entrapment sites of first branch (TO)sharp edge of deep fascia of abductor hallucis · just distal to medial edge of calcaneus

Second commonest (TO)medial calcaneal nerve

LPN (TO)supplies most foot muscles · skin of lateral ⅓ of plantar foot + 4th and 5th toes · entrapped between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae

MPN (TO)motor abductor hallucis, FHB, FDB, 1st lumbrical · skin medial ⅔ of plantar foot · entrapment less common than the others

Anterior tarsal tunnel (deep peroneal nerve)

Anterior tarsal tunnel Orthobullets OB
Roof (most superficial) Inferior extensor retinaculum Inferior extensor retinaculum
Floor (deep) Fascia over talus + navicular Talonavicular capsule
Medial / lateral — Medial malleolus / lateral malleolus

Commonest DPN entrapment siteunder the inferior extensor retinaculum = anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome
✗ Wrong options: EHB tendon · TN osteophytes · os intermetatarseum · base of 5th MT

Other DPN compressors (runners)dorsal talonavicular osteophytes · os intermetatarseum (between 1st + 2nd MT bases)

Causescontusion of dorsum · tight shoe laces / compressive shoes (commonest) · TN osteophytes · ganglion · pes cavus · scar · synovial cyst · hypertrophic extensor muscles · dorsalis pedis aneurysm · dorsal navicular avulsion fracture

Peroneal neuropathycommonest compressive neuropathy of lower limb · CPN at fibular prominence · SPN at exit from lateral compartment · DPN under extensor retinaculum

3Presentation

Painprolonged standing / walking · vague, misleading medial foot pain · sharp, burning · may radiate proximally up into the calf

Numbnessintermittent paraesthesia + numbness of plantar foot · lateral foot burning = lateral plantar nerve fibres · history of trauma or surgery

ExamTinel's over tibial nerve · sensory exam equivocal · pes planus · intrinsic wasting: abductor digiti quinti or abductor hallucis

Provocative test Manoeuvre
Compression test Plantar flexion + inversion + digital pressure over tunnel → highly sensitive + specific
Dorsiflexion–eversion test Ankle dorsiflexion + heel eversion + toe dorsiflexion → reproduces pain / paraesthesia

✗ Wrong options: sural · saphenous · SPN · DPN (not in the triad)

Diagnostic criteria

EMG / NCS (posterior TTS) Positive finding
Distal motor latency ≥ 7.0 ms
Sensory latency > 2.3 ms
Motor amplitude ↓ to abductor hallucis or abductor digiti minimi
Which first Sensory (SAP) abnormal before / more often than motor

Electrodiagnosticsnot very sensitive or specific, false negatives in symptomatic patients · still helpful to localise compression (nerve root vs tarsal tunnel vs more distal) · EMG confirms anterior TTS

    • Positive EMG + reproducible exam→TARSAL TUNNEL RELEASE
    • Traction neuritis→release, poorer response

Nonoperativeanti-inflammatories · SSRIs · orthosis / footwear to correct hindfoot alignment · period of short-leg cast · usually ineffective

Operative criteria

Release indicated after 3–6 months failed nonop and Outcome
Compressive mass (ganglion cyst) identified Best results — compressing anatomic structure removed
Positive EMG —
Reproducible physical findings Positive Tinel's pre-op → good results
Traction neuritis Responds less well

Success50–90% (Orthobullets) · 44–96% (OB, Ahmad) — read the options · early operation to prevent fibrosis

Deep fascia of abductor hallucis —

Anterior TTSnonop: activity modification, remove compressive shoes → surgical release · endoscopic for osteophytes / isolated ganglion · open for synovitis / unknown cause

1Basics

Definitionanterior ankle pain, most often osteophyte impingement in anterior tibiotalar joint · "footballer's ankle" (high incidence in soccer players)

2Mechanism

Causesrepetitive overuse · trauma · degenerative sequelae · excess anterolateral soft tissue · posterior soft-tissue / osseous abnormalities

Subtype (OB) Cause
Anteromedial Intra-articular exostoses of anterior tibia + talar neck pinch interposed synovium / capsule → chronic inflammation
Anterolateral AITFL catching on talus · or after ATFL sprain → fibrotic tissue in anterolateral gutter

✗ Wrong options: os trigonum = accessory ossification near posterolateral talar process → posterior impingement

Symptomsanterior ankle pain · worse crouching / squatting

Exampain with forced dorsiflexion · limited dorsiflexion (e.g. passive DF to 10° reproduces pain) · anterior joint-line point tenderness · soft-tissue swelling, effusion · subtalar joint pain-free

Anterolateral soft-tissue impingementold ankle sprain · pain anterolaterally at end-arc passive dorsiflexion · normal talar drawer · no tenderness at fibula, ATFL, CFL · no posterior pain with passive PF

Oblique view Reveals anteromedial talar spurs · better than standard series (Tol & van Dijk)
